q: Patient had in Coronary care unit with Myocardial infarction and associated with cardiac arrhythmia , patient now had numbness and paresthesia on right leg femoral pulse intact out below that was eitner diminished or absent, ler leg normal pulse. what to do next?
k: Acute limb ischaemia: heparin first, then imaging, then revascularisation; the cause picks the procedure. Embolus (AF, MI, valve disease, normal other leg): embolectomy Thrombosis (PAD, claudication, diabetic smoker): ca
r: A patient in the CCU with an MI and arrhythmia has an obvious cardiac source for an embolus. Sudden numbness and paresthesia with an intact femoral pulse but absent pulses below it and a normal other leg is acute embolic limb ischaemia lodged at the femoral bifurcation. Sensory loss means the limb i
kw: numbness and paresthesia on right leg
wo: A. Warfarin is long term anticoagulation after the event (e.g. for AF); the acute step is IV unfractionated heparin, and neither restores flow to a threatened limb. | C. Imaging (CT angiography or Doppler) helps when the cause is unclear or thrombosis on chronic PAD is suspected; with a clear cardiac embolic source and a threatened limb, it should not delay embolectomy. | D. Catheter directed thrombolysis is preferred for in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease (diabetic smoker with prior claudication); for a fresh embolus from a post MI cardiac thrombus, surgical removal is faster and more reliable.

q: Patient with right iliac fossa pain for 7 days . On examination: palpable mass in the iliac fossa , WBC high, ultrasound shows appendiceal mass with no collection . What to do?
k: Late appendicitis (more than about 5 days) with a mass: image first. Mass without collection (phlegmon): IV antibiotics, conservative Mass with collection (abscess): percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics Generalised per
r: RIF pain for 7 days with a palpable mass and ultrasound showing an appendiceal mass with no collection is an appendiceal phlegmon. A phlegmon has no fluid to drain and early surgery is hazardous (inflamed, adherent bowel), so it is managed conservatively with IV antibiotics , fluids and observation,
kw: palpable mass in the iliac fossa
wo: A. Non interventional management describes the same conservative approach, and an older version was keyed to it; when both appear, antibiotics is the more specific and active choice, which is why the compiler favoured E. | B. Laparoscopic appendectomy is right for acute appendicitis presenting early (within about 72 hours) without a mass; with a phlegmon it risks bowel injury and conversion. | C. Open appendectomy has the same problem as laparoscopy in a phlegmon; it is reserved for early appendicitis when laparoscopy is unavailable or for failure of conservative management. | D. Exploratory laparotomy is for generalised peritonitis or perforation with sepsis, not a localised mass in a stable patient.

q: Female Lactating with 6 days history of tender swelling 2x3 On US deep cystic lesion with thick fluid 3x4 among the differential abscess galactocele she is given floxacillin what should be added ?
k: Lactational breast infection: Mastitis (no fluctuation): flucloxacillin, continue breastfeeding or expressing No improvement on antibiotics: ultrasound for abscess Abscess, small, normal skin: needle aspiration (US guide
r: A lactating woman with a 6 day tender breast swelling and an ultrasound showing a deep cystic lesion with thick fluid, 3x4 cm has a breast abscess (or infected galactocele). Antibiotics alone do not clear a collection, so it must be drained; for an abscess under about 5 cm without thinned or necroti
kw: deep cystic lesion with thick fluid
wo: A. Antibiotics alone are enough for mastitis without a collection; once ultrasound shows fluid, drainage is needed. | C. Incision and drainage is for a large abscess (about 5 cm or more), multiloculated abscess, thinned, ischemic or necrotic overlying skin, or failure of repeated aspiration. | D. Unrecalled filler option; not a management choice.

q: A patient is hypotensive post MVA ( 70/40 mmHg). There is diffuse abdominal tenderness and rigidity . Next step?
k: Abdominal trauma pathway: Always ABC first: IV access, fluids and blood for shock Stable: CT abdomen Unstable blunt: FAST; positive leads to laparotomy Unstable penetrating: laparotomy Peritonitis, evisceration, gunshot:
r: After an MVA the patient is hypotensive at 70/40 with diffuse tenderness and rigidity (peritonitis). The lead in is next step : in the primary survey, circulation comes first, so large bore access and IV fluid resuscitation (with blood) start immediately. Laparotomy is the definitive step and follow
wo: A. Exploratory laparotomy is the definitive treatment for unstable blunt trauma with peritonitis and would be the answer to 'most appropriate' or 'definitive' management, but resuscitation begins first. | C. CT is only for hemodynamically stable patients; an unstable patient must never be sent to the scanner. | D. FAST is used in unstable blunt trauma to find intraperitoneal blood when the source is unclear; with frank peritonitis the indication for surgery is already clinical, and resuscitation still comes first.

q: Complicated appendicitis with generalized guarding and rigidity ; vital signs normal including BP ( not hypotensive ). most appropriate next step
k: Generalized peritonitis: Initial: IV fluids, analgesia, NPO, IV broad spectrum antibiotics Definitive: source control by surgery (laparotomy or laparoscopy) Localized abscess without peritonitis: percutaneous drainage Hi

q: A women with three perianal fistula with foul smelling discharge for 6 month, nothing found on proctoscopy What is most appropriate?
k: Anal fistula: Simple, low, near the anal verge: fistulotomy Complex, multiple, recurrent or high: pelvic MRI to map tracts Alternatives: endoanal ultrasound, examination under anaesthesia High or complex: seton, avoid sp
r: Three perianal fistulas with foul discharge for 6 months and nothing found on proctoscopy means a complex fistula whose tracts and internal openings are not visible. Pelvic MRI is the gold standard to map complex fistula tracts, their relation to the sphincters and any hidden abscess before surgery.
wo: B. Colonoscopy looks for Crohn's disease or colorectal pathology and is right when there are bowel symptoms (diarrhea, bleeding, weight loss); it does not map the fistula tracts, which is the immediate need.

q: A 10-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department after sustaining multiple punches to the face, resulting in severe facial trauma and bleeding. Multiple attempts at intubation have failed . What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Trauma airway ladder: Indications to intubate: GCS ≤8, SpO2 below about 88%, risk of aspiration (profuse oral bleeding) First choice: orotracheal intubation with in line neck stabilisation Failed intubation or severe max
r: A 10 year old with severe facial trauma and bleeding in whom multiple intubation attempts have failed is a 'cannot intubate' emergency, which needs an immediate front of neck surgical airway. Cricothyrotomy is the fastest emergency route; in children under about 12 needle cricothyrotomy is preferred
kw: Multiple attempts at intubation have failed
wo: A. Tracheostomy is slower and technically harder; it is the choice for a planned or prolonged airway, laryngeal fracture, or after an emergency cricothyrotomy is converted, not the immediate rescue. | C. Endotracheal intubation has already failed several times; repeating it wastes time and worsens hypoxia and airway trauma. | D. Orotracheal intubation is the same failed approach; with severe facial injury and bleeding, the oral route is also obscured.

q: Male adult complain of inguinoscrotal swelling What is type of hernia ?
k: Groin hernias by site. Indirect: deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, descends to scrotum, common in young males and children Direct: Hesselbach triangle, medial to inferior epigastric vessels, older men, r
r: An inguinoscrotal swelling in an adult male is an indirect inguinal hernia. It passes through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follows the spermatic cord down the canal, so it is the hernia that descends into the scrotum. Extension into the scrotum is the decisiv
wo: A. Femoral hernia: a swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, typically in elderly multiparous women, with the highest strangulation risk; it does not extend into the scrotum. | B. Option not recalled (lacunar hernia in a similar version): a rare variant through the lacunar ligament area, not a cause of inguinoscrotal swelling. | D. Direct inguinal hernia: bulges through Hesselbach triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels in older men; it is usually a broad bulge that rarely reaches the scrotum.

q: Women have bed sore after Deprivation She appears after two days confused other CNS symptom but forgot (maybe agitated) Low bp :maybe 86/56? But definitely map lower than 65 and hypotensive Temp: 38.9 Tachycardia: maybe 109?
k: Shock types. Septic (distributive): fever or hypothermia, infective source, warm peripheries early, low SVR Hypovolemic/hemorrhagic: fluid or blood loss, cold peripheries, high SVR Cardiogenic: low cardiac output, raised
r: A woman with an infected bed sore who had debridement and 2 days later develops confusion , fever 38.9 , tachycardia and MAP below 65 has septic shock from the wound source. Debridement of an infected ulcer can release bacteria into the bloodstream, and confusion reflects poor cerebral perfusion. Fe
wo: A. Pulmonary embolism: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia and tachycardia in an immobile or postoperative patient; fever this high with confusion and a known infected wound fits sepsis better. | C. Hypovolemic shock: follows fluid loss (vomiting, diarrhea, burns, poor intake) with cold peripheries and no fever. | D. Hemorrhagic shock: follows blood loss (trauma, surgery, GI bleeding) with falling hemoglobin; debridement of a bed sore is not a source of major bleeding and fever is not expected.

q: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a house fire. He has facial burns, singed nasal hairs , soot around his mouth, and a hoarse voice . He complains of difficulty breathing. His respiratory rate is 30/min, SpOz is 94% on room air, and carbonaceous sputum is noted.
k: Signs of airway burn = intubate early, before edema peaks. Facial burn, singed facial/nasal hair Soot in mouth/nose, carbonaceous sputum (highest diagnostic value) Hoarseness, stridor, respiratory distress Altered mental
r: House fire with facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot around the mouth, hoarse voice, carbonaceous sputum and respiratory distress (RR 30) is inhalation injury with impending upper airway obstruction. Airway edema progresses over hours and makes later intubation very difficult, so the airway is sec
wo: A. CPAP or NIV does not protect an airway that is swelling shut and the mask sits on burned facial skin; it suits cooperative patients with a patent airway, such as acute pulmonary edema or COPD exacerbation.

q: A patient has an aortic injury following trauma. Which associated trauma has the highest risk?
k: Blunt thoracic aortic injury = deceleration injury, look for multisystem trauma. Most frequent associated injury: head injury Others: pulmonary/cardiac contusion, rib and sternal fractures, abdominal bleeding, pelvic/lon
r: Blunt thoracic aortic injury comes from high energy deceleration, and the same mechanism injures many other regions. Among the associated injuries (head, lung and cardiac contusion, intra-abdominal bleeding, fractures, diaphragm rupture), severe head injury is the most frequent one reported, so the
wo: B. Pneumothorax and hemothorax do occur with chest trauma, but they are less often reported than head injury in blunt aortic injury series. | C. Concussion is a mild, functional brain injury; the association described is with significant (severe) head injury, so 'head trauma' is the broader and better answer. | D. Intra-abdominal injury is a well known associated injury, but it is reported less often than head injury.

q: he complain of vague lower abdomen and back heaviness , abdomen soft but there is plsatile mass . A patient presents with a pulsatile abdominal mass and complains of back pain. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: AAA imaging depends on symptoms and stability. Asymptomatic or screening: abdominal ultrasound Symptomatic and stable: CT angiography Unstable with known or highly suspected AAA: straight to theatre; bedside ultrasound o
r: A pulsatile abdominal mass with back and lower abdominal heaviness in a patient with a soft abdomen and no shock is a symptomatic, hemodynamically stable abdominal aortic aneurysm. Back symptoms raise concern for expansion or contained leak, and in a stable patient the next step is contrast CT (CT a
wo: B. Ultrasound is the screening and initial test for asymptomatic AAA and the bedside test in an unstable patient who cannot go to CT; it cannot reliably show retroperitoneal leak or plan repair.

q: An elderly woman presents to the ER after falling from a height . Her blood pressure is 88/50 mmHg, and she is found to have a pelvic hematoma . What is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Bleeding trauma patient in shock: replace blood with blood. Early pRBC (massive transfusion protocol with plasma and platelets if ongoing bleeding) Limit crystalloid; permissive hypotension in bleeding without head injur
r: An elderly woman after a fall from height with BP 88/50 and a pelvic hematoma is in hemorrhagic shock from pelvic bleeding. What she is losing is blood, so current trauma resuscitation (damage control resuscitation) replaces it with blood products early and avoids large volumes of crystalloid, which
wo: B. Normal saline is a bridge only when blood is not yet available or the patient is profoundly hypotensive; large crystalloid volumes cause dilutional coagulopathy in a bleeding patient. | C. Analgesia is part of care but does not treat shock; circulation comes first.

q: A 55-year-old female in ICU known case of diverticulitis underwent Hartman procedure , 2nd-day post-surgery patient developed a decrease in urine output to 20 ml/hr , and central venous pressure was 10 with lower limb edema. Other examinations were unremarkable, all vitals were stable , and normal blood pressure. What is the appropriate management?
k: Postoperative oliguria: first ask, is the patient filled? Low CVP: fluid challenge Adequate CVP after laparotomy: think abdominal compartment syndrome Check catheter patency first ACS confirmation: bladder (intra-abdomin
r: On day 2 after an emergency Hartmann procedure, oliguria ( 20 ml/h ) with an adequate CVP of 10 means the low urine output is not from hypovolemia, so a surgical cause must be suspected. In a postoperative ICU patient after a laparotomy for peritonitis, oliguria with edema and stable vitals fits abd
kw: decrease in urine output to 20 ml/hr
wo: B. Renal duplex looks for renal artery or vein thrombosis, which is rare here and would not explain the picture; it delays treatment. | C. Abdominal ultrasound is limited after laparotomy (dressings, gas, stoma) and cannot measure abdominal pressure; useful for fluid collections. | D. CT with contrast is used for suspected collection or leak in a stable patient with fever; contrast is also harmful in an oliguric patient and imaging delays decompression of ACS.

q: 55 year old obese woman in ICU for emergency hartmann procedure for perforated diverticulitis and fecal peritonitis . On 2nd post op day Urine output is 50 ml , CVP is 10 ml. BP: 130/78, HR: 98, RR: 22, Temp: 37.3, O2: 95%. What's the most appropriate next step in management?
k: ACS risk factors: emergency laparotomy, peritonitis, obesity, massive resuscitation, ileus. Early sign: oliguria despite adequate filling Others: tense abdomen, rising airway pressure, falling cardiac output Confirm: bla
r: An obese patient in ICU on day 2 after an emergency Hartmann for fecal peritonitis has low urine output despite an adequate CVP of 10 , so the oliguria is not from hypovolemia. Obesity, emergency laparotomy, peritonitis and large fluid resuscitation are all risk factors for abdominal compartment syn
wo: B. CT abdomen is right for suspected collection or anastomotic problem in a stable febrile patient; it delays decompression and contrast harms the kidneys. | C. Duplex ultrasound (renal or venous) does not address the likely cause and delays management. | D. Abdominal ultrasound is limited after laparotomy and cannot diagnose raised abdominal pressure.

q: Birad 4c mammography 1.5 cm calcified ; next step
k: BI-RADS action. 0: incomplete, more imaging 1-2: routine screening 3: probably benign, short interval follow up (about 6 months) 4 (A, B, C) and 5: core needle biopsy 6: known cancer, treat
r: BI-RADS 4C means a high suspicion of malignancy, and all BI-RADS 4 and 5 lesions need tissue diagnosis. Image guided core needle biopsy (stereotactic for calcifications) gives a histological diagnosis, separates in situ from invasive cancer and allows receptor testing, while avoiding an unnecessary
wo: B. Excisional biopsy is reserved for cases where core biopsy is not possible, is non diagnostic, or is discordant with imaging; as a first step it may leave positive margins and complicate later surgery.

q: Patient with MVA came with ( hemothorax clinical presentation , "diagnosis is not writtern") which is first :
k: Hemothorax in trauma. Treatment: large bore chest tube Thoracotomy: more than 1500 ml immediately, or more than 200 ml/h for 2 to 4 h, or unstable Tension pneumothorax: needle or finger decompression first, then chest tu
r: Per the compiler, a trauma patient with a hemothorax is treated with a chest tube (tube thoracostomy, usually large bore in the 5th intercostal space anterior to the mid axillary line), which drains the blood, re-expands the lung and measures ongoing bleeding. Intubation is needed only if there is a
wo: A. Intubation with cervical spine control is first when there is an airway problem (GCS 8 or less, obstructed airway, saturation not maintained); a patient talking with a patent airway does not need intubation.

q: A 25 years old male post motor cycle accident presented to the ER complaining of generalized body pain. On examination he looked anxoius with normal breathing and no signs of external bleeding. On pelvic exam he had unstable pelvic fracture and no blood at external meatus , drainage done by supra-pubic aspiration Vitals BP 110/80 Temp 36.6 RR/16 On x-ray revealed unstable pelvic rami fracture Which of the following is the initial imaging ?
k: Pelvic fracture imaging fork: Stable: CT with contrast (abdomen and pelvis) Unstable: pelvic binder, FAST, resuscitation, then angioembolization or preperitoneal packing Blood at meatus or high-riding prostate: retrograd
r: The patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 110/80, normal breathing) with an unstable pelvic rami fracture and no blood at the external meatus . In a stable trauma patient, contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the initial imaging to define the fracture, detect pelvic hematoma or active contrast e
wo: B. Retrograde urethrogram is indicated when urethral injury is suspected: blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal butterfly hematoma or inability to void. Here there is no meatal blood. | C. Pelvic angiography with embolization is for an unstable patient with pelvic arterial bleeding, or when CT shows active arterial extravasation; this patient is stable. | D. MRI is too slow and impractical in acute trauma and has no role as the initial study for a pelvic fracture.

q: A patient has a hard breast mass . Which type of biopsy is most appropriate?
k: Breast mass triple assessment: clinical exam, imaging, core biopsy. Under 30: ultrasound first; 30 or older: mammogram plus ultrasound BI-RADS 4 or 5: core needle biopsy Simple cyst: aspiration (FNA) Discordant or nondia
r: A hard breast mass is suspicious for carcinoma, and the biopsy of choice in triple assessment is a core needle (Tru-cut) biopsy . It provides tissue architecture to distinguish invasive from in situ disease and allows tumor grading and receptor testing (ER, PR, HER2) before planning surgery.
wo: B. Excisional biopsy removes the whole lump; it is used when core biopsy is nondiagnostic or discordant, or for small lesions, but it is not the first step for a suspicious mass because it can compromise later surgical planning. | C. Incisional biopsy takes part of a large mass surgically; it is reserved for cases where needle biopsy fails, such as some large fungating tumors. | D. FNA gives only cytology and cannot distinguish invasive from in situ cancer or provide receptor status; it is mainly for aspirating cysts and sampling axillary nodes.

q: A child has a midline neck swelling that moves upward with swallowing and protrusion of the tongue . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neck masses by position: Midline, moves with tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst Midline, moves with swallowing only: thyroid nodule or goiter Lateral, anterior to sternocleidomastoid: branchial cyst Posterior triangle,
r: A midline neck swelling in a child that moves up with swallowing and with tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst. The cyst is a remnant of the duct along which the thyroid descended from the foramen caecum, so it stays attached to the hyoid and tongue base. Treatment is the Sistrunk operation
wo: A. A branchial cyst lies laterally, at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, and does not move with tongue protrusion. | C. Zenker diverticulum occurs in elderly adults with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis, usually as a left-sided swelling, not a midline cyst in a child.

q: A patient is involved in a motor vehicle accident. While trying to avoid other vehicles, he swerves off the road and crashes into an object. Imaging reveals a widened mediastinum with pleural effusion . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Blunt aortic injury: Mechanism: rapid deceleration, injury at the isthmus (ligamentum arteriosum) CXR: widened mediastinum, obscured aortic knob, left hemothorax, tracheal or NG tube shift to the right, depressed left ma
r: A high speed deceleration injury (car swerving and crashing) shears the aorta at the isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery. On chest X-ray this gives a widened mediastinum , and a left pleural effusion represents hemothorax from the bleeding. CT angiography confirms the diagnosis.
wo: B. Pulmonary embolism is a delayed complication of trauma and immobility, presenting with sudden dyspnea and hypoxia; it does not widen the mediastinum. | C. Cardiac tamponade presents with Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) and an enlarged globular cardiac shadow, not a widened mediastinum with effusion. | D. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation away, raised JVP and hypotension; imaging would show a collapsed lung with mediastinal shift, not widening.

q: Hard breast mass type of biopsy?
k: Breast mass workup: Triple assessment: exam, imaging, core biopsy Imaging first: ultrasound under 30, mammogram plus ultrasound 30 and older Suspicious solid mass (BI-RADS 4 or 5): core needle biopsy Simple cyst: aspirat
r: A hard breast mass is suspicious for carcinoma, and the biopsy of choice is a core needle biopsy . It gives tissue architecture to confirm invasive cancer and allows grading and receptor testing (ER, PR, HER2) to plan treatment, as part of triple assessment with clinical examination and imaging.
wo: B. Excisional biopsy is used when core biopsy is nondiagnostic or discordant with imaging; doing it first may compromise definitive surgery. | C. Incisional biopsy is reserved for large masses where needle biopsy has failed. | D. FNA gives cytology only and cannot separate invasive from in situ cancer or reliably give receptor status; it is used for cysts and axillary nodes.

q: Large open fracture , most appropriate management
o: Debridement external fixation , delay wound closure
k: Open fracture pathway: IV antibiotics + tetanus, then debridement and irrigation, then stabilisation, then delayed closure or flap cover. Gustilo I: wound under 1 cm, clean Gustilo II: 1 to 10 cm, moderate soft tissue da
r: A large open fracture (high Gustilo grade) is contaminated and has a soft tissue defect. After antibiotics and tetanus cover, the wound needs surgical debridement , the bone is stabilised (external fixation is the classic temporary choice when the wound is large and dirty) and the wound is left open
wo: A. Intramedullary fixation and wound closure: there is no debridement and primary closure of a large contaminated wound traps bacteria and risks deep infection and osteomyelitis; nailing is acceptable only after thorough debridement.

q: Adult after MCV had IIIa fracture femur with open contaminated wound X ray show combunated mid femur fracture with mid displacement What is this most appropriate
o: Debridement , Extramedullary fixation with delayed wound closure
k: Open fracture: antibiotics + tetanus, then debridement and irrigation, then fixation, then delayed closure. IIIa: adequate soft tissue for coverage despite extensive injury IIIb: periosteal stripping, needs flap cover II
r: This is a Gustilo IIIa open femoral fracture with a contaminated wound and a comminuted displaced shaft fracture after a motor vehicle crash. The essential step is debridement , followed by stabilisation and delayed wound closure , and option C is the only choice that includes debridement and avoids
wo: A. Primary internal fixation: inserting hardware into a contaminated wound without debridement invites deep infection; internal fixation is done only after the wound is debrided. | B. Intramedullary fixation with primary closure: nailing after debridement is common for femoral shafts, but here debridement is missing and primary closure of a contaminated IIIa wound is unsafe.

q: 38 y came to clinic with ulcer in medial aspect of leg Which most risk factors
k: Leg ulcer by site: medial gaiter area = venous; foot and toes = arterial or neuropathic. Venous: shallow, irregular, sloughy, edema, hemosiderin, lipodermatosclerosis, pulses present Arterial: punched out, painful, toes
r: An ulcer over the medial aspect of the leg (gaiter area, above the medial malleolus) is the classic site of a venous ulcer . Venous hypertension from valvular incompetence or prior DVT is its underlying cause and by far the commonest cause of leg ulcers.
kw: ulcer in medial aspect of leg
wo: B. Buerger disease: a young male heavy smoker with painful ulcers or gangrene of the fingertips and toes, not the medial leg. | C. Diabetes: causes neuropathic ulcers on pressure points of the foot (metatarsal heads, heel), painless with a punched-out base. | D. Atherosclerosis: arterial ulcers are painful, punched out, on the toes, foot or over the lateral malleolus, with absent pulses.

q: (Around 37 years old) patient with depression come to ER complaining of dysuria , unable to urinate for 12 hours , destended bladder on the prostate is small, soft and tender , what is the diagnosis ?
k: Prostate on DRE tells the diagnosis. Tender, boggy, warm: acute prostatitis (avoid vigorous massage) Smooth, enlarged, non-tender, older man: BPH Hard, nodular, irregular: prostate cancer Fluctuant with persistent fever
r: A man in his late 30s with dysuria and acute urinary retention (distended bladder) whose prostate is tender on rectal exam has acute prostatitis . Inflammatory swelling obstructs outflow, and tenderness is the decisive clue; the retention is relieved (suprapubic catheter is often preferred), and the
kw: prostate is small, soft and tender
wo: A. BPH: a disease of older men (usually over 50) with gradual LUTS and a smooth, enlarged, NON-tender prostate. | B. UTI (cystitis): causes dysuria and frequency but not a tender prostate or retention in a young man; prostatitis is the specific diagnosis here.

q: A woman is brought to the Emergency Department after a traumatic injury. Examination and imaging reveal a posterior elbow dislocation with a (complex comminuted ) radial head fracture . What should be the next step in management?
k: Dislocation with fracture: reduce first, then deal with the fracture. Check and document neurovascular status before and after reduction Posterior dislocation + radial head fracture + coronoid fracture = terrible triad (
r: A posterior elbow dislocation must be reduced as an emergency to protect the brachial artery and nerves, whatever the associated fracture. The next step is closed reduction under analgesia and sedation , followed by a neurovascular check and imaging; a comminuted radial head fracture is then address
wo: A. Apply cast only: immobilising a dislocated joint leaves it unreduced, risking neurovascular compromise and stiffness. | C. Internal fixation with nail (no reduction): fixing a fracture without reducing the dislocation is never correct; reduction comes first, then ORIF. | D. Observation: a dislocated elbow is an urgent injury; observation is not an option.

q: A 32-year-old patient is positive for the BRCA1 gene . Her mother had breast cancer at the age of 45. What is the method of surveillance ?
o: Start mammogram at the age of 35
k: BRCA carrier surveillance (high risk): Breast awareness from 18; clinical breast exam every 6 to 12 months from 25 Annual breast MRI from 25 Annual mammogram added from 30 (with MRI) Discuss risk-reducing mastectomy and
r: A BRCA1 carrier aged 32 is above the age (30) at which annual mammography is added to surveillance, so screening should begin now rather than at a later age. This recall's key is starting mammography immediately; in practice it is combined with annual breast MRI, which is the most sensitive test in
wo: A. Ultrasound every six months: an adjunct for symptoms or dense breasts, not the recommended surveillance for BRCA carriers. | C. Start mammogram at 35: delays screening in a very high risk woman who is already past the starting age. | D. Start MRI immediately: annual MRI is a core part of BRCA surveillance (from age 25); it is the main competitor to the key here.

q: A patient was admitted with right lower quadrant pain and diagnosed with ruptured appendicitis with a localized abscess . WBC is 13.6. What is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Complicated appendicitis: match the treatment to the finding. Uncomplicated: appendectomy Phlegmon or small abscess: antibiotics, observe Localized drainable abscess, stable: percutaneous drainage + antibiotics, then con
r: The decisive clues are ruptured appendicitis with a localized abscess and a stable patient (WBC 13.6, no generalized peritonitis). A walled-off appendiceal abscess is treated first by percutaneous (image-guided) drainage plus IV antibiotics, which controls sepsis without operating in an inflamed, ad
wo: A. Interval appendectomy is the step done weeks AFTER the abscess has been drained and the inflammation settled; it is not the initial management. | B. Emergency appendectomy is right for uncomplicated appendicitis or for perforation with generalized peritonitis/instability; operating on a localized abscess carries higher risk of bowel injury and extended resection. | C. Antibiotics alone suit a phlegmon or a small collection (under about 3 to 4 cm); a defined abscess needs source control by drainage.

q: A female post-laparoscopic cholecystectomy 2 weeks ago presents to the emergency room complaining of vague abdominal pain. Labs show elevated total and direct bilirubin. CT abdomen reveals a 10 x 15 cm subhepatic collection found to be a biloma . What is the most appropriate management?
k: Bile leak after cholecystectomy: drain the collection, then control the leak. Small asymptomatic collection: observe Large or symptomatic biloma/abscess: image-guided percutaneous drainage Persistent leak: ERCP, sphincte
r: A large ( 10 x 15 cm ) subhepatic collection 2 weeks after laparoscopic cholecystectomy , already identified as a biloma , must be evacuated. Image-guided percutaneous drainage is the first-line management because it is minimally invasive, both diagnostic and therapeutic, and avoids reoperation. If
wo: A. MRCP is a diagnostic study to map the biliary tree or locate the leak; it does not treat a large established collection. | C. Open (operative) drainage is reserved for failed percutaneous drainage, bile peritonitis, or an inaccessible or complex collection. | D. Conservative care fits only small, asymptomatic collections; a 10 x 15 cm symptomatic biloma with elevated bilirubin needs drainage.

q: A 21-year-old man came with generalized abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. He is a heavy smoker . On examination, the abdomen is scaphoid and rigid . Blood pressure is 110/70, heart rate is 105, temperature is 38.5, and oxygen saturation is 95%. What is the most appropriate initial test?
k: Suspected hollow viscus perforation: erect CXR first. Free air under diaphragm: perforation, go to surgery Negative CXR, high suspicion: CT abdomen Risk factors for perforated ulcer: smoking, NSAIDs, steroids, H. pylori
r: A young heavy smoker with generalized pain, a rigid, scaphoid abdomen, tachycardia and fever has peritonitis most likely from a perforated peptic ulcer. The first test is an upright (erect) chest x-ray , which is quick, cheap and shows free air under the diaphragm, confirming perforation and the nee
wo: B. An erect abdominal x-ray is used for obstruction (air-fluid levels); it is less sensitive than an erect chest film for subdiaphragmatic free air. | C. Abdominal ultrasound is first line for biliary disease, pediatric appendicitis or pregnancy, not for detecting pneumoperitoneum. | D. CT is the most sensitive test and is used when the chest x-ray is negative but suspicion remains; it is not the initial test in suspected perforation.

q: A patient presents with acute pancreatitis . Which of the following is most useful for assessing severity and prognosis ?
k: Acute pancreatitis severity assessment. CRP at 48 hours: best single lab marker of severity Hematocrit above 44% (hemoconcentration), rising BUN: poor prognosis Scores: Ranson, Glasgow (Imrie), APACHE II, BISAP Amylase a
r: Among the options, C-reactive protein is the single laboratory marker validated for severity and prognosis in acute pancreatitis: a markedly raised CRP at about 48 hours predicts severe or necrotizing disease. ALP, ESR and procalcitonin are not established severity markers for pancreatitis.
wo: A. Procalcitonin has been studied to predict infected necrosis but is not the standard marker for assessing overall severity. | C. ESR is a nonspecific, slow-changing inflammatory marker with no validated role in grading pancreatitis. | D. Alkaline phosphatase points to biliary obstruction (gallstone etiology) but does not grade severity.

q: 24 year old complain of RLQ pain nausea and vomiting ( symptoms of appendicitis) examination show right iliac fossa mass CT SCAN. Shows periappendicular collection 10x12 of abscess with fecalith and it extends to right flank
k: Appendiceal mass or abscess. Phlegmon (no collection): antibiotics, conservative Drainable abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics Later: interval appendectomy (especially with appendicolith or recurrent symptoms
r: A tender right iliac fossa mass with CT showing a 10 x 12 cm periappendiceal abscess with a fecalith is complicated (perforated, walled-off) appendicitis. The first intervention is percutaneous (image-guided) drainage with IV antibiotics, which controls sepsis without operating in an inflamed field,
wo: A. Open appendectomy at this stage risks bowel injury and an ileocecal resection in an inflamed, adherent field; surgery is for generalized peritonitis, instability or failed drainage. | B. Laparoscopic appendectomy is the treatment of uncomplicated appendicitis; for a large localized abscess, drainage comes first and appendectomy is deferred. | C. No intervention ignores a large abscess that needs source control; antibiotics alone fit only a phlegmon or a small collection.

q: 44 years male patient came with Painless hematuria only , on P\ E normal What to do next ?
o: Follow up and repeat urinalysis after 2weeks
k: Painless hematuria in adults: rule out urothelial cancer. Confirm on urinalysis, exclude infection Lower tract: cystoscopy (+ cytology) Upper tract: CT urography Risk factors: smoking, age over 35, occupational dyes, cyc
r: Painless hematuria in a 44-year-old man with a normal exam is malignancy until proven otherwise (bladder urothelial carcinoma most commonly). Evaluation of the lower tract is by cystoscopy , the gold standard for bladder tumors, with urine cytology as an adjunct; upper tract imaging (CT urography) i
wo: A. Antibiotics treat a proven UTI (dysuria, frequency, positive culture); empirically treating painless hematuria delays a cancer diagnosis. | B. Non-contrast CT is the test for suspected stones (painful hematuria with colicky flank pain); hematuria workup needs CT urography with contrast plus cystoscopy. | D. Repeating the urinalysis suits isolated microscopic hematuria in a young low-risk patient (or after exercise, menses, infection); painless hematuria in a man over 35 needs full evaluation now.

q: 61 years old complaining of bloody nipple discharge , examination of right breast normal , what is the next step?
k: Pathologic nipple discharge (bloody, spontaneous, unilateral, single duct). Age 40 or older: diagnostic mammogram + ultrasound Under 30 to 40: ultrasound first Lesion seen: image-guided core biopsy Imaging negative: MRI
r: In a 61-year-old woman with bloody nipple discharge and a normal exam, the first imaging is a diagnostic mammogram (usually with targeted retroareolar ultrasound), because in women over 40 mammography best detects an underlying carcinoma or microcalcifications. Age decides the modality: ultrasound f
wo: A. Ultrasound is the initial test under about 30 to 40 years (dense breasts), as in younger women with suspected intraductal papilloma; at 61 it complements, not replaces, mammography. | B. Ductography is a second-line test, considered when mammogram and ultrasound are negative and the discharge persists; it is not the first step. | D. CT has no role in evaluating nipple discharge; it is used for staging established cancer.

q: 45-year-old woman with bloody nipple discharge alone . Did mammogram and this is the finding: Heterogeneously dense breast tissue with microcalcification . What is the next step?
k: Bloody nipple discharge workup. Mammogram + ultrasound first (age 40 or older) Suspicious finding (e.g. microcalcification, mass): image-guided biopsy Imaging negative: MRI (or ductogram) Persistent discharge with negati
r: This recall's key is breast MRI . The compiler explains that suspicious microcalcification on mammogram should really go to biopsy, but biopsy and ultrasound are not offered; ductogram and MRI share the same indication (bloody discharge with a negative mammogram), so among the listed choices MRI is
kw: Heterogeneously dense breast tissue with microcalcification
wo: A. Interval mammography (short-term follow-up) is for probably benign findings (BI-RADS 3); bloody discharge with microcalcification needs active workup. | C. Ductography outlines an intraductal lesion when imaging is negative; it does not evaluate microcalcification and has been largely replaced by MRI. | D. Observation is unsafe with pathologic (bloody) nipple discharge and a mammographic abnormality.

q: 32 year old patient was undergoing elective thyroidectomy . What preop antibiotic should be given?
k: Wound classes and prophylaxis. Clean (thyroid, hernia without mesh): no prophylaxis Clean with implant (mesh, joint, vascular graft): single dose cefazolin Clean-contaminated (biliary, gastric): single dose cefazolin Col
r: Elective thyroidectomy is a clean procedure (no entry into respiratory, GI, genital or urinary tracts) with a very low infection rate, so routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated in a healthy 32-year-old . Prophylaxis is used for clean-contaminated or contaminated surgery, or clean surgery wi
wo: A. A single preoperative dose of cefazolin is the standard prophylaxis for clean-contaminated cases (e.g. cholecystectomy) or clean surgery with prosthetic implants; not needed for thyroidectomy. | B. Cefazolin plus metronidazole adds anaerobic cover for colorectal or appendiceal (contaminated) surgery. | D. Prophylaxis, when indicated, is a single dose (redosed only for long surgery or major blood loss); a routine second dose adds no benefit.

q: A 50-year-old man is 6 days post-uneventful subtotal colectomy and ileocolic anastomosis when he develops sudden-onset shortness of breath and one episode of hemoptysis . Chest X-ray: Left basilar atelectasis. ECG: Sinus tachycardia and a new finding of a right bundle branch block . Which of the following is the most appropriate test?
k: Suspected PE: decide by probability and stability. Low/intermediate probability: D-dimer; negative rules out High probability, stable: CT pulmonary angiography Unstable: bedside echo, then thrombolysis if RV strain CT co
r: Postoperative day 6 after major abdominal surgery with sudden dyspnea, hemoptysis , sinus tachycardia and a new right bundle branch block (right heart strain) makes pulmonary embolism highly likely. With high pretest probability in a stable patient, the test to confirm is CT pulmonary angiography .
kw: new finding of a right bundle branch block
wo: A. D-dimer is useful only to rule out PE in low or intermediate probability; it is almost always raised after surgery and adds nothing when probability is high. | B. Echocardiography shows RV strain and is used at the bedside in unstable patients who cannot go to CT; it does not confirm PE in a stable patient. | D. Lower limb Doppler diagnoses DVT and is used when CT is contraindicated (e.g. pregnancy, contrast allergy, renal failure) or when there are leg symptoms; here there are none.

q: Following a head-on motor vehicle collision, a 21-year-old unrestrained passenger presents to ER with dyspnea and respiratory distress. She is intubated and physical examination reveals subcutaneous emphysema and decreased breath sounds. Chest X-ray reveals cervical emphysema, pneumomediastinum , and a right-sided pneumothorax . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Air in the wrong places after chest trauma. Pneumomediastinum + cervical/subcutaneous emphysema + pneumothorax: tracheobronchial injury Persistent air leak or failed lung re-expansion after chest tube: suspect bronchial
r: In blunt high-energy trauma, the triad of subcutaneous/cervical emphysema , pneumomediastinum and pneumothorax points to a tracheobronchial injury : air escaping from a torn airway tracks into the mediastinum and neck. A pneumothorax alone explains decreased breath sounds, but not the extensive medi
wo: A. Tension pneumothorax causes hypotension, raised JVP and tracheal shift away from the affected side; it does not explain pneumomediastinum and cervical emphysema. | B. Open pneumothorax requires a chest wall defect (sucking chest wound), which is not described. | D. Pulmonary contusion produces hypoxia and patchy alveolar opacities developing over hours, not free air in the mediastinum and neck.

q: Day 5 post sigmoidectomy , no mention of the surgical site , fever only 38.5 Next most important initial step ?
k: Postoperative fever by timing (5 Ws). Day 1 to 2: atelectasis (wind) Day 3: UTI (water), also pneumonia Day 5: wound infection; days 5 to 7 anastomotic leak/abscess Day 7 and beyond: DVT/PE, deep collection (CT abdomen)
r: Fever on postoperative day 5 after sigmoidectomy falls in the window when surgical site infection and anastomotic leak/intra-abdominal collection become likely. The most important initial step is to examine the surgical site (wound and abdomen), because it is the commonest source at this time and is
wo: B. Reviewing drugs (drug fever) is considered after the wound and other infectious sources are excluded, in an otherwise asymptomatic patient.

q: Patient with haemoroid that reduce spontaneously Hg = 8 What is the definitive ttt ?
k: Hemorrhoid ladder: conservative, then office procedure, then surgery; complications or failure jump to surgery. Grade I to II: fiber, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths Grade III (manually reducible): rubber band ligati
r: The lead-in asks for the definitive treatment, and the patient has symptomatic bleeding hemorrhoids with Hb 8 , i.e. anemia from chronic blood loss. Significant anemia is a complication that moves hemorrhoids past the conservative and office-procedure steps of the ladder, and hemorrhoidectomy is the
wo: A. Observation: acceptable only for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic hemorrhoids; a patient bleeding enough to drop the Hb to 8 cannot be observed. | B. Band ligation: the outpatient choice for grade I to III internal hemorrhoids with uncomplicated bleeding, but it has higher recurrence and is not the definitive answer when bleeding has caused significant anemia.

q: Pt. For appendectomy (Uncomplicated) , the question was about when to give Abx. ?
k: Antibiotics in appendicitis depend on the operative finding: Uncomplicated: single preoperative prophylactic dose, stop after surgery Complicated (perforation, abscess, peritonitis): continue a short therapeutic course a
r: For uncomplicated appendicitis, antibiotics are prophylactic: a single dose given before incision covers the operation, and once a non-perforated appendix is removed there is no residual infection to treat. Postoperative courses add no benefit in infection rates and increase resistance, side effects
wo: A. 1 dose preoperative, 3 days postoperative: a short therapeutic course is used for complicated (perforated or gangrenous) appendicitis, not uncomplicated disease. | B. 1 dose preoperative, 5 days postoperative: unnecessary in uncomplicated cases; a postoperative course is reserved for perforation, abscess or peritonitis. | C. 1 dose preoperative, 7 days postoperative: too long even for most complicated cases after adequate source control.

q: A 70-year-old women p7+1 with chronic constipation presented to Emergency Room with abdominal distension and vomiting. Examination revealed abdomen is distended, tympanic, with round tender nonreducible swelling in the right groin bellow and lateral to pubic tubercle (see report). X-ray abdomen: Distended small bowel with multiple fluid levels . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Groin swelling: locate it relative to the pubic tubercle. Above and medial: inguinal hernia (direct or indirect) Below and lateral: femoral hernia Femoral: more common in women, highest strangulation risk, always repair
r: An elderly multiparous woman with chronic constipation has a tender, irreducible groin swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle , plus small bowel distension with multiple fluid levels. That position marks the femoral canal, so this is an obstructed femoral hernia; the narrow rigid femoral r
kw: bellow and lateral to pubic tubercle
wo: B. Direct inguinal hernia: emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle through Hesselbach triangle, typically in older men, and rarely strangulates because its neck is wide. | C. Metastatic lymph node: a firm, non-reducible node does not cause small bowel obstruction with fluid levels; the obstruction picture points to a hernia. | D. Indirect inguinal hernia: passes through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle, often extending into the scrotum or labium.

q: A 72 year old man otherwise healthy came complaining of left inginal hernia reducible with moderate pain What's the most appropriate management
k: Inguinal hernia management: Symptomatic, fit patient: elective tension-free mesh repair (open Lichtenstein) Recurrent after open repair or bilateral: laparoscopic mesh repair Minimal symptoms or unfit: watchful waiting i
r: A healthy 72-year-old with a symptomatic (moderate pain) primary unilateral reducible inguinal hernia should have elective repair. The standard is a tension-free mesh repair (for example Lichtenstein), which has the lowest recurrence; age alone is not a reason to avoid surgery in a fit patient.
wo: A. Bassini ("bandini") repair: a tissue repair that sutures structures under tension; it has higher recurrence and is now reserved for situations where mesh cannot be used, such as a contaminated field. | C. Do nothing: watchful waiting is acceptable only for minimally symptomatic hernias or patients unfit for surgery; this patient has pain and is otherwise healthy. | D. Not recalled: cannot be assessed.

q: A patient underwent appendectomy for acute appendicitis. One week later, histopathological examination revealed an appendiceal carcinoid tumor . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Appendiceal carcinoid after appendectomy: <2 cm, tip, no invasion: appendectomy alone, observe >2 cm, base, high grade, mesoappendix or lymphovascular invasion, positive nodes: right hemicolectomy Appendiceal adenocarcin

q: 65-year-old man is scheduled for colon surgery. He has a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus , both well-controlled with medications. He is physically active and walks to the mosque daily without limitations . What is his ASA physical status classification?
k: ASA physical status: I: healthy II: mild, controlled systemic disease III: severe systemic disease, functional limitation IV: severe disease that is a constant threat to life V: moribund, not expected to survive without
r: He has hypertension and diabetes, but both are well-controlled and he has no functional limitation (walks daily without difficulty). Systemic disease that is mild and controlled, without functional limitation, is ASA II.
wo: A. ASA I: a normal healthy patient with no systemic disease; his hypertension and diabetes exclude it. | C. ASA III: severe systemic disease with functional limitation, such as poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, morbid obesity or COPD limiting activity. | D. ASA IV: severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, such as recent MI or decompensated heart failure.

q: During excision of a back lipoma under local lidocaine, the surgeon suspects an excessive dose . Earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity ? (p. 37)
k: Lidocaine toxicity progression: Early: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness Then: visual disturbance, muscle twitching, confusion Then: seizures, coma, respiratory depression Late: bradycardia, hypotens
r: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity starts with CNS excitation at the lowest blood levels, before cardiovascular effects. The earliest symptoms are perioral numbness, metallic taste, lightheadedness and tinnitus ; with rising levels the patient progresses to muscle twitching, seizures, CNS depression
wo: A. Skin rash: suggests an allergic reaction, which is rare with amide anesthetics like lidocaine and is not a sign of toxicity. | B. Bradycardia: a late cardiovascular sign (with hypotension, arrhythmia and arrest) at high plasma levels. | C. Seizures: occur after the early warning symptoms, as levels rise further; a late CNS sign.

q: A male patient after MVA a head injury associated with a temporal bone fracture . He initially experiences a period of unresponsive interval but arusable but later becomes unconscious again while in the hospital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Lucid interval + temporal fracture = extradural. Extradural: middle meningeal artery, biconvex, does not cross sutures Subdural: bridging veins, crescent, crosses sutures, elderly/alcoholics Signs of herniation: ipsilate
r: Temporal bone fracture after trauma with a lucid interval (initially rousable, then deteriorating in hospital) is the classic extradural (epidural) haematoma. The fracture tears the middle meningeal artery , and arterial bleeding expands quickly to cause secondary loss of consciousness; CT shows a b
wo: A. Subdural haematoma comes from torn bridging veins, typically in the elderly or alcoholics after deceleration injury, with gradual decline and a crescent shaped collection; it is not classically tied to temporal fracture and lucid interval.

q: A patient presents to the emergency department after sustaining a stab wound to the right side of the chest. On examination, the trachea is deviated to the left , breath sounds are absent on the right side , and the neck veins are distended . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Chest trauma: read the neck veins and percussion. Tension pneumothorax: hyperresonant, absent breath sounds, trachea away, raised JVP, hypotension Massive haemothorax: dull, absent breath sounds, flat neck veins, shock C
r: Penetrating right chest trauma with absent right breath sounds , trachea deviated to the left (away from the injury) and distended neck veins is tension pneumothorax. A one way valve traps air, shifts the mediastinum and kinks the great veins, so venous return falls and the JVP rises. It is a clinic
kw: trachea is deviated to the left
breath sounds are absent on the right side
wo: A. A simple haemothorax causes dullness and reduced breath sounds but is usually too small to shift the trachea or raise the JVP. | B. Massive haemothorax (over 1500 mL) gives dullness and shock, but the neck veins are typically flat from blood loss; distended veins favour tension. | C. Simple pneumothorax reduces breath sounds without mediastinal shift, raised JVP or haemodynamic compromise.

q: at screening clinic mamgram show dense breast , posative family history of cancer , BARCA posative
o: do a biopsy guided by ultrasound
k: High risk breast screening = MRI. Indications: BRCA1/2 carrier, lifetime risk about 20% or more, chest irradiation at young age, strong family history BRCA carriers: annual MRI from about 25 to 30, add mammogram from 30
r: A BRCA positive woman with dense breasts is high risk, and dense tissue lowers mammogram sensitivity because it masks tumours. High risk women are screened with annual breast MRI (in addition to mammography), which is the most sensitive test in this group. With no focal lesion seen, MRI is the next
wo: B. Repeating the mammogram adds nothing; the limitation is the dense tissue itself, which will mask lesions again. | C. Ultrasound guided biopsy needs a target lesion; there is no focal abnormality to biopsy here.

q: Pt with mets have bowle incontenance , MRI show cord compression . despite medical management what appropriate next step
k: Malignant cord compression is an emergency. Red flags: back pain in cancer, leg weakness, sensory level, sphincter dysfunction Investigation: urgent whole spine MRI Immediate: high dose dexamethasone Definitive: surgical
r: Metastatic spinal cord compression with bowel incontinence (autonomic involvement) that is progressing despite medical management (high dose steroids) needs urgent surgical decompression to save neurological function. Surgery followed by radiotherapy gives better outcomes than radiotherapy alone in
wo: B. Dexamethasone is started at once to reduce cord oedema, but escalating steroids does not relieve mechanical compression when deficits keep worsening.

q: Teenage with testicular torsion after detorsion what is appropriate next step ?
k: Testicular torsion: time is testis. Sudden severe scrotal pain, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex Strong clinical suspicion: straight to surgery (salvage best within about 6 hours) Manual detorsion
r: Manual detorsion is only a temporising manoeuvre; the testis can twist again because the underlying bell clapper anomaly persists. The next step is surgical exploration with orchidopexy , and because the anomaly is usually bilateral the contralateral testis is fixed too (bilateral orchidopexy, as ke
wo: A. Doppler ultrasound is used only when the diagnosis is uncertain and must never delay surgery; after detorsion the diagnosis is already made and fixation is still required.

q: breast lump which type of biopsy .
k: Breast lump: triple assessment = exam + imaging + core biopsy. Age under 30: ultrasound first; 30 or older: mammogram ± ultrasound BI-RADS 4/5: core needle biopsy Simple cyst: aspirate (FNA) ADH or discordant core: wire
r: Tissue diagnosis of a suspicious ("hard") breast lump is made by core needle biopsy , the biopsy step of triple assessment after clinical exam and imaging. A core gives tissue architecture, so it distinguishes invasive from in situ cancer and allows grading and receptor testing (ER, PR, HER2) before
wo: B. Excisional biopsy removes the whole lump as a diagnostic first step; it is reserved for discordant or nondiagnostic core results or atypia (e.g. ADH needing wire localization excision), not as the first biopsy. | C. Incisional biopsy (removing part of the mass surgically) is open surgery and has been replaced by core needle biopsy; it is rarely needed in breast work-up. | D. FNA gives cytology only, with no architecture, so it cannot separate in situ from invasive disease and has more false negatives; it is used to aspirate cysts or sample axillary nodes.

q: case presentation: mostly likely Choledocholithiasis and asked about initial management :
k: Suspected CBD stone, by probability: High (stone seen on US, bilirubin > 4 with dilated CBD, cholangitis): ERCP Intermediate (abnormal LFTs or dilated CBD alone): MRCP or EUS Low: lap cholecystectomy ± intraoperative cho
r: When choledocholithiasis is likely (ultrasound showing a dilated common bile duct or stone with cholestatic labs: raised bilirubin and ALP), the next step is ERCP , which both confirms the stone and removes it (sphincterotomy and extraction). It decompresses the duct before definitive cholecystectom
wo: B. MRCP is diagnostic only; it is used when the probability of a CBD stone is intermediate (e.g. raised LFTs but normal duct size), not when the stone is already likely. | C. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but leaves the duct stone; it follows ERCP (ideally in the same admission).

q: A 45-year-old woman presented with postprandial right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and emesis for few days that became persistent for the last 20 hours (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 87 /min, Temperature 37.2 °C. WBC 11 (normal 4.5-10.5 x 109/L), Direct bilirubin 9.5 (1.5-6.5 mol/L), Total bilirubin 18.5 (3.5-16.5 mol/L), Alkaline phosphatase 463 (39-117 IU/L). Ultrasound: Cholelithiasis, gallbladder wall thickening, and a common bile duct of 12 mm . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Biliary picture by clues: Biliary colic: brief pain, normal labs: elective lap chole Cholecystitis: fever, raised WBC, Murphy sign, normal bilirubin: lap chole within 72 hours Choledocholithiasis: raised bilirubin/ALP, d
r: The key clues are raised direct bilirubin and ALP 463 (cholestasis) plus gallstones with a CBD of 12 mm on ultrasound: this recall's key reads that as choledocholithiasis needing duct clearance, so the answer is ERCP , followed by cholecystectomy. She is afebrile (37.2) and stable, so it is not seve
wo: B. MRCP only images the duct; it is chosen when the probability of a stone is intermediate, whereas a 12 mm duct with cholestatic labs already justifies therapeutic ERCP. | C. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is right for acute cholecystitis or biliary colic without duct obstruction; here the CBD stone must be cleared first. | D. Conservative treatment leaves an obstructing stone that risks cholangitis and pancreatitis.

q: Patient present to the clinic with request of sick leave he has backpain felt when awaking from sleep. Yesterday he was playing football and had no injuries or trauma . PE there was localized tenderness and no limitation of movement in flexion?
o: Give him sick leave for 3 days …
Give analgesia and avoid (long or bed) rest
k: Acute mechanical low back pain: Reassure, stay active, avoid bed rest First line: NSAIDs or paracetamol; topical NSAIDs; heat No imaging in the first 6 weeks without red flags Red flags: age > 50, cancer history, fever,
r: This is acute non specific (mechanical) low back pain: pain after football without trauma, localized tenderness , normal range of movement and no red flags. Management is reassurance, simple analgesia (NSAIDs or paracetamol, topical agents) and staying active; bed rest is avoided because it slows re
wo: A. Urgent MRI is only for red flags: cauda equina features (saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention), progressive neurological deficit, suspected cancer, infection or fracture. | B. Sick leave for rest encourages inactivity; patients with simple back pain should keep up normal activities, with work modified if needed, rather than resting. | D. Not recalled; it cannot beat analgesia with advice to stay active in uncomplicated back pain.

q: 54-year-old male with history of DM and CKD , recently admitted for acute coronary syndrome , presents to clinic for follow-up. He has high creatinine, slightly high cholesterol, low HDL, and high LDL . Which of the following medications should be added to his regimen?
k: Statin benefit groups (adults over 21): Clinical ASCVD (ACS, stroke, PAD): high intensity statin LDL ≥190 mg/dL: high intensity statin Diabetes aged 40 to 75: moderate to high intensity statin High 10 year risk: statin p
r: A recent acute coronary syndrome means clinical ASCVD, which is an indication for high intensity statin therapy regardless of the baseline LDL. His diabetes and CKD add risk and strengthen the indication. Atorvastatin is the standard choice and needs no renal dose adjustment.
kw: recently admitted for acute coronary syndrome
wo: B. Niacin raises HDL but has not reduced cardiovascular events when added to statins and causes flushing; it is not used for secondary prevention. | C. Ezetimibe is an add on when LDL stays above target despite a maximally tolerated statin, or in statin intolerance; it is not first line. | D. Doing nothing is wrong: every patient after ACS needs a statin, and his raised LDL makes it even clearer.

q: A patient presents with pneumonia (productive cough, fever and pain; the picture shows a lobar pneumonia). Treatment is started with IV ceftriaxone , azithromycin, paracetamol and tramadol. After one day he is stable and improving, but the platelet count has fallen to about 70 . Which drug should be stopped ?
k: New thrombocytopenia after starting drugs: think drug induced immune thrombocytopenia and stop the culprit. Classic culprits: heparin (HIT), beta lactams such as ceftriaxone and piperacillin, vancomycin, quinine, sulfona
r: The patient is improving on standard CAP therapy, then the platelets fall to about 70 after starting new drugs , which suggests drug induced immune thrombocytopenia. Among the four drugs, ceftriaxone (a beta lactam) is the one classically associated with drug induced immune thrombocytopenia, so it i
kw: platelet count has fallen to about 70
wo: A. Paracetamol at normal doses rarely affects platelets; its main toxicity is hepatic in overdose. | B. Tramadol causes nausea, seizures and serotonin syndrome, not thrombocytopenia. | D. Azithromycin's concerns are QT prolongation and GI upset; it is not a typical cause of thrombocytopenia.

q: A patient with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis three times per week develops a pericardial effusion . Blood pressure is 83/60 mmHg and heart sounds are muffled . What is the next step?
k: Uremic pericardial effusion: decide on tamponade first. No tamponade (stable BP): dialysis is initial, next and definitive treatment Tamponade (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds, pulsus paradoxus): pericardiocentes
r: ESRD on dialysis with a pericardial effusion points to a uremic or dialysis associated effusion. The decisive clues are BP 83/60 and muffled heart sounds : hypotension makes this tamponade, not a simple effusion. An unstable tamponade needs immediate pericardiocentesis for rapid stabilization; inten
wo: A. Urgent or intensified dialysis is the right answer for a uremic effusion WITHOUT tamponade (normal BP); a hypotensive patient may not tolerate dialysis and needs drainage first. | C. Furosemide reduces preload, which worsens tamponade (filling depends on preload), and it does little in an anuric ESRD patient. | D. Doing nothing is wrong: hypotension from tamponade can progress to cardiac arrest.

q: A 45-year-old woman known to have end-stage renal disease secondary to type 1 diabetes mellitus came to the clinic for a routine follow-up. She had no complaints but was found to have abnormal blood results (see lab results; the laboratory panel was not captured in the recall). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: CKD mineral bone disease: the kidney cannot activate vitamin D, so phosphate rises, calcium falls and PTH rises. Low Ca, high PTH, low vitamin D in ESRD: calcitriol (active vitamin D) High phosphate: dietary restriction
r: A 45 year old with ESRD from type 1 DM on routine follow up with abnormal labs is the classic picture of secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH and low vitamin D. The failing kidney cannot make active vitamin D, so calcitriol (1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D) is given
wo: A. Sevelamer is a phosphate binder; it is right when the main issue is hyperphosphatemia, but it does not correct low active vitamin D or suppress PTH directly. | C. Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic for persistently high PTH with normal or high calcium; it lowers calcium further and is avoided when calcium is low. | D. 25 hydroxy vitamin D (calcidiol) still needs renal 1 alpha hydroxylation, which fails in ESRD; it fits nutritional vitamin D deficiency with normal kidneys.

q: Elderly patient came to hospital with dysuria and UTI symptoms , known to have hypertension, diabetes and COPD, with a previous admission for urosepsis with shock. Now he is agitated and aggressive on the ward. Vitals mostly normal but temperature high and oxygen saturation 92% . What is the most appropriate management?
k: Delirium in the elderly: find and treat the cause, then non drug measures first. Causes: infection (UTI, pneumonia), drugs, hypoxia, retention, constipation, electrolytes Non drug: reorientation, sleep wake cycle, glasse
r: An elderly patient with a UTI who becomes agitated and aggressive on the ward with fever has hyperactive delirium from infection. Treating the cause (antibiotics) is not offered, so the best answer is non pharmacological delirium care, here sleep cycle regulation (day night orientation, lights, mini
wo: A. Sedation (antipsychotic or benzodiazepine) is a last resort only when the patient endangers himself or others after non drug measures fail; benzodiazepines worsen delirium and may depress breathing in COPD. | B. Physical restraint increases agitation, injury and delirium duration; it is avoided except briefly in an emergency. | D. Oxygen would be right if SpO2 were below 88% in COPD; at 92% he is on target, and long term oxygen needs two ABGs with chronic hypoxemia when stable.

q: Young man 30 years smoker . Has pulmonary nodule . Risk factor for pulmonary nodule to be malignant *in this patient * Culture send for TB
k: Nodule malignancy risk: size, smoking, age, spiculated margin, upper lobe, growth. ≤4 mm: no follow up (low risk) more than 4 to 8 mm: CT at 3 to 6 months more than 8 mm to 2 cm: PET/CT then biopsy more than 2 cm: surger
r: Of the options, size is the strongest independent predictor of malignancy in a pulmonary nodule, and a lesion over 2 to 3 cm is treated as malignant until proven otherwise (a 'mass'). The mention of a TB culture shows TB is on the differential, and TB also explains apical position and hypercalcemia,
wo: A. Older age (over about 40 to 50) raises risk, but this patient is a young man, so age argues against malignancy here. | B. High serum calcium may occur with squamous cell cancer (PTHrP) but also with TB and sarcoidosis granulomas, and it is not part of nodule malignancy risk models; benign calcification patterns in the nodule favour benign disease. | D. Upper lobe location is a recognized cancer risk feature, but apical disease is also classic for reactivation TB, which is being investigated here.

q: An older postoperative patient receives D5W and develops hyponatremia ( Na 125 mmol/L), serum osmolality 266 mOsm/kg and mildly elevated urine sodium . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Hyponatremia step by step: Step 1 serum osmolality: low (below 280) means true hypotonic hyponatremia Step 2 urine osmolality: below 100 means excess water intake; above 100 means ADH is acting Step 3 volume status and u

q: A 55-year old man with stable COPD , presents with sudden onset left-sided pleuritic chest pain and exertional dyspnea. On examination, he is not in distress . the trachea is central and breath sounds are equal in both sides with occasional mild expiratory wheezes (see report). Blood pressure 130/70 mmHg Heart rate 80 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 93 % Chest X-ray: Shows a left sided pneumothorax measuring 2 cm between the lung and chest wall . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (lung disease, older than 50, smoker): Breathless or more than 2 cm: chest drain 1 to 2 cm, not breathless: needle aspiration, admit below 1 cm, not breathless: high flow oxygen, observ
kw: 2 cm between the lung and chest wall

q: A 64-year-old man with liver cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis C completed treatment for HCV and now has undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment. He is asymptomatic (see lab results). Which of the following is the most diagnostic ?
o: Triphasic CT scan of the abdomen
k: HCC in cirrhosis: Surveillance: ultrasound every 6 months, with or without AFP, continues after HCV cure Nodule below 1 cm: repeat ultrasound in 3 months Nodule ≥1 cm or rising AFP: multiphasic CT or contrast MRI Arteria
r: This recall's key is triphasic CT because the lead in asks for the most diagnostic test: triphasic (multiphasic) contrast CT shows the arterial enhancement and venous washout that diagnose HCC without biopsy. Even after HCV cure (undetectable RNA at 12 weeks), established cirrhosis keeps the HCC ris
wo: A. Contrast MRI is at least as accurate as triphasic CT for diagnosing HCC, but this option is a yearly surveillance schedule, which is not standard; surveillance is ultrasound every 6 months. | B. Liver ultrasound every 6 months (with or without AFP) is the surveillance (screening) test after HCV cure in cirrhosis; it is the answer when the question asks for follow up or screening. | C. AFP alone is not sensitive enough and is not used every 3 months; it is an adjunct to ultrasound every 6 months.

q: 50-52 y/o female patient came to the screening clinic , medically and surgically free, No family history , what to do?
k: Average risk CRC screening starts at 45 (choose 50 if 45 is not offered). Colonoscopy: every 10 years (gold standard) FIT / high sensitivity FOBT: annually Stool DNA: every 3 years Flexible sigmoidoscopy: every 5 years C
r: A 50 to 52 year old woman with no family history and no risk factors is average risk, so she needs routine colorectal cancer screening. Annual stool testing for blood (FOBT/FIT) is a valid average risk strategy with the correct interval. The other listed options carry the wrong interval for an avera
wo: A. Sigmoidoscopy: per the recaller's correction this option was every 10 years, a wrong interval for sigmoidoscopy alone; as printed (every 5 years) it would be a guideline interval, which is why the correction matters. | C. Colonoscopy every 5 years: the average risk interval is every 10 years; 5 years is for higher risk (e.g. first degree relative with CRC, prior adenomas). | D. Option not recalled; no basis to choose it.

q: 20 year old male KC of DM1 and diabetic nephropathy had a tonic colonic seizure lated for 4 minutes after 2 hour EEG show wave ( I can't remember) and tha labs was Na 132 RBG 4
k: First seizure: is it provoked? Check glucose, Na, Ca, Mg, toxins, head imaging Provoked only if the abnormality is severe: Na below about 120, glucose clearly low, marked hypocalcemia Unprovoked + epileptiform EEG: epile
r: The labs are Na 132 and RBG 4 : a sodium of 132 is only mildly low and a glucose of 4 mmol/L is normal, so neither can explain a 4 minute tonic clonic seizure . Provoked metabolic seizures need much more marked derangements, and the EEG showing epileptiform wave discharges points to a primary genera
wo: B. Hypoglycemia seizure: right when glucose is clearly low (around 2.5 mmol/L or less, or about 45 mg/dL), common in type 1 diabetics on insulin; a glucose of 4 mmol/L is normal. | C. Hyponatremia: seizures usually occur with severe (Na below about 120) or rapidly falling sodium; 132 is mild and not a seizure cause. | D. Option not recalled (hypocalcemia in the earlier version): Ca 2.1 is only slightly low; hypocalcemic seizures need marked hypocalcemia with tetany signs.

q: A patient with DM, non-compliant with medications, presents with confusion Na 121 HbA1c = 8.something What is the most likely cause?
k: Hyponatremia symptoms track severity and speed. Mild (130 to 134): usually asymptomatic Moderate (125 to 129): nausea, headache, malaise Severe (below 125): confusion, seizures, coma Work-up: serum osmolality, then volum
r: The only value given that is markedly abnormal is Na 121 , and significant hyponatremia causes confusion. HbA1c around 8 shows poor long term control but is not an acute cause of altered mental status, and the other labs were said to be about normal. So the confusion is best explained by hyponatremi
wo: A. Hypokalemia: causes muscle weakness, ileus and arrhythmias (flat T waves, U waves), not confusion, and no low potassium was reported. | C. Hypocalcemia: causes tetany, perioral tingling, Chvostek and Trousseau signs and prolonged QT; no low calcium was reported. | D. Hypoglycemia: a classic cause of confusion in diabetics, but on treatment (insulin or sulfonylurea); a patient non compliant with medications with HbA1c 8 is more likely hyperglycemic.

q: A patient was diagnosed with pneumonia and treated with antibiotics. His condition improved, and he was discharged. He later returned with severe respiratory distress and worsening clinical status. On examination: SpO2: 85% Bilateral crackles on auscultation pH: 7.27 What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Worsening after pneumonia: name the process. Bilateral infiltrates + severe hypoxemia within 1 week of insult, non cardiac: ARDS (Berlin) ARDS severity by PaO2/FiO2: mild 200 to 300, moderate 100 to 200, severe ≤ 100 Hyp

q: A woman with a BMI of 35 kg/m² and a family history of diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic. She is concerned about her risk of developing diabetes. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Follow a diet with reduced carbohydrate intake.
Undergo bariatric surgery because losing weight may be difficult.
Engage in regular physical activity and maintain a healthy diet.
k: Obesity and diabetes prevention. First line: diet + exercise (at least 150 minutes per week of moderate activity) for weight loss Bariatric surgery (classic exam criteria): BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with comorbidity; newer crite
r: She has BMI 35 and a family history of diabetes but no diabetes or other obesity related complication of her own. The first and most effective recommendation for diabetes prevention is lifestyle modification: regular physical activity combined with a healthy diet, aiming for weight loss. Option C co
wo: A. Reduced carbohydrate diet: only one part of lifestyle change; diet without regular exercise is less effective than the combined approach. | B. Bariatric surgery: not the first recommendation for diabetes prevention before any lifestyle trial; classic exam criteria are BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with her own obesity related comorbidity (diabetes, hypertension, OSA), and a family history does not count (newer 2022 surgical society criteria allow BMI ≥ 35 alone, but lifestyle still comes first).

q: Female with melena and epigastric pain no history of nsaid endoscopy performed and urea test antrum biopsy negative appropite next diagnostic test
k: No NSAID + bleeding ulcer = assume H. pylori until proven otherwise; a negative biopsy test during the bleed needs a second test. Active bleed or on PPI: serology is unaffected Off PPI 2 weeks, off antibiotics 4 weeks: u

q: A 55-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of recurrent epigastric pain that resolves spontaneously, associated with nausea but no vomiting and unintentional weight loss . He has no family history of GI malignancy. Examination reveals epigastric tenderness on deep palpation. Labs show anemia with low MCV . What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Dyspepsia + any alarm feature = endoscopy. Unintentional weight loss Iron deficiency anemia or GI bleeding Progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting Palpable mass, new symptoms in older age No alarm features and young:
r: Recurrent epigastric pain in a 55-year-old with unintentional weight loss and iron deficiency (microcytic) anemia has alarm features for upper GI malignancy or a bleeding ulcer. Alarm features mandate direct visualisation and biopsy, so upper GI endoscopy is the next step regardless of family histor
wo: B. CT abdomen is used for staging once a cancer is found or for suspected complications; it cannot see mucosa or take biopsies. | C. Test and treat for H. pylori is for young dyspeptic patients without alarm features; with weight loss and anemia it would delay a cancer diagnosis (biopsies at endoscopy can test for H. pylori anyway).

q: A 51-year-old man presents to the ER with vomiting blood . He has a previous history of two gastrointestinal bleeds of unknown site . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step?
k: Upper GI bleed sequence. 1. ABC, two large bore cannulas, fluids or blood 2. Risk score and medical therapy (PPI; terlipressin and antibiotics if variceal suspected) 3. Endoscopy within 24 h (sooner if unstable) 4. Faile
r: Hematemesis with two previous GI bleeds of unknown site needs a diagnosis of the source, and upper GI endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic (it can inject, clip, band). The true first action is ABC and resuscitation, but that is not offered, so among these options endoscopy (after stabilisati
kw: two gastrointestinal bleeds of unknown site
wo: B. A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is a temporary rescue for uncontrolled variceal bleeding when endoscopic therapy fails or is unavailable; the source here is not even known. | C. Laparotomy is reserved for bleeding that endoscopy (and interventional radiology) cannot control, or for perforation. | D. Barium studies cannot treat bleeding, are poor at finding the source and coat the mucosa, making later endoscopy harder.

q: A 20-years-old male patient with sickle cell disease presented to the ED with acute vaso-occlusive crisis. He was managed with IV fluids, morphine and enoxaparin . His thrombocytopenia (80) . Creatinine and urea were normal. What's the cause of his thrombocytopenia?
k: Thrombocytopenia after heparin: think HIT. Timing: typically 5 to 10 days after start (earlier if heparin exposure in the past 100 days) Fall in platelets about 50% or more, rarely below 20 Thrombosis, not bleeding Stop
