r: The new drop in platelets ( 80 ) appeared after the patient received enoxaparin , a heparin, and he has normal creatinine and urea . Heparin induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction to heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes, causing thrombocytopenia (typically 5 to 10 days after starting) with a
wo: A. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion with isolated thrombocytopenia in a well patient (often after a viral illness); a clear drug trigger is present here. | B. HUS needs microangiopathic hemolysis plus acute kidney injury; renal function is normal. | C. TTP presents with hemolysis, fever, neurological signs and severe thrombocytopenia; nothing points to it, and no drug trigger is needed.

q: A 49-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history presents for lung cancer screening. What is the best screening test ?
o: Low-dose CT scan of the chest
k: Lung cancer screening (USPSTF 2021). Who: age 50 to 80 with 20 pack-years or more, current smoker or quit within 15 years How: annual low dose CT Stop: quit 15 years or more, or health limits curative surgery
r: The question asks for the best screening test in a heavy smoker (30 pack-years). Annual low dose CT of the chest is the only lung cancer screening test shown to reduce lung cancer mortality, and it uses a fraction of the radiation of a diagnostic CT.
wo: B. Chest X-ray (with or without sputum) was studied as a screening tool and did not reduce lung cancer mortality; it is for symptomatic patients. | C. Spirometry diagnoses COPD in a smoker with symptoms; it does not screen for cancer. | D. Sputum cytology has poor sensitivity and no mortality benefit for screening.

q: Pneumonia Pneumonia with X-ray picture patient had shock : Vital : hypotension Fever He started on vasopressin , antibiotics What will you find?
k: Shock hemodynamic profiles. Hypovolemic: low CO, high SVR, low CVP/PCWP Cardiogenic: low CO, high SVR, high CVP/PCWP Septic (early): high CO, low SVR, low or normal CVP Neurogenic: low SVR with bradycardia Obstructive: l
r: Pneumonia with fever and hypotension needing vasopressors is septic shock, a distributive shock. Widespread vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance, and the heart compensates with tachycardia, producing the classic hyperdynamic picture of high cardiac output (warm shock).
wo: A. Systemic vascular resistance is low in septic shock; high SVR is seen in hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock (cold, clamped down). | C. Raised central or venous pressures fit cardiogenic or obstructive shock; in sepsis filling pressures are normal or low.

q: Female after mastectomy Na increased Urine osmilairy decreased
k: Read sodium and urine osmolality together. High Na + dilute urine = DI (central or nephrogenic) Low Na + concentrated urine, euvolemic = SIADH Low Na + very dilute urine = psychogenic polydipsia Water deprivation then de
r: High sodium with low urine osmolality means the kidney is losing free water despite a concentrated plasma, which is diabetes insipidus. In the fuller version (post mastectomy with lung metastases, polyuria and thirst, Na 150, urine osmolality 110), breast cancer metastasis to the pituitary or hypoth
wo: B. SIADH causes water retention, so it gives hyponatremia with an inappropriately concentrated urine (high urine osmolality). It is the answer when Na is low with euvolemia, as in small cell lung cancer or CNS disease.

q: Patient with increased cough and SOB i think
k: VTE prophylaxis choice: Normal renal function, normal weight: enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily Severe renal impairment or dialysis: UFH Severe obesity: higher dose regimens History of HIT: fondaparinux (if kidneys allow) H

q: Best recommendation for UTI patient :
k: UTI management priority: Symptomatic cystitis: empiric antibiotics Complicated, recurrent, pregnancy or pyelonephritis: culture first, then antibiotics Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only in pregnancy or before urologic
r: Between the two listed options, this recall's key is cranberry juice, a commonly recommended measure that may reduce UTI recurrence by limiting bacterial adherence to the urothelium. The compiler notes that if antibiotics (ideally with culture when indicated) appear among the options, they take prio
wo: A. Hydration flushes the bladder and is reasonable general advice, but it is nonspecific; this recall keys cranberry as the targeted measure against bacterial adherence. Hydration is the expected answer for rhabdomyolysis, hypercalcemia or kidney stone prevention.

q: A 28-year-old woman referred to the clinic with 3-week history of generalized fatigability. malaise, arthralgia, back pain and fever. Positive history of raw milk ingestion . Abdominal examination, mild hepato-splenomegaly (see lab results and reports). Temperature 38.5 °C Test Result Normal Values Hb 10.5 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 120 150-400 x 109/L Blood culture: Gram negative cocco-bacilli Which of the following is the optimal duration of therapy ?
k: Brucellosis duration by complication: Uncomplicated (including sacroiliitis): 6 weeks Spondylitis: 12 weeks First line: doxycycline plus rifampicin or streptomycin Children under 8 or pregnancy: avoid doxycycline MRI sep
r: Raw milk ingestion, fever, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly and Gram negative coccobacilli on blood culture mean brucellosis. With no imaging showing spondylitis, this is treated as uncomplicated brucellosis, for which the standard regimen (doxycycline plus rifampicin or streptomycin) is given for 6 w
wo: A. 3 weeks is too short; brucella is intracellular and short courses have high relapse rates. | C. 12 weeks is the duration for complicated brucellosis such as spondylitis; choose it when the stem gives MRI evidence of spondylitis or another focal complication. | D. 24 weeks is not a standard brucellosis duration; prolonged courses are individualized for neurobrucellosis or endocarditis, which are not described.

q: Young adult admitted to isolation. Bone marrow biopsy showed AML M5 . One day before start of chemotherapy he developed fever . Vitals normal. Temperature 38.9 C Hgb low. What is the treatment?
k: Febrile neutropenia: cultures then IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam within the first hour. Options: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, carbapenem (or ceftazidime) Add vancomycin for catheter infection, skin infection, MRSA
r: A patient with AML , whose marrow is replaced by leukemic cells, who spikes 38.9 C is treated as febrile neutropenia even before chemotherapy. After cultures, the treatment is prompt empiric IV broad spectrum antipseudomonal monotherapy, classically an extended spectrum penicillin such as piperacill
kw: One day before start of chemotherapy
wo: B. G-CSF can shorten neutropenia and is used in selected prophylaxis, but it is not a treatment for fever and it is generally avoided in myeloid leukemia; antibiotics are the urgent step. | C. Oral fluoroquinolone (often with amoxicillin-clavulanate) is for low-risk outpatient febrile neutropenia or for prophylaxis; an admitted AML patient is high risk and needs IV therapy. | D. Most third generation cephalosporins (for example ceftriaxone) lack antipseudomonal cover; only ceftazidime is an accepted option, so the generic class is not the best answer.

q: A patient with pneumonia develops sepsis/septic shock/ SIRS . Which of the following hemodynamic changes would most likely be seen?
k: Shock profiles (CO, SVR, CVP): Septic (distributive): CO up, SVR down, CVP low or normal Hypovolemic: CO down, SVR up, CVP down Cardiogenic: CO down, SVR up, CVP and PCWP up Obstructive: CO down, SVR up, CVP up Neurogeni
r: Sepsis from pneumonia causes distributive shock : inflammatory mediators produce widespread vasodilation, so systemic vascular resistance falls and the heart compensates with tachycardia and a high cardiac output (the warm, hyperdynamic phase). This is the hallmark profile of early septic shock.
wo: B. CVP is usually low or normal in sepsis because vasodilation and capillary leak reduce venous return; a raised CVP suggests cardiogenic or obstructive shock (tamponade, tension pneumothorax). | C. SVR is decreased in septic shock; increased SVR is seen in hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock as compensatory vasoconstriction. | D. This option was not recalled, so it cannot be assessed.

q: A patient with asthma was prescribed for the first time inhaler and the doctor was busy to refer him to the education clinic what is the most likely consequence of this action ?
k: Asthma education is part of treatment: Teach and recheck inhaler technique at every visit Spacer for children and poor coordination Rinse mouth after inhaled steroid (prevents candidiasis, dysphonia) Written asthma actio
r: Without inhaler education, patients commonly use the device wrongly (poor technique, poor coordination, not rinsing after steroid). The fuller version confirms the result: inhalers used incorrectly and repeated ER visits for exacerbations. Poor technique means poor drug delivery and more local side
kw: busy to refer him to the education clinic
wo: A. Decreased confidence may occur, but it is a soft secondary effect; the exam focuses on the clinical harm of incorrect inhaler use. | B. Increased self-efficacy is the result of proper education, the opposite of what happens when it is skipped. | C. Maximized daily productivity reflects good asthma control, which is expected after education, not after it is omitted.

q: 25 YO complain of 3 months abdominal pain, bloody DIARRHEA, weight loss. Mother and brother have same complain Guaiac stool test: positive
k: Young adult with rectal bleeding and family history: FAP: autosomal dominant, APC gene, hundreds of adenomas, colectomy by early adulthood Peutz-Jeghers: hamartomas plus perioral and lip pigmentation Lynch (HNPCC): few p
r: This recall's key is FAP because of the young age (25) with bloody stools, weight loss and the same complaint in the mother and brother , a vertical pattern consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. FAP produces hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomas that bleed, and colonoscopy shows a colo
kw: Mother and brother have same complain
wo: A. Ulcerative colitis causes chronic bloody diarrhea with urgency and tenesmus and has only a modest familial tendency; it is the answer when there is no strong first degree pattern and there are extraintestinal features such as arthritis or a raised CRP. | C. Diverticulosis affects older adults, is usually asymptomatic or causes painless large bleeds, and has no autosomal dominant family pattern in young people.

q: A 70 YO patient presents with right-sided weakness that started 12 hours ago . Vitals Within Normal Range. Coagulation profile is normal and platelet normal (I missed numbers) Imaging shows a proximal Anterior circulation occlusion with a Small-moderate-sized infarct core . What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Acute ischemic stroke by time: Check glucose, then non-contrast CT to exclude hemorrhage Within 4.5 h: IV tPA if no contraindication Large vessel occlusion within 6 h: thrombectomy (plus tPA if within 4.5 h) 6 to 24 h: t
r: Onset 12 hours ago puts him outside the thrombolysis window (up to 4.5 hours), but a proximal anterior circulation (large vessel) occlusion with a small to moderate infarct core and a persistent deficit meets criteria for mechanical thrombectomy, which is beneficial in selected patients up to 24 hou
wo: A. IV tPA is given within 4.5 hours of onset (or last known well) with hemorrhage excluded; at 12 hours it is outside the window. | C. Observation (with aspirin and secondary prevention) is right when there is no large vessel occlusion, a large established core, or presentation beyond 24 hours. | D. Combined tPA plus thrombectomy is right for a large vessel occlusion presenting within 4.5 hours; here only thrombectomy is still possible.

q: 63 year old man with poorly controlled hypertension, when with sitting with family became unresponsive, only moves eyes vertically and does not move limbs (bilaterally) . Where is the lesion ?
k: Quadriplegia + mute + conscious + only vertical eye movement/blinking = locked-in syndrome = ventral pons. Cause: basilar artery thrombosis or pontine hemorrhage (hypertension) Pontine bleed: pinpoint pupils, coma or qua
r: This is locked-in syndrome : a hypertensive man suddenly becomes "unresponsive" with quadriplegia but keeps vertical eye movements and consciousness. A lesion of the ventral pons (classically basilar artery occlusion or hypertensive pontine hemorrhage) cuts both corticospinal and corticobulbar tract
wo: B. Medulla: gives lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome with crossed sensory loss, dysphagia and ataxia, or medial medullary hemiparesis with tongue deviation; it does not spare only vertical gaze. | C. Midbrain: the vertical gaze centres sit here, so a midbrain lesion would LOSE vertical gaze (Parinaud) or give Weber syndrome (CN III palsy plus contralateral hemiplegia). | D. Left cerebral cortex: produces contralateral (right) hemiparesis and aphasia, not bilateral limb paralysis with preserved eye movements.

q: Patient newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, Hb1C 7.9. His BMI 34 . What is the first line for him? (SGLT2 inhibitors wasn't mentioned)
k: New T2DM: lifestyle + metformin first, then add an agent chosen by comorbidity. Obesity: add GLP-1 agonist ASCVD, heart failure or CKD: add SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist Weight neutral add-on: DPP-4 inhibitor Very hig
r: In a newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic with HbA1c 7.9% the first-line drug is metformin together with lifestyle change, regardless of BMI. Obesity (BMI 34) makes a GLP-1 agonist attractive, but in this recall it is added to metformin rather than replacing it; the recaller notes SGLT2 inhibitors were s
wo: A. DPP-4 inhibitor: weight neutral add-on (second line) when metformin is not enough or not tolerated; not first line. | B. Liraglutide: GLP-1 agonist favoured as an add-on in obese patients or those with established cardiovascular disease; it is started with metformin, not instead of it. | D. Sulfonylurea: causes weight gain and hypoglycemia, an especially poor choice with BMI 34; used as a cheap second-line add-on.

q: 60-year-old man found to have elevated blood pressure during a routine checkup ( 155/90 ). No symptoms, unremarkable exam. ECG, CBC, electrolytes, renal function tests, and urine analysis normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Repeat office blood pressure measurement in 3 months
k: Raised office BP without end-organ damage: confirm before labelling or treating. Preferred confirmation: ambulatory BP monitoring (home BP is an alternative) JNC 7 follow-up for 140-159/90-99: confirm within 2 months Ver
r: A single raised office reading (155/90) in an asymptomatic man with a normal exam, ECG and labs (no end-organ damage) does not establish hypertension. The next step is to confirm the diagnosis out of office, and ambulatory BP monitoring is the preferred confirmatory test because it excludes white co
wo: A. Echocardiogram: not a routine test in uncomplicated hypertension; used if heart failure or LVH is suspected clinically or on ECG. | B. Start antihypertensive medication: drugs are started after the diagnosis is confirmed, or immediately only for very high readings (around 180/110) or evident end-organ damage. | D. Repeat office BP in 3 months: too long a delay; a reading of 140-159/90-99 should be confirmed within about 2 months, and office readings alone do not exclude white coat effect.

q: An elderly patient on lisinopril develops several days of vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. His creatinine rises from 60 to 160 µmol/L. Investigations: Urine Na+ = 68 mmol/L Urine osmolality = 220 mOsm/kg Urine specific gravity ≈ 1.009 Urea = 11 mmol/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Urine indices separate pre-renal from intrinsic (ATN) AKI. Urine Na: pre-renal below 20; ATN above 40 FeNa: pre-renal below 1%; ATN above 2% Urine osmolality: pre-renal above 500; ATN below 350 Specific gravity: pre-rena
r: Vomiting and diarrhea on an ACE inhibitor start as pre-renal injury, but the urine shows the tubules have stopped working: urine Na 68 (above 40), urine osmolality 220 (dilute, below 350) and specific gravity about 1.009 (isosthenuria). Loss of sodium retention and concentrating ability is the signa
wo: A. Pre-renal AKI: tubules are intact, so urine Na is below 20, urine osmolality above 500 and specific gravity above 1.020; this patient's indices are the opposite. | B. (forgot): the option was not recalled; whatever it was, the dilute, sodium-wasting urine after a hypoperfusion insult points to ATN. | D. Acute-on-chronic CKD: the baseline creatinine of 60 µmol/L is normal, and the rise followed an acute insult, so there is no evidence of prior CKD.

q: 19 years old female presented to the ER with vomiting and (other signs of dehydration), she's conscious but appears in distress, she admits mephetamin overuse , (No vitals), Labs: Low Na (I can't remember the rest but it was abnormal) Which of the following is known complication of her drug abuse?
k: Amphetamine and MDMA toxicity: sympathomimetic picture with metabolic complications. Hyponatremia: SIADH plus high water intake Hyperthermia, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis Rhabdomyolysis leading to acut
r: Amphetamine-type drugs (methamphetamine and especially MDMA or mephedrone) cause hyponatremia through inappropriate ADH release and excessive water drinking, plus volume loss from vomiting. A young woman with vomiting, dehydration and low Na after use therefore shows the known complication of electr
wo: A. Liver toxicity: amphetamines can occasionally injure the liver (usually with hyperthermia), but nothing in the stem suggests hepatic injury; it would be right with jaundice or raised transaminases. | B. (forgot): the option was not recalled; the given low sodium still anchors the answer to electrolyte imbalance. | C. CKD: a chronic condition and not an acute complication; amphetamines cause acute kidney injury mainly via rhabdomyolysis.

q: Iron Deficiency Anemia in young medically free lady? I think she was symptomatic like palpitations or SOB but Hb levels was "not" very severe drop , i forgot the ferritin level, management ?
k: IDA: oral iron first, IV iron for failure or malabsorption, transfusion for instability. Confirm: low ferritin, microcytosis, high TIBC Response: reticulocytes rise within about a week, Hb rises over weeks Continue oral
r: A young, otherwise healthy woman with iron deficiency anemia and only mild symptoms (palpitations or breathlessness) and a not severe hemoglobin drop is treated with oral iron (for example ferrous fumarate) first. It is effective, cheap and safe, and is continued for about 3 months after Hb normalis
kw: Hb levels was "not" very severe drop
wo: B. IV iron: for intolerance or failure of oral iron, malabsorption (celiac disease, bariatric surgery, IBD), ongoing losses exceeding oral replacement, or late pregnancy needing rapid repletion.

q: From the following medications used to treat esophageal varices in vitally unstable (I mean he has tachycardia and hypotension) patient, which one is improving the mortality :
k: Acute variceal bleed bundle: resuscitate, vasoactive drug, antibiotics, endoscopy within 12 hours. Mortality benefit: prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone) Vasoactive: octreotide or terlipressin Restrictive transfusion:
r: The lead-in asks which drug improves mortality , not which stops bleeding. In cirrhotic patients with variceal bleeding, prophylactic antibiotics (IV ceftriaxone) reduce bacterial infections, rebleeding and death, and are one of the clearest survival benefits in the bundle.
wo: B. PPI: reduces post-banding ulcer bleeding and helps in peptic ulcer bleeding, but has no proven survival benefit in variceal bleeding. | C. Octreotide: lowers portal pressure and helps control bleeding before endoscopy, but its mortality benefit is not established (terlipressin has more evidence); it is the answer when asked for the IV pharmacological treatment. | D. Packed RBC: needed in an unstable patient, but a restrictive strategy (target Hb about 7 to 8 g/dL) is used because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding; it is not the mortality-reducing drug here.

q: A patient presents with Cushingoid features . Laboratory results show elevated cortisol (4pm around 800, 8pm around 500) and elevated ACTH ( 17 and the reference was 15). What is the most likely cause?
k: Cushing syndrome: confirm, then use ACTH to localise. Screen: 24-hour urine cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, 1 mg dexamethasone suppression Low ACTH: adrenal source, CT adrenals (or exogenous steroids) High ACTH,
r: High cortisol with loss of diurnal variation (evening values still high) and an ACTH that is high or inappropriately normal (17 with an upper limit of 15) means ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. The mildly raised ACTH is typical of Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma, the most common cause of en
wo: B. Adrenal tumor: autonomous cortisol secretion suppresses ACTH, so ACTH would be low or undetectable. | C. Carcinoid (ectopic ACTH): usually very high ACTH with rapid onset, hypokalemia and weight loss rather than a mildly raised ACTH. | D. Iatrogenic corticosteroid use: exogenous steroids suppress ACTH; it is the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome overall but does not fit a high ACTH.

q: A woman presents with galactorrhea . (She also have bitemporal hemianopia and headache) Her serum prolactin level has already been measured and is elevated. What is the first investigation to order now to establish the diagnosis?
k: Galactorrhea work-up order. 1: pregnancy test 2: TSH and prolactin (hypothyroidism raises prolactin) 3: pituitary MRI if prolactin high and other causes (drugs, pregnancy, hypothyroidism) excluded Visual fields for macro
r: The lead-in stresses that prolactin has already been measured and is high, and she has bitemporal hemianopia and headache , so a pituitary macroadenoma compressing the chiasm is suspected. The next investigation to establish the diagnosis is MRI of the pituitary , the imaging of choice for the sella
kw: prolactin level has already been measured
wo: A. CT of the head: poorer soft tissue resolution for the pituitary; used only when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. | B. Serum prolactin: already done and raised; repeating it adds nothing here (it is the first test in galactorrhea when not yet measured). | C. Mammography: galactorrhea is a hormonal, bilateral milky discharge; mammography is for a breast lump or suspicious unilateral bloody discharge.

q: Female with idiopathic dvt came for follow up , warfarin 6 weeks and INR = 6 In addition to stop warfarin what to do?
k: Supratherapeutic INR on warfarin. No bleeding, INR above range but under 10: hold/reduce dose, recheck INR No bleeding, INR above 10: hold + oral vitamin K Minor bleeding: hold + vitamin K Major bleeding: IV vitamin K +
r: The patient is seen in follow-up clinic with an INR of 6 and no bleeding . For a non-bleeding patient with INR between about 4.5 and 10, the management is to hold warfarin and recheck the INR within a short interval, then resume at a lower dose once in range. Routine vitamin K is not needed at this
wo: A. Vitamin K is given when INR is above about 10 without bleeding (oral), or with any bleeding (IV); at INR 6 without bleeding it is not routinely required. | C. Fresh frozen plasma is for major bleeding on warfarin when prothrombin complex concentrate is unavailable. | D. Prothrombin complex concentrate with IV vitamin K is the reversal for major or life-threatening bleeding (e.g. intracranial hemorrhage).

q: Patient with Idiopathic dvt on warfarin came for followup , INR = 6 In addition to stop the warfarin , what to do ?
k: High INR on warfarin: first ask, is the patient bleeding? Major or life-threatening bleeding (any INR): admit, IV vitamin K plus PCC (or FFP) No bleeding, INR >10: hold warfarin plus oral vitamin K No bleeding, INR 4 to
r: A routine follow-up visit with no mention of bleeding means a non-bleeding patient, and INR 6 falls in the 4 to 10 band. For a non-bleeding patient in this band the management is to hold warfarin and arrange close follow-up with a repeat INR; vitamin K is only considered, not mandatory. So stopping
kw: In addition to stop the warfarin
wo: A. Administer vitamin K: routinely given orally when INR is >10 without bleeding (or considered at 4 to 10 if bleeding risk is high); not required at INR 6 in a stable patient. | C. Administer fresh frozen plasma: reserved for active bleeding on warfarin, together with IV vitamin K; this patient is not bleeding. | D. Administer prothrombin complex concentrate: the preferred rapid reversal for major or life-threatening bleeding (for example intracranial), not for an isolated high INR.

q: A 47-year-old sexually active woman has a 5-year history of hypertension treated with medication. Her BMI is 37 kg/m². Which of the following screening tests is most appropriate?
k: Pick the screen that matches the risk factors in the stem: Obesity or overweight plus HTN, dyslipidemia, family history: diabetes (FPG or HbA1c) Average risk age ≥45: colorectal cancer screening Women 21 to 65: cervical
r: She is 47 with hypertension and BMI 37 , two strong risk factors for type 2 diabetes and features of metabolic syndrome. Adults who are overweight or obese with an additional risk factor such as hypertension, and all adults from age 35, should be screened for diabetes, so fasting blood glucose is th
wo: A. CT chest: not a screening test here; low-dose CT is for lung cancer screening in heavy smokers aged 50 to 80, and she has no smoking history. | B. Pap smear: routine cervical screening is still due every 3 to 5 years at her age, but nothing in the stem raises her cervical risk, whereas her obesity and hypertension point to diabetes screening as the targeted answer. | C. Annual fecal occult blood test: colorectal screening is due from 45, but the question is built around her metabolic risk factors; the targeted screen is glucose.

q: Man with Tonic-clonic movement more than 4 hours without regaining consciousness he known case of epilepsy not complain to medication
k: Status epilepticus: seizure ≥5 minutes or ≥2 seizures without recovery between them. ABC, oxygen, finger-stick glucose First line: IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam) or IM/buccal midazolam if no IV access Second lin
r: Continuous tonic-clonic activity without regaining consciousness in a non-compliant epileptic is status epilepticus. After airway, oxygen and a glucose check, the first-line drug is an IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam or midazolam), which terminates seizures quickly; the long duration does not
wo: B. IV infusion phenytoin: second line, given after (or alongside) the benzodiazepine if seizures persist; not the first drug. | C. Propofol: third line for refractory status epilepticus after benzodiazepines and a second-line agent fail, requiring intubation and ICU care. | D. Forgot (another version had phenobarbital): phenobarbital is a later-line agent, not first line.

q: Pt 80 year old brought by his family with worsening forgetfulness he forget place that he was familiar with and he is struggling to manage his finances . What do or how to manage this pt ?
k: Approach to suspected dementia: Step 1: history from patient and family, cognitive testing (MMSE, MoCA) Step 2: reversible causes: TSH, B12, glucose, electrolytes, calcium, renal and liver function, consider syphilis/HIV
r: An 80-year-old with progressive memory loss, getting lost in familiar places and struggling with finances has a pattern of dementia (likely Alzheimer type) with impaired daily function. Dementia is a clinical diagnosis , so the first step is a formal cognitive assessment (such as MMSE or MoCA plus f
wo: A. CT brain: part of the dementia work-up to exclude structural causes (subdural hematoma, tumor, normal pressure hydrocephalus), but it does not diagnose dementia and follows the clinical assessment; first choice if acute onset, head trauma or focal signs. | C. MRI: the preferred structural imaging when available (shows atrophy or vascular change), but again supports rather than makes the diagnosis.

q: Elder women with cancer in paltive care Become agateded Despite repeated attempts by the healthcare team to settle her, she remains agitated how to manage
k: Delirium/agitation in the elderly or palliative patient: Look for reversible causes: pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, drugs, infection First: non-pharmacological (reorientation, family, quiet room) Then: a
r: An elderly cancer patient in palliative care who becomes agitated has terminal delirium until proven otherwise. When non-pharmacological measures have failed , the drug of choice is an antipsychotic, and haloperidol is the standard first-line agent because it calms agitation without the respiratory
wo: B. Benzodiazepines: can worsen delirium and confusion in the elderly; reserved for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, seizures, or as an add-on (or for palliative sedation) when antipsychotics fail. | C. Propofol: a general anesthetic needing airway monitoring; not used for agitation on a palliative ward.

q: Pt with urine retention ,on amitriptyline what is the cause ?
k: Anticholinergic side effects: dry as a bone, red, hot, blind, mad, full bladder. Drugs: TCAs (amitriptyline), antihistamines, antipsychotics, oxybutynin, antiparkinson anticholinergics Effects: retention, constipation, d
r: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant with strong anticholinergic effects: it blocks muscarinic receptors on the detrusor, so the bladder cannot contract and urinary retention follows, often with constipation and abdominal distension. Underlying BPH makes this much more likely. Management is s
wo: B. Increased sympathetic activity can tighten the bladder neck (e.g. pain, decongestants), but the stem names an anticholinergic drug that explains retention and constipation together.

q: Pt with 3 sezure attack , na 121 plasma osmolarity 240 ,k 3.4 Urine osmolality 840 diagnosis?
k: Hypotonic hyponatraemia: check urine osmolality and volume status. SIADH: low serum osm, urine osm >100 (often >300), euvolaemic, urine Na >30, normal K Addison: low Na, high K, hypotension Conn and Cushing: normal/high
r: Hyponatraemia (Na 121) severe enough to cause seizures , with low plasma osmolality (240) and an inappropriately concentrated urine (840), is the SIADH pattern: excess ADH retains free water and dilutes sodium. The mildly low potassium (3.4) does not fit Addison disease, which typically raises potas
wo: A. Addison disease causes hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypotension, hyperpigmentation and often hypoglycaemia; here potassium is low (3.4).

q: Yong lady jundice , no family history of similar condition high bilirubin , low HB , normal plt .no results related to combs test or information about hx of gall stone or cholecystectomy or recent infect .diagnosis?
k: Haemolysis with spherocytes: HS vs warm AIHA. HS: family history, splenomegaly, gallstones, chronic course; osmotic fragility/EMA test, Coombs negative Warm AIHA: acquired, IgG, Coombs positive; associated with SLE, CLL,
r: A young woman with jaundice, low Hb and high bilirubin has haemolysis, and the stem goes out of its way to say there is no family history and no mention of gallstones or splenomegaly. Without the clues of a chronic inherited haemolysis, an acquired cause, warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia , is the
kw: no family history of similar condition
wo: B. Hereditary spherocytosis is autosomal dominant in most cases, so a family history, splenomegaly or pigment gallstones from chronic haemolysis would be expected; all are absent here.

q: A 35-Year-Old Man Presents To The Emergency Department Complaining Of Sudden-Onset Fatigue, Generalized Weakness, And Yellow Discoloration Of The Eyes And Skin. He Denies Recent Infections Or New Medications. On Physical Examination, He Is Mildly Icteric. No Lymphadenopathy Or Splenomegaly Is Noted. Investigations Reveal The Following: Hemoglobin: Low, Reticulocyte Count: Elevated , Platelet Count: Normal, Indirect (Unconjugated) Bilirubin: Elevated, Haptoglobin: Decreased. Abdominal Ultrasound: Multiple Gallstones . What Is The Most Likely Diagnosis?
k: Pick the haemolytic anaemia by the extra clue. Gallstones, splenomegaly, family history: HS None of these, young woman, Coombs positive: warm AIHA Dark morning urine, thrombosis, pancytopenia: PNH Low platelets + coagulo
r: The labs show haemolysis (low Hb, high reticulocytes, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin) with normal platelets. The decisive clue is multiple gallstones in a 35 year old man: pigment stones signal long standing haemolysis, which points to an inherited chronic cause, hereditary spherocytosis,
wo: A. PNH classically gives dark morning urine (intravascular haemolysis), thrombosis in unusual sites and often cytopenias; platelets are normal here and none of these features are described. | C. Warm AIHA is acquired and usually acute, with no reason for gallstones; it would be favoured if gallstones, splenomegaly and family history were all absent, as in NOV-0769. | D. DIC causes low platelets, prolonged PT/APTT and schistocytes in a severely ill patient (sepsis, trauma, obstetric); platelets are normal here.

q: 60 YO COPD with 4 yr cough . Wbc 3.8 temp 36.6 What to do?
k: COPD investigation ladder. Symptoms suggest COPD: spirometry (post bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7) COPD confirmed: test alpha 1 antitrypsin once Bronchiectasis features: HRCT Exacerbation with fever/purulent sputum: sputum
r: The recaller clarified this is a known case of COPD with a chronic stable cough and no exacerbation (afebrile 36.6, WBC 3.8 not raised) and no features of another disease. Current GOLD and WHO advice is that every patient diagnosed with COPD should be tested once for alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency ,
wo: B. Sputum culture is for an infective exacerbation (fever, purulent sputum, raised WBC) or suspected TB/bronchiectasis; this patient is stable and afebrile. | C. HRCT is chosen when the diagnosis is not yet made or another disease is suspected, e.g. bronchiectasis (large purulent sputum, recurrent infection, clubbing) or fibrosis; lung cancer screening uses low dose CT, not HRCT.

q: A 60 year old man has symptoms suggestive of COPD . He has a 40 year history of smoking but stopped smoking 5 years ago . What is the next appropriate step in management?
k: Diagnosed vs suspected COPD decides the answer. Suspected: spirometry (if absent from options, HRCT per this recall) Spirometry shows obstruction or known COPD: AAT level Bronchiectasis features: HRCT Lung cancer screeni
r: The stem says only symptoms suggestive of COPD , so the diagnosis is not yet established. Alpha 1 antitrypsin testing is done after COPD is diagnosed, so this recall's key is HRCT as the available test to confirm the structural picture (emphysema) and exclude other causes in a 40 year smoker. In pra
wo: A. Bronchoscopy is for suspected endobronchial tumour, haemoptysis or sampling; it does not diagnose COPD. | B. Sputum culture is for infective exacerbations or suspected TB; no infection is described. | C. Alpha 1 antitrypsin level is ordered once COPD is diagnosed (as in NOV-0772 and NOV-0774); here the diagnosis is not yet made.

q: A patient presented to the clinic with a 3-year history of dyspnea and cough with sputum , the patient quit smoking 5 years ago "It was a long case"+ temperature was normal The pulmonary function test showed an FEV1/FVC ratio <0.6 and FEV1 around 55% (not sure about the FEV1 value but around this number) What is the next or most appropriate investigation?
k: After spirometry confirms COPD. Classify severity: GOLD 1 FEV1 ≥80%, GOLD 2 50 to 79%, GOLD 3 30 to 49%, GOLD 4 <30% Check AAT once in every patient Think AATD especially if young, basal emphysema, minimal smoking, liver
r: Spirometry is already done and shows FEV1/FVC <0.6 with FEV1 about 55% : fixed airflow obstruction in an ex smoker with chronic productive cough, i.e. COPD is diagnosed (moderate, GOLD 2). Afebrile with no exacerbation features, so the next investigation is a one time alpha 1 antitrypsin level, reco
wo: A. Bronchoscopy is for suspected malignancy, haemoptysis or foreign body; nothing here suggests these. | B. HRCT is for suspected bronchiectasis (large purulent sputum, recurrent infections, clubbing) or interstitial disease, not routine in confirmed COPD; lung cancer screening uses low dose CT. | D. Sputum culture fits an infective exacerbation with fever and purulent sputum; temperature is normal.

q: Pneumonia admitted to ICU what to add to azithromycin ?
k: CAP empiric therapy by setting. Outpatient healthy: amoxicillin or macrolide/doxycycline Outpatient comorbid: amoxicillin clavulanate + macrolide, or respiratory FQ alone Ward: beta lactam + macrolide, or respiratory FQ
r: Severe community acquired pneumonia needing ICU is treated with a beta lactam plus a macrolide (or beta lactam plus respiratory fluoroquinolone). The patient is already on azithromycin for atypical cover, so the missing piece is a beta lactam: ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus and gram negatives.
wo: A. Moxifloxacin duplicates the atypical cover of azithromycin and both prolong QT; a fluoroquinolone replaces the macrolide alongside a beta lactam, it is not added to one.

q: Meningitis prophylaxis for household contacts ?
k: Meningococcal contact prophylaxis. Who: household and close contacts, those exposed to oral secretions Rifampicin: 2 days, twice daily Ceftriaxone: single IM dose (safe in pregnancy) Ciprofloxacin: single oral dose Hib c
r: Close household contacts of meningococcal meningitis need chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible. Accepted options are single dose IM ceftriaxone , single dose oral ciprofloxacin, or rifampicin twice daily for 2 days. Ceftriaxone is the listed valid option and is the choice in pregnancy.
wo: B. Doxycycline plus rifampicin is the regimen for brucellosis, not meningitis prophylaxis; rifampicin alone (2 days) would be correct.

q: ejection systolic murmur , increase with inspiration , jvp a wave
k: Murmur that increases with inspiration = right sided lesion. Ejection systolic, left 2nd ICS, ejection click, RV heave: pulmonary stenosis Ejection systolic, right 2nd ICS, radiates to carotids: aortic stenosis (louder o

A prominent JVP a wave means a stiff, hypertrophied right ventricle that the right atrium has to contract hard against, which is typical of pulmonary stenosis. The f
wo: A. Tricuspid stenosis also raises the a wave and increases with inspiration, but its murmur is a mid diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal edge, not an ejection systolic murmur.

q: ascitic tap show polymorph 400 management

SBP is treated immediately with intravenous antibiotics , a third generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone (or cefotax
wo: A. Fluid restriction is only for cirrhotic ascites with significant hyponatraemia; it does not treat an infection. | B. Oral spironolactone is the first diuretic for uncomplicated cirrhotic ascites (neutrophils below 250) after salt restriction; it does nothing for SBP. | D. Therapeutic large volume paracentesis is for tense or diuretic refractory ascites; with untreated SBP the priority is antibiotics.

q: alcholic came with hematamesis what is the cause?
k: Haematemesis in an alcoholic: think varices, Mallory-Weiss, ulcer. Chronic liver disease signs + massive bleed: varices (portal hypertension) Repeated retching or vomiting after binge, then blood: Mallory-Weiss tear Epig

q: 71 years male no DM no medication not smoking BP 171/90 Cholesterol 6.1 HDL 1 Calculate cardiovascular risk based on picture:
k: Reading a risk chart: pick the right table, then row, then column. Table: sex, diabetes, smoker Block: age band (use nearest) Row: systolic BP; column: TC/HDL ratio Biggest drivers: age, then SBP and smoking 10 year risk
r: On a 10 year cardiovascular risk chart, risk is read from sex, diabetes, smoking, age, systolic BP and total cholesterol to HDL ratio. A man over 70 with systolic BP 171 and a total cholesterol/HDL ratio of about 6 (6.1/1) sits in the highest band even as a non diabetic non smoker, because age and S
wo: A. 10 to 19% would fit a younger man or one with lower BP or a lower cholesterol ratio; at over 70 with SBP above 160 the chart moves to the top band. | B. 20 to 24% underestimates the combined effect of age over 70, SBP of 171 and a ratio of 6. | C. 25 to 29% is still one band too low; the combination of high SBP and high ratio at this age reaches the highest colour.

q: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with chronic pain and stiffness of his fingers. Physical examination reveals joint tenderness with limited range of motion. Laboratory tests show ESR within normal limits and negative rheumatoid factor . See the photo Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Hand OA vs RA: OA: DIP (Heberden) and PIP (Bouchard), first CMC; spares MCP and wrist OA: morning stiffness under 30 minutes, normal ESR, negative RF RA: MCP, PIP, wrist; DIP spared; stiffness over 1 hour Psoriatic: DIP
r: A 68 year old with chronic finger pain and stiffness, normal ESR and negative RF has a non inflammatory arthritis, and the photo shows bony interphalangeal nodes (Heberden at DIP, Bouchard at PIP). This is hand osteoarthritis , a degenerative cartilage disease with short morning stiffness and pain w
wo: B. Diabetic neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy affects weight bearing joints, mainly the foot and ankle, with a swollen, deformed, relatively painless joint, not the fingers. | C. Rheumatoid arthritis involves MCP, PIP and wrists symmetrically with spared DIPs, prolonged morning stiffness, raised ESR/CRP and usually positive RF or anti CCP. | D. Gout presents with acute, red, hot attacks (often the first MTP) or tophi, with raised inflammatory markers during flares; not chronic nodal finger stiffness.

q: 52 years old patient, pain affecting PIP and DIP and his left knee Rheumatoid factor is normal ESR elevated No skin manifestation
k: DIP joint involvement: OA or psoriatic arthritis, not RA. OA: DIP + PIP + knee/hip, bony nodes, mechanical pain Psoriatic: DIP + nails/skin, dactylitis, pencil in cup on X ray RA: MCP, PIP, wrist, symmetric, RF/anti CCP
r: Pain in the PIP and DIP joints with a weight bearing joint ( left knee ) in a 52 year old , with normal RF, no skin disease and nodal hand changes on the photo, is the typical pattern of osteoarthritis . A mildly raised ESR is non specific at this age and does not override the joint pattern; erosive
wo: B. Rheumatoid arthritis spares the DIP joints and affects MCPs and wrists symmetrically with long morning stiffness; normal RF also argues against it. | C. Psoriatic arthritis does involve DIPs and can be asymmetric with a knee, but needs psoriasis, nail pitting or dactylitis; the stem stresses "no skin manifestation".

q: Patient came with SOB and fatigue . He was stable . ECG: showed bradycardia (same pic, Dx not written). Next step in the management?
k: Symptomatic bradycardia (HR < 50 with symptoms): ABCs, oxygen, IV access, 12 lead ECG, look for reversible causes (drugs, hyperkalaemia, ischaemia) First: atropine 1 mg IV, repeat to max 3 mg Atropine fails: transcutaneo
r: A patient with bradycardia causing symptoms ( shortness of breath and fatigue ) needs treatment, and the first drug in the bradycardia algorithm is IV atropine (1 mg, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes up to 3 mg). If atropine fails, the next steps are transcutaneous pacing or infusions of dopamine or ep
wo: A. Cardioversion treats tachyarrhythmias (unstable SVT, AF, VT); it has no role in bradycardia, where pacing is the electrical therapy. | C. Aspirin is for acute coronary syndrome; it does not raise the heart rate, though an inferior MI causing bradycardia would also need it after rate support. | D. Dual antiplatelet therapy is for ACS or after stenting, not first line for symptomatic bradycardia.

q: (Recall context written in Arabic on the page: a female patient, clearly iron deficiency anaemia.) Which of the following Definitive to confirmed the cause of her underlying condition:
k: Iron studies: IDA: low ferritin, low iron, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation, low MCV, high RDW Anaemia of chronic disease: high/normal ferritin, low iron, low TIBC Best initial test: serum ferritin Gold standard: bo
r: The red word is definitive . Serum tests can only infer body iron stores, whereas a bone marrow biopsy with Prussian blue iron stain directly shows absent stainable iron and is the gold standard for confirming iron deficiency. It is invasive and rarely needed in practice (ferritin is the best first
wo: A. Serum ferritin is the best initial and most useful non invasive test (low ferritin is diagnostic), but it is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal in inflammation, so it is not the definitive test. | B. Serum iron is low in IDA but fluctuates through the day and with meals and is also low in anaemia of chronic disease, so it is not specific. | D. TIBC is high in IDA (low in anaemia of chronic disease) and helps differentiate them, but it is an indirect marker.

q: 60 years old male present with jaundice for 2 months (he was asymptomatic no added info just us finding it was very short Q) Us showed liver cirrhosis with 2 lesions What is the cause of his condition?
k: HCC risk factors: Hepatitis B (most common worldwide; can cause HCC without cirrhosis) Hepatitis C, alcohol, NAFLD via cirrhosis Aflatoxin (Aspergillus, peanuts/grains), haemochromatosis Marker: AFP; lesion > 1 cm in cir
r: A cirrhotic liver with focal lesions in a 60 year old with jaundice is hepatocellular carcinoma until proven otherwise. Among the options, aflatoxin (a mycotoxin from Aspergillus contaminating stored grains and peanuts) is a recognized hepatocarcinogen that causes p53 mutations and acts synergistica
wo: B. Lead poisoning causes microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling, abdominal colic, neuropathy (wrist drop) and encephalopathy; it is not a cause of cirrhosis or HCC. | C. Not recalled; if it was hepatitis B or C, that would be the stronger association (HBV most common worldwide, HCV and alcohol common in the West).

q: A man presents to a family medicine clinic with multiple pustular lesions involving his beard area after shaving . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Follicle infections by depth: Folliculitis: superficial pustules on hair follicles (beard after shaving) Furuncle: deep painful nodule around one follicle Carbuncle: several furuncles joined together Pseudofolliculitis b
wo: A. Option not recalled. If it was furuncle (offered in earlier versions): a deep, painful, tender nodule with pus around one follicle, chosen when the lesion is deep or discharging. | B. Option not recalled. If it was carbuncle (offered in earlier versions): several furuncles joined into a large tender mass with multiple draining points, often on the back of the neck in diabetics. | C. Option not recalled. If it was impetigo (offered in earlier versions): honey crusted erosions, usually in children around the nose and mouth, not pustules centred on hairs. | D. Ingrown hair reaction (pseudofolliculitis barbae) is a foreign body reaction to curly hairs re entering the skin after close shaving; it would be right if the stem stressed curly hair, papules more than pustules, and visible ingrown hairs.

q: A women presented to the ER due to physical injuries caused by severe beating from her husband what is the most Appropriate next action ?
k: ER approach to intimate partner violence: Treat injuries and assess immediate safety Interview alone, document injuries carefully Safety plan and referral to social services or protection programs Know local law: mandato

q: 55 women opd, abdominal injury after fall during gardening , and gp provided preventative strategies , which prevents methods is preferred?
k: Fall prevention in older adults, evidence based measures: Exercise for strength and balance (e.g. tai chi): the most effective single intervention Medication review (sedatives, antihypertensives) Home hazard modification
r: This recall's key is maintain healthy weight , chosen as general preventive counselling for a 55 year old woman after an injury from a fall while gardening . Weight control supports mobility, balance and joint health, and in a postmenopausal woman both obesity and very low weight contribute to fall
wo: A. Increasing calcium intake (with vitamin D) helps prevent fractures from osteoporosis after menopause, but it does not prevent falls themselves. | B. Hand hygiene prevents infection spread and is unrelated to preventing a fall injury. | C. Avoiding aggressive sports is irrelevant here: the injury happened during gardening, a low intensity activity.

q: Child old boy fall in school and injured his head , teacher took him to hospital . The doctor found 6 cm laceration in his scalp . The boy is stable and the doctor want to suture the wound . What is most appropriate course of action?
o: Wait for consent from one of parents
k: Consent in minors. Non emergency: consent from at least one parent or legal guardian Emergency (life or limb threatening): treat without waiting Teacher, neighbor, relative escort: cannot consent Minor exceptions: contra
r: The child is a minor, he is stable , and suturing a 6 cm scalp laceration is not a life saving emergency, so the doctor must obtain consent from a parent or legal guardian. The consent of one parent is enough; both are not needed. Waiting for a parent is the appropriate course while the wound is cle
wo: A. Patient can give consent: minors cannot consent to routine treatment, except for specific exceptions (contraception, STD care, prenatal care, substance abuse treatment) or emancipated minors. | C. Take consent from teacher: a teacher, neighbor or other adult escort is not a legal guardian and cannot consent. | D. Option not recalled; if it was 'proceed without consent', that is right only in a true emergency where delay would threaten life or limb.

q: it was a patient who did surgery (i think it was appendictomy, im not sure but it was a small surgery), he was admitted to the hospital, day 3 post surgery you made rounds with the team, he was alert and communicating well with the team, what should be done at this point?
k: Daily postoperative round checklist: review and remove unnecessary devices. Urinary catheter: remove as early as possible (prevent CAUTI) IV lines: remove or resite if not needed (prevent phlebitis/CLABSI) Drains: remove
r: On day 3 after a minor operation, an alert, communicating patient no longer needs indwelling devices. Routine postoperative rounds include reviewing lines and urinary catheters and removing those that are not needed, because every extra catheter day raises the risk of catheter associated urinary tra
wo: A. Reassurance alone skips a concrete patient safety task; it would fit only if the question were about an anxious patient with no devices in place. | B. Option not recalled; choices such as routine labs or imaging are not indicated in a well, alert patient. | C. Option not recalled; anything that adds intervention rather than de-escalating care does not fit a patient recovering normally.

q: A patient with hypertension was taking an ACE inhibitor and another medication with a name similar to morphine . The patient underwent surgery. Postoperatively, he was given morphine FOR pain The question asked: Where was the error something like this
o: Inadequate assessment/evaluation of the patient postoperatively
k: Medication reconciliation: complete, compare, resolve at every care transition. Done at admission, transfer between units and discharge Prevents omissions, duplications, interactions and look-alike sound-alike errors Loo
r: The patient's home medication (with a sound-alike name to morphine) was not captured and compared against the new postoperative orders, so morphine was prescribed without accounting for it. That is a failure of medication reconciliation , the process of obtaining a complete medication list at each t
wo: A. A pharmacist error would be dispensing the wrong drug or dose from a correct order; here the prescriber's order itself was made without a reconciled medication list. | C. Inadequate postoperative assessment would be the answer if the harm came from missed clinical signs (for example unrecognized respiratory depression); the root error here is the undocumented home medications. | D. This option was not recalled, so it cannot be assessed; in the other version the remaining options (manufacturer error, poor postoperative assessment) do not address the missing medication list.

q: Patient with wood stick injury question mentioned it involves the sclera and the eye was bleeding and patient was unable to move his eye and in severe pain. On examination, he has Teardrop pupil and Cloudy anterior chamber What is the type of injury? (It Was Metallic Object In Another Recall)
k: Open globe: protect, do not press. Signs: teardrop pupil, shallow or cloudy anterior chamber, hyphema, positive Seidel test, low intraocular pressure Do not measure IOP or apply pressure; place a rigid shield Do not remo
r: Penetrating trauma by a stick involving the sclera , with a teardrop (peaked) pupil , bleeding and a cloudy anterior chamber (hyphema or exudate), indicates a full-thickness wound of the eye wall, an open globe injury. The pupil peaks toward the wound because the iris is drawn into or prolapses thro
wo: A. A corneal laceration is limited to the cornea; this injury involves the sclera, and the umbrella diagnosis for any full-thickness corneal or scleral wound is open globe injury. | C. q: A 67-year-old woman presents for cervical cancer screening. She has a history of normal Pap smear results over the past 10 years . What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue Pap smear screening every 3 years
k: Cervical cancer screening (average risk). Start at 21 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years 30 to 65: co-test or primary HPV every 5 years (or cytology every 3) Stop after 65 if adequate negative prior screening History of CI
r: She is 67 years old (older than 65) with normal Pap results over the past 10 years , which counts as adequate negative prior screening. Cervical cancer screening stops after age 65 in women with adequate negative screening and no history of high grade lesions. Continuing screening adds no benefit at
kw: normal Pap smear results over the past 10 years
wo: B. Pap every 3 years: the schedule for ages 21 to 29 (or 30 to 65 with cytology alone); it does not apply after 65 with negative history. | C. Annual Pap smear: not recommended at any age for average risk women; intervals are 3 to 5 years. | D. HPV testing: primary HPV or co-testing every 5 years is used between 30 and 65; after 65 with adequate negative screening no further testing is needed.

q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester presents with dyspnea . What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Reassure her that dyspnea is a normal physiological change during pregnancy due to increased blood volume.
Explain that it is due to physiological anemia of pregnancy and advise her to increase her intake of iron-rich foods.
k: Physiological dyspnea of pregnancy. Common from the first trimester Main driver: progesterone increases respiratory drive and tidal volume (mild respiratory alkalosis) Blood volume rises 40 to 45% by 32 to 34 weeks Red f
r: Breathlessness in early pregnancy without other alarming features is a common physiological change, so the appropriate advice is reassurance. Pregnancy brings major cardiorespiratory changes, including blood volume rising from about 6 weeks and increased ventilation, and many women feel short of bre
wo: B. Physiological anemia of pregnancy: is a dilutional effect (plasma rises more than red cells) that does not usually cause dyspnea, and iron rich food advice would be for true iron deficiency, not this complaint.

q: A woman presents with amenorrhea for 9 months . Her evaluation is otherwise normal, except for an elevated Labs:- serum FSH level of 60 IU/L. LH 60 Testosterone, TSH ARE normal Which of the following long term complications is she most at risk of developing?
k: High FSH/LH + amenorrhea = ovarian failure = low estrogen = bone and heart risk. High FSH, high LH, low estrogen: POI / menopause, risk osteoporosis Normal or high estrogen, anovulation (PCOS): risk endometrial hyperplas
r: Secondary amenorrhea for 9 months with FSH 60 and LH 60 (both high) and normal TSH and testosterone means the ovaries have failed: hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, i.e. premature ovarian insufficiency in a young woman. The defining hormonal problem is estrogen deficiency , and the classic long term c
wo: A. Endometrial cancer is driven by unopposed estrogen (anovulation as in PCOS, obesity, estrogen-only HRT); here estrogen is low, so the endometrium is not stimulated. | B. Ovarian cancer risk rises with incessant ovulation, nulliparity and BRCA mutations; ovarian failure does not raise it. | D. Fourth option not recalled; any choice not linked to estrogen deficiency would not fit this hormone picture.

q: Pregnant woman BMI 37 , will do total hysterectomy what is the best VTE prophylaxis
k: VTE prophylaxis in pregnancy and postpartum. Agent of choice: LMWH (no placental transfer) Warfarin: avoid in pregnancy (teratogenic), safe in breastfeeding Risk factors: obesity, cesarean or pelvic surgery, previous VTE
r: This woman stacks major VTE risk factors: pregnancy (a hypercoagulable state), obesity (BMI 37) and major pelvic surgery (hysterectomy) . High risk surgical patients need pharmacological prophylaxis, and LMWH is the agent of choice in pregnancy and the puerperium because it does not cross the placen
wo: B. Compression stockings alone are for patients with low risk or a contraindication to anticoagulation (active bleeding, high bleeding risk); with this many risk factors they are an adjunct to LMWH.

q: Missed abortion at 8 weeks what is the management:
k: Miscarriage management by type. Threatened: reassurance Missed (stable): expectant, misoprostol, or suction evacuation Inevitable or incomplete with heavy bleeding or instability: surgical evacuation (D&C / suction) Sept
r: A missed abortion at 8 weeks (non viable pregnancy with a closed cervix and retained products) in a stable woman can be managed expectantly, medically or surgically. Expectant management is not offered, so medical evacuation with misoprostol (a prostaglandin E1 analogue that ripens the cervix and ca
wo: B. Hysterectomy is never a treatment for miscarriage; it is reserved for life threatening hemorrhage not controlled by other means. | C. Methotrexate is for an ectopic pregnancy (stable, unruptured, criteria met) or for some gestational trophoblastic disease, not an intrauterine miscarriage. | D. Hypertonic saline instillation is an obsolete second trimester termination method with serious risks; it has no role at 8 weeks.

q: 39wks gestation Spontaneus rupture for 24 hours ; everything else is normal. What is the next step:
k: PROM management by gestational age. At or after 37 weeks: induction of labor (oxytocin) 34 to 36 weeks: delivery is generally advised Below 34 weeks without infection: expectant, steroids, latency antibiotics (erythromyc
r: Rupture of membranes at 39 weeks without labor for 24 hours is term PROM. The risk of chorioamnionitis and neonatal infection increases with time from rupture, and at term there is no benefit to prolonging the pregnancy, so with a cephalic fetus and otherwise normal findings the next step is inducti
wo: A. Conservative (expectant) management is an option only for a short period after term PROM, or is the standard for preterm PROM (PPROM) without infection where fetal maturity is the aim; after 24 hours at term it raises infection risk.

q: 21 years old female , complains of heavy menstrual bleeding for the previous 2 years. Low hb There is US pic of uterus What is the diagnosis:
k: Fibroid types and symptoms. Submucosal: heavy menstrual bleeding and infertility Intramural: bleeding and bulk symptoms Subserosal: pressure symptoms only Diagnosis: pelvic ultrasound; hysteroscopy for submucosal Enlarge
r: A young woman with heavy menstrual bleeding for 2 years causing anemia and an ultrasound showing a uterine lesion fits uterine leiomyoma (fibroid). Fibroids, especially submucosal ones, enlarge the endometrial surface and impair contraction, causing heavy regular periods; ultrasound is the initial i
wo: A. Pregnancy causes amenorrhea, not 2 years of heavy menses; ultrasound would show a gestational sac. | B. Ovarian cysts are adnexal masses that usually cause pain or no symptoms, not heavy regular menstrual bleeding with a uterine lesion. | C. Endometrial cancer typically presents with postmenopausal bleeding in older women with estrogen excess; very unlikely at 21.

q: female with vulvar pain, on examination there is an ulcer in labia minora , ragged edges , necrotic center , and regional lymphadenopathy (pic provided) What is the Diagnosis?
k: Genital ulcer: decide by pain, base and nodes. Chancroid: painful, ragged, necrotic/purulent base, tender suppurative nodes Primary syphilis: painless, clean base, indurated sharp edge, non-tender nodes HSV: multiple pai
r: A painful vulvar ulcer with ragged edges , a necrotic base and regional (inguinal) lymphadenopathy is the classic picture of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi . The nodes may become fluctuant buboes that can rupture. Vulvar pain plus a dirty, undermined ulcer is the decisive pairing.
wo: B. HIV is not a cause of a single necrotic genital ulcer; acute HIV gives a flu-like illness with generalized lymphadenopathy. Think HIV when there is fever, generalized nodes and opportunistic infections such as oral candidiasis. | C. Herpes zoster gives grouped vesicles in a dermatomal band with burning pain, not a single ragged necrotic ulcer. Genital herpes (HSV) would show multiple small painful shallow ulcers on an erythematous base.

q: Female has progressive dysmenorrhea and pelvic heaviness in US THERE IS palpable mass
o: ovarian cyst or utuerine cyst (one of them)
k: Dysmenorrhea plus pelvic finding: Firm palpable mass, heaviness, menorrhagia = leiomyoma Diffusely bulky tender uterus, older multiparous = adenomyosis Dyspareunia, dyschezia, infertility, chocolate cyst = endometriosis
r: Progressive dysmenorrhea with pelvic heaviness and a palpable (firm) pelvic mass fits a uterine leiomyoma (fibroid). Fibroids enlarge the uterus, causing pressure symptoms, heavy and painful periods, and a mass that moves with the uterus on examination and ultrasound.
wo: A. An ovarian cyst is usually asymptomatic or causes unilateral adnexal pain; it does not typically cause progressive dysmenorrhea. Choose it when a separate adnexal cystic mass is described, especially with acute pain from torsion or rupture. | C. PID presents with pelvic pain, fever, discharge and cervical motion tenderness, not a palpable firm mass with gradually progressive dysmenorrhea. A tubo-ovarian abscess would be a tender complex adnexal mass with fever. | D. This option is an unclear or garbled recall item and does not describe a diagnosis; in the lookalike the fourth option was anovulation, which causes irregular bleeding without a mass or dysmenorrhea.

q: A 28-year-old woman complains of pelvic pressure and heavy bleeding .after marriage . On examination, she has pelvic tenderness . What is the diagnosis?
k: Young, sexually active, pelvic tenderness = think infection first. PID: pelvic pain, tenderness, abnormal bleeding, discharge, fever Adenomyosis: age 40 to 50, multiparity, prior uterine surgery, bulky tender uterus Endo
r: This recall's key is PID because of the young age (28) , onset after marriage (new sexual exposure) and pelvic tenderness . Pelvic pressure is nonspecific and occurs in subacute PID, and abnormal or heavy uterine bleeding is reported in a substantial share of PID patients. Adenomyosis is less likely
wo: B. Adenomyosis gives heavy painful periods with a diffusely bulky tender uterus, but usually in older multiparous women or after C-section, D&C or myomectomy. Choose it when those risk factors and a bulky uterus are described. | C. Endometriosis presents with cyclic pain, dyspareunia, dyschezia and infertility rather than heavy bleeding after marriage. Choose it for a nulliparous woman with the 3 Ds or a chocolate cyst on ultrasound.

q: Baby delivered dead at 38 wks ( Stillbirth case). Placenta and baby appear normal Which of the following is best to sent for investigations for chromosomal analysis ?
k: Stillbirth genetic testing sample: Before delivery: amniocentesis (highest yield) After delivery: placental tissue (chorionic plate below cord insertion) Additional: umbilical cord segment, fetal skin or internal tissue
r: After a stillbirth, fetal cells in blood and skin may be nonviable, so culture often fails. Placental tissue (a sample of the chorionic plate near the cord insertion) has the highest yield of viable cells for karyotype or chromosomal microarray after delivery, even when the placenta looks normal, be
wo: A. A segment of umbilical cord is an acceptable additional sample, but it gives a lower yield of viable cells than placental tissue. | B. Amniotic fluid (by amniocentesis) is the best sample before delivery, when the fetal death is diagnosed in utero; after the baby is delivered it is no longer available. | C. Fetal cord blood is often clotted and contains no viable dividing cells after fetal death, so it frequently fails to culture.

q: Question about 30 years G2p1 with past hx of pph and now 50% singlton pregnancy What the risk of pph in her current pregnancy
k: PPH causes (4 Ts) and risk factors: Tone (atony, most common): overdistension (twins, macrosomia, polyhydramnios), prolonged or precipitous labor, grand multiparity, chorioamnionitis Trauma: lacerations, instrumental del
r: The stem gives a past history of PPH and a singleton pregnancy in a G2P1 aged 30. A previous PPH is one of the strongest predictors of PPH in a subsequent pregnancy, so it is her risk factor. The other options are excluded by the stem itself.
wo: B. Multiple pregnancy overdistends the uterus and causes atony, but this pregnancy is a singleton; choose it when twins are described. | C. Grand multiparity (usually 5 or more births) is a risk factor, but she is only para 1. | D. Advanced maternal age (35 or older) raises PPH risk; at 30 she is not in that group.

q: Patient with ovarian cancer asking what is the best form of contraception?
k: Contraception in gynecologic cancers (eligibility): Ovarian cancer: hormonal methods, including combined pills, Category 1 Endometrial cancer: hormonal methods allowed; IUD insertion restricted while awaiting treatment C
r: Ovarian cancer is Category 1 (no restriction) for combined hormonal contraception in the medical eligibility criteria, because combined pills do not worsen ovarian cancer and in fact long-term use lowers ovarian cancer risk. The compiler's key is the OCP as a safe, highly effective method while the
wo: A. The vaginal ring is also combined hormonal contraception and has the same eligibility category; it is not wrong medically, but the classic expected answer in this recall is the OCP. | B. Male condoms are safe for anyone but have a much higher typical-use failure rate, so they are not the best form when an effective hormonal method is allowed.

q: A 25-year-old woman, known to have a left ovarian cyst , presented to the Emergency Room with 3 hours of severe left lower quadrant pain associated with nausea. Ultrasound Doppler: Diminished blood flow toward the left ovary . Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
k: Ovarian torsion: clinical diagnosis supported by reduced Doppler flow, treated by urgent laparoscopy. Clues: sudden unilateral pelvic pain, nausea and vomiting, adnexal mass (often over 5 cm) Normal Doppler flow does not
r: A young woman with a known ovarian cyst , sudden severe unilateral pain with nausea , and diminished Doppler flow to that ovary has ovarian torsion . This is a surgical emergency: laparoscopy to detort the ovary and remove the causative cyst (cystectomy) to preserve the ovary.
kw: Diminished blood flow toward the left ovary
wo: A. Conservative management: delay leads to ovarian necrosis and loss; conservative care fits an uncomplicated simple cyst with normal flow. | B. Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours: wastes the window to salvage the ovary; repeat imaging is for a stable, asymptomatic simple cyst. | D. Ultrasound-guided drainage: does not untwist the pedicle and simple cysts recur; it has no role in torsion.

q: A woman in her thirties had a Pap smear 3 years ago that was negative . She now asks about cervical cancer screening. What is the recommended screening?
o: Co-testing (Pap smear and HPV) every year
k: Cervical screening (average risk): Under 21: no screening 21 to 29: Pap (cytology) every 3 years 30 to 65: Pap every 3 years, HPV every 5 years, or co-test every 5 years Over 65 with adequate negative history: stop After
r: For a woman in her thirties with a negative last Pap, the accepted screening intervals are cytology alone every 3 years , primary HPV testing every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years. Of the listed options only Pap smear every 3 years matches a recommended schedule.
kw: Pap smear 3 years ago that was negative
wo: A. HPV testing every year alone: primary HPV testing is done every 5 years from age 30 (25 in some guidelines), not yearly. | C. Co-testing every year: co-testing is every 5 years; annual screening adds harm without benefit. | D. No further screening: screening continues to 65 provided prior results are adequate and negative.

q: A female with a history of ectopic pregnancy is asking about the chance of recurrence in a future pregnancy. What is the chance of recurrence?
k: Ectopic pregnancy recurrence and risk factors. General population: about 1 to 2% of pregnancies After one ectopic: about 10 to 15% After two or more: about 25% or higher Strongest risk factor: previous ectopic; commonest
r: After one previous ectopic pregnancy the risk of recurrence in a later pregnancy is about 10 to 15% , which falls within the 6 to 15% option. It rises further (around 25% or more) after two ectopics, so early ultrasound is advised in every future pregnancy.
wo: A. 1-5%: closer to the background rate of ectopic pregnancy in the general population (about 1 to 2%), not the risk after a previous ectopic. | C. 50-60%: greatly overstates the risk; most women with a prior ectopic go on to have an intrauterine pregnancy. | D. (forgot): the option was not recalled; the accepted figure of about 10 to 15% still points to 6 to 15%.

q: A 25-year-old woman was diagnosed with a complete abortion at 10 weeks of gestation. She is a heavy smoker , smoking more than 20 cigarettes a day, and was not taking any folic acid or dietary supplements. Which of the following is the most likely risk factor that caused the miscarriage?
o: Smoking more than 20 cigarettes a day
k: Miscarriage risk factors. Most common cause overall: fetal chromosomal abnormality Maternal age over 35 and prior miscarriage Smoking, alcohol, cocaine, heavy caffeine Uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid disease, antiphosphol
r: Of the options, heavy smoking (over 20 cigarettes a day) is the identifiable, established risk factor for first-trimester miscarriage. Nicotine and carbon monoxide cause placental vasoconstriction and uteroplacental insufficiency, raising the risk of miscarriage, growth restriction and abruption.
wo: A. Diet low in carotene: not an established cause of miscarriage. | B. Diet low in folic acid: folate deficiency mainly raises the risk of neural tube defects; it is not the main miscarriage risk here. | C. No known risk factor: most sporadic early losses are chromosomal, but this stem gives a clear modifiable risk factor, so this is not the best answer.

q: A 31-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 had an uneventful pregnancy and went into spontaneous vaginal delivery. She delivered a healthy boy weighing 3000 g. After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in managing this patient?
o: Start blood transfusion with O negative blood
Send blood tests and manage accordingly
Take her to the operating room for surgical management
Call for help and make sure there is cross-matched blood
k: PPH: resuscitate and treat the cause (4 Ts) in parallel. Call for help, 2 large-bore IV lines, cross-match blood Check tone: uterine massage, oxytocin, then other uterotonics Tissue, trauma, thrombin as causes Refractory
r: Heavy bleeding after placental delivery is primary postpartum hemorrhage, an obstetric emergency where the first actions are to call for help (mobilize the team) and secure blood by cross-matching , alongside checking uterine tone, IV access and uterotonics. Among the options, this is the initial st
kw: After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily
wo: A. Emergency O negative transfusion is for massive hemorrhage with instability when cross-matched blood is not yet available; it is not the first step in a patient not yet assessed. | B. Sending blood tests and waiting to 'manage accordingly' delays active resuscitation; labs are drawn while the team acts, not before. | C. Theatre (surgical management) is for PPH that fails uterine massage, uterotonics and balloon tamponade, or for retained tissue or tears needing repair under anesthesia.

q: A 33-year-old G3 at 24 weeks of gestation presents with vaginal discharge and PPROM is assessed by sterile speculum examination. Which protein helps diagnose PPROM?
k: Diagnosing rupture of membranes. Sterile speculum: pooling in posterior fornix (confirms) Nitrazine (alkaline pH) and ferning: supportive, false positives with blood, semen, infection Protein assays: PAMG-1, IGFBP-1 when
r: Placental alpha-microglobulin-1 (PAMG-1) is a protein present in high concentration in amniotic fluid and very low in cervicovaginal secretions, so its detection in a vaginal swab (a commercial bedside immunoassay) supports rupture of membranes. PPROM is primarily diagnosed clinically by sterile spe
wo: A. Placental protein 14 (glycodelin) is a decidual/endometrial protein not used to diagnose ROM; do not confuse it with placental protein 12 (IGFBP-1), which is the other validated rupture test besides PAMG-1. | B. Placental alkaline phosphatase is a placental enzyme (and tumor marker) with no role in diagnosing membrane rupture. | C. Placental vasopressinase degrades ADH and explains transient diabetes insipidus of pregnancy; it is not used to diagnose PPROM.

q: 40 years old woman with lower abdominal pain , no bleeding , pregnancy test was negative on examination cervical motion tenderness and closed What the diagnosis
k: PID diagnosis (minimum criteria in a sexually active woman with pelvic pain): Cervical motion tenderness, OR uterine tenderness, OR adnexal tenderness Supportive: fever, mucopurulent discharge, raised WBC or CRP Always r
r: Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness and a negative pregnancy test (ectopic excluded) is the classic picture of pelvic inflammatory disease. Cervical motion tenderness reflects inflammation of the upper genital tract and is a minimum clinical criterion for PID; a closed cervix and no
wo: B. UTI: causes dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain; it does not produce cervical motion tenderness on pelvic examination. | C. Cystitis: a lower UTI with suprapubic pain and urinary symptoms, again without cervical motion tenderness. | D. Forgot (recaller says it was not ectopic): ectopic would require a positive pregnancy test; endometriosis, if offered, fits cyclic pain, dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia, not acute pain with CMT.

q: woman in her 30s presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure. On examination, an enlarged uterus with irregular a palpable mass in the uterine fundus is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Uterine shape on examination points to the cause of AUB: Enlarged, irregular, focal mass: leiomyoma Diffusely enlarged, regular, boggy, tender: adenomyosis Normal-size uterus with intermenstrual bleeding: endometrial pol
r: A woman in her 30s with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure and an enlarged, irregular uterus with a palpable fundal mass has a leiomyoma (uterine fibroid). Fibroids are focal benign smooth muscle tumors, so they enlarge the uterus asymmetrically and produce bulk symptoms (pressure, frequen
kw: palpable mass in the uterine fundus
wo: B. Endometriosis: presents with cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and infertility, with a fixed retroverted uterus or nodules; it does not cause an irregular enlarged uterus with a fundal mass. | C. Adenomyosis: causes heavy, painful periods in a multiparous woman in her 40s with a DIFFUSELY enlarged, regular, boggy and tender uterus, not an irregular focal mass. | D. Uterine cancer: classically postmenopausal bleeding in an older woman with risk factors (obesity, diabetes, unopposed estrogen); unlikely in her 30s with a focal fundal mass.

q: A 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of heavy menstrual bleeding lasting more than 10 days . Pregnancy test is negative , and pelvic ultrasound is normal . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Acute AUB in a non-pregnant woman: First: pregnancy test, CBC, assess stability Medical: IV conjugated estrogen, COCP or high-dose oral progestin, tranexamic acid Severe or refractory bleeding: D&C Age ≥45 or risk factor
r: Heavy bleeding for more than 10 days with a negative pregnancy test and a normal ultrasound is acute abnormal uterine bleeding without structural cause, in a patient not described as unstable. Medical therapy comes first, and tranexamic acid (an antifibrinolytic) is the only effective medical option
kw: heavy menstrual bleeding lasting more than 10 days
wo: A. Dilatation and curettage: reserved for severe or refractory bleeding, or hemodynamic instability, after medical treatment fails; in a 45-year-old, endometrial sampling is also indicated for diagnosis, but it is not the first management here. | B. Hysterectomy: definitive treatment for chronic AUB after failed medical and conservative therapy when fertility is not desired; not the first step for an acute episode with a normal uterus. | D. Oxytocin: a uterotonic for postpartum hemorrhage; it has no role in non-pregnant AUB.

q: pregnant woman with preeclampsia has just delivered and has a lax uterus with moderate postpartum hemorrhage . Physical examination reveals no laceration or retained product of conception. Which of the following medical therapies is most recommended?
o: 20 units oxytocin in a 500 mL of D5W given intravenous
k: Uterotonic ladder for atonic PPH (with uterine massage, call for help, cross-match): 1st: oxytocin IV or IM 2nd: ergometrine 0.5 mg IM or methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM; avoid in hypertension or preeclampsia 3rd: carboprost
r: A lax uterus after delivery with no laceration or retained tissue means atonic PPH, and oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic. The patient has preeclampsia , which rules out ergometrine because it causes vasoconstriction and can provoke a hypertensive crisis, so an IV oxytocin infusion is the correc
