wo: A. 5 units of oral oxytocin: oxytocin is not given orally because it is destroyed in the gut; it is given IV or IM. | B. 0.2 mg intravenous ergometrine: an effective second-line uterotonic in normotensive women, but contraindicated in preeclampsia or hypertension. | C. 0.5 mg intramuscular ergometrine: the correct route and dose for ergometrine in a normotensive woman, but ergot alkaloids are contraindicated in preeclampsia or hypertension because they cause vasoconstriction and can provoke a hypertensive crisis.

q: 23-year-old woman develops postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) following a normal vaginal delivery, with an estimated blood loss of 1500 mL . All uterotonic medications have been administered but failed to control the bleeding. Which of the following is the first-line surgical intervention ?
k: Refractory atonic PPH escalation: Massage plus uterotonics, tranexamic acid Intrauterine balloon tamponade Laparotomy: compression sutures (B-Lynch), uterine or internal iliac artery ligation Embolization if stable and a
r: After a vaginal delivery with atonic PPH and failure of all uterotonics , the next step is the least invasive mechanical measure, intrauterine balloon tamponade (for example a Bakri balloon). It is quick, can be placed at the bedside, often stops the bleeding, and preserves fertility in a 23-year-ol
kw: All uterotonic medications have been administered
wo: A. Uterine artery embolization: an option when the patient is stable and interventional radiology is immediately available, usually after tamponade fails. | B. Hysterectomy: the last resort when all conservative and surgical measures fail or life is threatened; it ends fertility in a young woman. | D. Dilatation and curettage: used for retained products of conception, not for atony after uterotonics have failed.

q: Pregnant female with fetal hydrobe and they ask which of the following arteries is used to detect fetal anemia ?
k: Fetal Doppler: which vessel for which question: MCA PSV: fetal anemia (>1.5 MoM = moderate to severe), then cordocentesis and intrauterine transfusion Umbilical artery: placental insufficiency in IUGR Ductus venosus: fet
r: Fetal hydrops can result from severe fetal anemia (for example alloimmunization). Doppler of the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is the non-invasive test for fetal anemia: anemic blood is less viscous and the fetus increases cardiac output, so MCA flow velocity rises, and a value above
wo: B. Renal artery: not used to assess fetal anemia. | C. Umbilical artery: Doppler assesses placental resistance in fetal growth restriction (absent or reversed end-diastolic flow), not anemia. | D. Hepatic: not a standard vessel for anemia screening.

q: 6 weak pregnant woman has a previous child with hydrocephalus . What dose of folic acid should she take?
k: Folic acid dose by NTD risk: Average risk: 0.4 mg daily, from at least 1 month before conception through the first trimester Moderate risk (family history of folate-sensitive anomalies such as hydrocephalus, diabetes): 1
r: A previous child with hydrocephalus (a folate-sensitive congenital anomaly, but not a neural tube defect itself) places her at moderate risk. Moderate risk women take 1 mg (1,000 micrograms) folic acid daily until 12 weeks, then drop to the standard 0.4 mg; she is 6 weeks , so she is still in the hi
wo: A. 400 micrograms: the dose for average-risk women, and the dose for this moderate-risk woman after 12 weeks (another recall at 16 weeks was keyed 400). | C. 5000 micrograms: the high-risk dose (4 to 5 mg) for a previous pregnancy with a neural tube defect, antiepileptic drug use, sickle cell disease or similar. | D. 2000 micrograms: not a standard recommended dose.

q: year-old primigravida at 12 weeks ; electrolytes and renal function were requested. Most expected finding? (p. 147)
k: Normal pregnancy dilutes and filters more: most renal markers go DOWN. GFR and renal plasma flow: up about 50% Creatinine: down (by about 0.3 mg/dL) BUN: down Sodium and osmolality: down slightly Albumin: down about 1 g/
r: Early in pregnancy renal plasma flow and GFR rise sharply (by about 50%), so creatinine is cleared faster and its serum level falls . At 12 weeks this change is already established, making a lower creatinine the most expected result on routine renal function.
wo: B. Plasma sodium falls slightly in pregnancy because water retention exceeds sodium retention (dilution); it does not rise. | C. BUN also falls with the higher GFR and plasma dilution; a raised BUN would suggest dehydration or renal impairment, not normal pregnancy. | D. BUN is not unchanged; it drops in the first trimester for the same reason creatinine does.

q: 25-year-old woman in her mid-trimester of pregnancy presents with a sudden unexpected rupture of membranes followed by painless expulsion of the products of conception. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Painless second trimester dilation or loss = cervical incompetence. Risk factors: prior cone biopsy/LEEP, repeated dilation, cervical trauma, previous mid-trimester loss Diagnosis: history plus short cervix on transvagin
r: Mid-trimester loss that begins with sudden unexpected rupture of membranes and ends in painless expulsion is the classic picture of cervical incompetence: the weak cervix dilates silently without contractions. The absence of pain, fever and preceding bleeding is the decisive clue.
wo: A. Septic miscarriage presents with fever, uterine tenderness and foul discharge, usually after retained products or instrumentation; this patient is painless and well. | C. Threatened miscarriage is bleeding with a closed os and a continuing pregnancy; here the products have already been expelled. | D. Incomplete miscarriage is an open os with partial passage of tissue and usually painful bleeding with cramps; it describes the outcome of passage, not a painless second trimester mechanism.

q: A 30-year-old woman is referred by a medical clinic with a complaint of vulvar pain . Examination reveals one ulcer on the left lower labia majora. The lesion has a ragged edge , necrotic base , and palpable adenopathy on the left inguinal region. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Genital ulcers: decide by pain and base. Syphilis: single, painless, clean indurated base, rubbery non-tender nodes Chancroid: painful, ragged undermined edge, necrotic/purulent base, tender suppurative nodes Herpes: mul
r: A painful vulvar ulcer with a ragged edge , necrotic base and tender unilateral inguinal adenopathy is chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi . The undermined, dirty base and painful node (which may suppurate into a bubo) are the decisive features.
wo: A. Primary syphilis gives a painless ulcer with a clean, indurated base and sharp margins with non-tender nodes; this ulcer is necrotic and ragged. | C. Herpes causes multiple small painful vesicles that erode into shallow ulcers, often with systemic symptoms; it is not a single necrotic ulcer. | D. A Bartholin abscess is a tender fluctuant swelling at the 4 or 8 o'clock position of the posterior vestibule, not an ulcer on the labia majora.

q: A 35-year-old woman, G3P2 diabetic patient at 38 weeks of gestation, is planned to have induction of labor. She has no abdominal or pelvic pain, and no vaginal loss. Examination revealed the uterine size corresponds to gestational age, soft, and not tender. Pelvic examination shows the cervix is closed and uneffaced . CTG is done . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Read a CTG with DR C BRAVADO; reassuring = all features normal. Baseline 110 to 160 bpm Variability 5 to 25 bpm Accelerations present No decelerations Early: head compression (benign); Variable: cord; Late: placental ins
r: The woman is not in labour : no pain, no vaginal loss, soft non-tender uterus and a closed uneffaced cervix. Without contractions there is nothing to cause periodic decelerations, and the trace with a baseline of about 140 bpm is reassuring. Induction is planned only because of diabetes at 38 weeks.
wo: A. Late decelerations start after the contraction peak and reflect uteroplacental insufficiency; they need contractions and an abnormal trace, neither described here. | B. Early decelerations mirror contractions from head compression, typically in active labour with an engaged head; this woman has no contractions. | D. Variable decelerations are abrupt dips from cord compression (e.g. cord prolapse, oligohydramnios); nothing in the stem suggests this.

q: Recently married women with sudden iliac fossa pain ?
k: Acute pelvic pain in a woman of childbearing age: hCG first, then pelvic US. Positive hCG + empty uterus + adnexal mass/free fluid = ectopic Sudden pain + adnexal mass + vomiting = torsion (Doppler) Ruptured cyst: free f
r: A recently married woman of reproductive age with sudden iliac fossa pain must have pregnancy related and adnexal causes excluded first: ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ruptured or haemorrhagic cyst. Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal, with beta hCG) is the first imaging test: it is fast, radiation
wo: A. CT pelvis uses radiation that is undesirable in possible pregnancy and is inferior for adnexal and early pregnancy assessment; it is reserved for unclear cases or suspected non gynaecological pathology. | B. Erect and supine abdominal X ray is used for suspected obstruction or perforation, not for sudden iliac fossa pain in a woman of childbearing age.

q: Hypertensive lady worried about still birth what decrease the risk ?
k: Chronic hypertension in pregnancy. High risk for pre eclampsia: chronic HTN, prior pre eclampsia, CKD, diabetes, SLE/APS Aspirin 75 to 150 mg nightly from 12 weeks (before 16) to delivery Safe antihypertensives: labetalo

q: DM pregnant lady OGTT normal in first hr , high after 2 hr ...?
k: Gestational diabetes: diagnose by OGTT, then treat. Screen 24 to 28 weeks (earlier if previous GDM or high risk) 75 g OGTT: one abnormal value is enough (fasting, 1 h or 2 h) First step: diet and exercise with home gluco

q: Endometriosis defenetive management
k: Endometriosis management ladder. Diagnosis gold standard: laparoscopy (visualisation ± biopsy) First line pain control: NSAIDs + combined pill or progestin Second line: GnRH agonist with add back HRT Fertility wish: lapa
r: The lead in asks for the definitive management of endometriosis. Endometriosis is oestrogen dependent, so removing the uterus and both ovaries ( TAH with BSO ) with excision of visible disease is the treatment with the lowest recurrence; it is reserved for women who have completed their family and f
wo: B. Endometrial ablation destroys the uterine lining to treat heavy menstrual bleeding; it does not treat ectopic endometrial implants. | C. Not recalled; if it was laparoscopic excision or ablation of implants, that is first line surgery and preserves fertility but is temporising, with many patients needing reoperation. | D. Not recalled; if it was medical therapy (combined pill, progestins, GnRH agonists), that suppresses symptoms but is not curative and symptoms recur after stopping.

q: infertility laparoscop show absence of dye filling bilateral tubal blockage management
k: Infertility treatment by cause. Tubal patency: HSG first, laparoscopy and dye confirms Bilateral tubal block: IVF Unilateral block with ovulation issue: clomiphene Anovulation (PCOS): letrozole or clomiphene, then gonado
r: Laparoscopy with dye showing no spill from both tubes confirms bilateral tubal blockage : sperm and egg cannot meet, so any treatment that relies on the tubes will fail. IVF bypasses the tubes by fertilising the egg outside the body and transferring the embryo to the uterus.
wo: A. Clomiphene induces ovulation in anovulatory women (e.g. PCOS) or is used with one patent tube; ovulation is useless if both tubes are blocked. | C. IUI places sperm in the uterus and still needs at least one patent tube; it suits mild male factor or unexplained infertility. | D. Gonadotropin ovulation induction is for anovulation resistant to clomiphene/letrozole; it cannot overcome blocked tubes.

q: 67 yr women with negative 3 pap smear. A 67 year old woman , had 3 consecutive negative pap smear and no evidence of CIN 2 (or 3, im not sure), which one of the following is the recommended step:
o: pap smear and HPV co-testing every 5 years
k: Cervical screening schedule: Start at 21 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years 30 to 65: co-test every 5 years (or cytology every 3) Over 65 with adequate negative history and no CIN 2+ in 25 years: stop After hysterectomy fo
r: Cervical screening stops after age 65 in a woman with adequate prior negative screening (for example 3 consecutive negative Pap smears, or 2 negative co-tests, within the past 10 years) and no history of CIN 2 or worse in the last 25 years. She is 67 with 3 consecutive negative smears, so she needs
wo: A. Not recalled; whatever it was, it cannot beat stopping screening once the age and negative history criteria are met. | B. Pap smear every 3 years is the schedule for ages 21 to 29 (and an option up to 65); it does not apply after 65 with adequate negative history. | C. Co-testing every 5 years is the preferred schedule for ages 30 to 65, not for a 67 year old who qualifies to stop.

q: after abortion risk of reoccurrence. Female had one ABORTION , risk of 2nd abortion ?
k: Miscarriage recurrence after one loss ≈ baseline risk. Baseline clinical miscarriage: about 10 to 15% under 35 Risk rises with each further loss and steeply with maternal age over 40 Recurrent miscarriage = 3 or more con
r: After a single sporadic miscarriage, the risk of miscarriage in the next pregnancy is about the same as the background rate, roughly 15 to 20% (mainly from random chromosomal errors), and rises only modestly with more losses. 10 to 25% is the range that contains this figure, and the card notes it as
wo: A. 1 to 9% is below even the baseline miscarriage rate of clinically recognized pregnancies (about 10 to 15% under age 35). | C. 25 to 45% fits a woman after two or three consecutive losses (recurrent miscarriage) or of advanced maternal age, where the risk rises steeply after 40; it does not apply after one abortion.

q: A 26-year-old G4 P3 presented at 31 weeks gestation with labor pain. She had preterm premature rupture of membranes 4 weeks ago . Today, the cervix is 3 cm dilated with clear liquor noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: High vaginal swab for bacterial culture and sensitivity
k: Preterm labour after PPROM: look for infection first. High vaginal swab for culture; antibiotics (erythromycin is the latency antibiotic after PPROM) Chorioamnionitis (fever, fetal tachycardia, tender uterus, foul liquor
r: She is in preterm labour at 31 weeks after prolonged PPROM (4 weeks) , which carries a high risk of ascending infection (chorioamnionitis) even with clear liquor. The next step is a high vaginal swab for culture and sensitivity to identify the organism and guide antibiotic therapy for mother and neo
kw: preterm premature rupture of membranes 4 weeks ago
wo: B. Antipyretics and review delays the work-up; fever or fetal tachycardia after PPROM suggests chorioamnionitis that needs antibiotics and a delivery decision, not symptom masking. | C. Immediate caesarean section is for obstetric indications such as fetal distress, cord prolapse or malpresentation; chorioamnionitis itself is an indication for delivery, usually vaginal, not for caesarean. | D. Fetal blood sampling is contraindicated under 34 weeks, and it assesses fetal acidosis in labour; the issue here is infection after prolonged PPROM, not acidosis.

q: A 23-year-old single woman presented with heavy menstruation during the first 4 days of her period for the last 2 years (see image and lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Heavy menstrual bleeding causes (PALM-COEIN): Structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy Non structural: coagulopathy, ovulatory, endometrial, iatrogenic, not classified Fibroid on US: well defined hypoechoic
r: Heavy menstrual bleeding for 2 years with an ultrasound showing a uterine mass (arrow) points to uterine leiomyomas (fibroids), the commonest cause of structural menorrhagia. Submucosal and intramural fibroids enlarge the endometrial surface and cause heavy, regular periods; ultrasound is the first
wo: A. Pregnancy causes amenorrhoea, not 2 years of regular heavy periods; bleeding in pregnancy would suggest miscarriage or ectopic with a positive hCG. | B. An ovarian cyst is an adnexal mass, usually asymptomatic or causing pain or torsion, and does not typically cause heavy periods. | C. Endometrial cancer presents mainly with postmenopausal bleeding in older women with risk factors (obesity, PCOS, unopposed oestrogen); it is very unlikely at 23.

q: A 30-year-old woman with a history of infertility for 6 years complains of severe dysmenorrhea unrelieved by naproxen . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Endometriosis: cyclic pain + infertility. 3 Ds: dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia (deep), dyschezia Exam: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodules Diagnosis: laparoscopy (powder burn, red/white lesions); endometrioma = cho
r: Infertility (6 years) plus severe dysmenorrhoea not relieved by NSAIDs (naproxen) in a woman of 30 is the classic combination for endometriosis ; the laparoscopic photo of peritoneal "powder burn" lesions confirms it. Endometriosis causes the 3 Ds (dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, dyschezia) and infertil
wo: A. Endometritis is an infection of the endometrium, usually after delivery, miscarriage or instrumentation, with fever, pelvic pain and discharge; it is not years of cyclic pain. | B. Leiomyomata mainly cause heavy menstrual bleeding and pressure symptoms; submucosal ones can affect fertility, but refractory dysmenorrhoea with powder burn lesions is endometriosis. | D. Pelvic congestion syndrome is chronic dull pelvic pain worse on standing and premenstrually, with pelvic varices, typically in multiparous women; it is not linked to infertility.

q: A woman comes to the clinic for having a history of increasing pelvic pain. which is cyclic in nature and increasing in intensity just before menses . Which of the following is an acceptable method for diagnosing endometriosis ?
k: Endometriosis diagnosis: Initial: transvaginal ultrasound (endometrioma = chocolate cyst, ground glass) Gold standard / confirmatory: laparoscopy ± biopsy MRI: deep infiltrating disease, surgical planning CA-125 may rise
r: Cyclic pelvic pain building just before menses suggests endometriosis, and the question asks for an acceptable method of diagnosing it. Diagnostic laparoscopy with direct visualization (ideally with biopsy of lesions) is the gold standard and confirmatory test, because peritoneal implants are usuall
kw: increasing in intensity just before menses
wo: A. MRI helps map deep infiltrating endometriosis and endometriomas before surgery, but it misses superficial peritoneal disease and cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis. | C. Endometrial biopsy samples the uterine lining and is the test for abnormal bleeding over 45 or suspected hyperplasia/cancer; endometriosis lies outside the uterus. | D. Transvaginal ultrasound is the initial test and can show an endometrioma (ground glass cyst), but a normal scan does not exclude endometriosis.

q: A 33-year-old woman, nulliparous , complaining of cyclic pelvic pain and dyschezia underwent diagnostic laparoscopy (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Cyclic pain + dyschezia/dyspareunia + infertility = endometriosis. Most common site: ovary; then uterosacral ligaments, pouch of Douglas Exam: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodularity Adenomyosis: older, multipar
r: A nulliparous woman with cyclic pelvic pain and dyschezia has two of the 3 Ds of endometriosis (dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, dyschezia); dyschezia reflects implants in the pouch of Douglas or rectovaginal septum. Laparoscopy, the confirmatory test, shows the typical peritoneal implants (powder burn,
wo: A. Pelvic TB causes infertility, menstrual disturbance (often amenorrhoea) and constitutional symptoms, with tubercles and dense adhesions at laparoscopy, usually in endemic settings; not cyclic pain. | B. Adenomyosis is endometrium within the myometrium, seen in older multiparous women with heavy painful periods and a bulky tender uterus; it is not visible as peritoneal lesions on laparoscopy. | D. PID gives non cyclic pelvic pain, fever, discharge and cervical motion tenderness in a sexually active woman, with inflamed tubes or adhesions rather than cyclic symptoms.

q: Mother pregnant with twin , in U/S there's lambda sign What type of twins pregnancy ?
k: Chorionicity on ultrasound: Lambda (twin peak) sign, thick membrane: DCDA T sign, thin membrane: MCDA No membrane: MCMA Different sexes or two separate placentas: dichorionic Cleavage timing: 0 to 3 days DCDA, 4 to 8 day
r: The lambda (twin peak) sign is a triangular projection of placental tissue into the base of a thick inter twin membrane; it means two separate chorions, i.e. dichorionic diamniotic twins. It is best assessed in the first trimester (around 11 to 14 weeks), when chorionicity is most reliable.
wo: A. Monochorionic monoamniotic twins have no dividing membrane at all and are recognized by cord entanglement in a single sac. | B. Monochorionic diamniotic twins show the T sign: a thin membrane meeting the single placenta at a right angle, without placental tissue between the layers. | D. Conjoined twins have no membrane and fused fetal bodies that move together; they result from very late cleavage (after about day 13).

q: 8yrs boy with fever, pain & redness in left leg after examination : tenderness, redness what is the appropriate next step ?
k: Suspected acute osteomyelitis in a child: Initial imaging: X ray (often normal early) Most sensitive and diagnostic: MRI Bone scan: site unclear or multiple sites Labs: CBC, ESR, CRP, blood culture Most common organism:
r: An 8 year old with fever, pain, redness and tenderness of the leg raises cellulitis versus acute osteomyelitis. The lead in is the next step , and plain X ray is the first imaging: it is cheap, quick, excludes fracture, foreign body or tumour, and gives a baseline, even though bone changes of osteom
kw: fever, pain & redness in left leg
wo: B. MRI is the best diagnostic test for early osteomyelitis and is chosen when the question asks for the most sensitive or confirmatory imaging, not the initial step. | C. CT gives radiation and is less sensitive than MRI for marrow changes; it is used for cortical detail or sequestrum, or when MRI is unavailable. | D. Option not recalled; another version listed a nuclear bone scan, which is used when the site is unclear or multifocal or MRI is not possible.

q: 8yrs boy with fever, pain & redness in left leg, parenteral antibiotic is given and after (i think 4 days) pt still feverish , what may be the cause ?
k: Infection not improving despite appropriate antibiotics: look for a collection. Cellulitis or osteomyelitis: ultrasound or MRI for abscess or subperiosteal collection Pyelonephritis: renal ultrasound for obstruction or r
r: A child with fever, pain and redness of the leg treated with parenteral antibiotics who is still febrile after about 4 days has failed appropriate treatment. The commonest reason for persistent fever despite correct IV antibiotics in a soft tissue or bone infection is a collection (abscess) that ant
wo: A. Non adherence is a cause of failure for oral outpatient treatment; with parenteral antibiotics given in hospital, adherence is not the issue. | B. An organism not covered (e.g. MRSA) is possible, but empirical regimens cover the usual Staph and Strep; the first thing to exclude in a non responding infection is an abscess, and cultures guide any change. | C. Option not recalled; other causes of persistent fever (drug fever, wrong diagnosis) are less likely than a collection here.

q: Pediatric patient with leg localized redness and warmth. Was admitted and given parental antibiotics . Patient condition deteriorated with high grade fever and increased redness and hotness ( no mention of induraion or fluctuating mass ). What is the cause of deterioration?
k: Refractory cellulitis: ultrasound to look for an abscess even without fluctuation. Abscess: incision and drainage (plus antibiotics) No collection and still worsening: broaden cover (MRSA), reconsider diagnosis Rapid spr
r: Localized leg redness and warmth treated with parenteral antibiotics that deteriorates with high grade fever and spreading redness suggests the cellulitis has formed a deep abscess . The stem deliberately gives no induration or fluctuant mass : deep abscesses are often not clinically apparent, which
kw: no mention of induraion or fluctuating mass
wo: A. A resistant organism (e.g. MRSA) is a cause of failure, but it is considered after excluding a collection, and is favoured when cultures show resistance or an abscess has already been drained without improvement.

q: due to poor feeding and failure to thrive. The mother reports that the infant becomes sweaty and cyanotic during feeding . On examination, the infant's weight is below the 3rd percentile , and a systolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border . What is the most appropriate next step regarding infant's failure to thrive?
k: Failure to thrive: look for the organic clue and treat the cause. Sweating, cyanosis or tachypnea with feeds plus murmur: cardiac, refer cardiology (echo) Large VSD: pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal border, heart
r: An infant with failure to thrive (weight below the 3rd percentile) who becomes sweaty and cyanotic during feeding and has a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border has a cardiac cause of poor growth (large VSD or a cyanotic lesion such as tetralogy of Fallot). Sweating with feeds is a sign
wo: B. Gastroenterology referral fits FTT with vomiting, diarrhea, malabsorption or GERD symptoms; nothing here points to the gut. | C. Endocrinology fits short stature with preserved weight (growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism); in this infant weight is affected and the clues are cardiac. | D. Nasogastric feeding supports nutrition in infants who cannot feed enough and may be used later, but it does not address the underlying heart disease causing the FTT.

q: A 10-year-old boy presents with frontal headache , fever, and nasal congestion he had runny nose and sore throat since two days . On examination, he has left cheek tenderness . What is the next best management?
k: Acute bacterial sinusitis in children: needs one of three patterns. Persistent: nasal discharge or cough ≥10 days without improvement Severe onset: fever ≥39 °C plus purulent discharge for ≥3 consecutive days Worsening:
r: This recall's key is amoxicillin clavulanate for 10 days , treating the picture as acute bacterial sinusitis: frontal headache, fever, nasal congestion and cheek tenderness point to maxillary sinus involvement. Amoxicillin with or without clavulanate is the antibiotic of choice when a child meets cr
wo: A. Sinus X ray is not recommended in children; sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis, and CT or MRI is used only for suspected orbital or intracranial complications. | B. Reassurance with symptomatic care is the guideline answer for a viral URTI with sinus symptoms under 10 days without severe features; the other version of this recall was keyed to this. | D. Intranasal antihistamine fits allergic rhinitis (sneezing, itching, clear rhinorrhea, no fever); it does not treat infection.

q: A 2-year-old child presents with cough and fever for 1 week duration following flu-like symptoms. On examination, well looking with decreased air entry and crackles in right lower lung on auscultation and just below this finding there is stony dullness on percussion . Blood pressure 98/65 mmHg, Heart rate 105 /min, Respiratory rate 22 /min, Temperature 38.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 95 %. Which of the following is the expected finding in chest X-ray match child's chest finding?
k: Percussion note and chest X ray: Stony dull: pleural effusion (meniscus, blunted angle) Dull with bronchial breathing: consolidation (air bronchogram) Dull with shift toward the lesion: collapse Hyperresonant: pneumothor
r: A 2 year old with a week of cough and fever after a flu like illness , decreased air entry and crackles at the right base and stony dullness just below has pneumonia complicated by a parapneumonic effusion. Stony dullness is specific to pleural fluid, so the chest X ray will show a homogeneous lower
wo: A. Bronchopneumonia gives patchy bilateral infiltrates with generalized fine crackles; percussion is normal or only mildly dull, never stony dull. | C. Pneumothorax gives a hyperresonant note with absent breath sounds, the opposite of stony dullness. | D. Lung collapse causes a dull (not stony dull) note with the trachea and mediastinum pulled toward the affected side.

q: A preschool child presents for his routine preschool-entry examination (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: HB 90 (112-165), RDW 20 (11.5-16%), Platelets count 490 (150-400 x 109/L), MCV 68 (80-95 fl), MCH 26 (28-33 pg/cell), MCHC 241 (260-340 g/L), Reticulocyte 1.1 (0.2-1.2 %), WBC 7.5 (4.5-10.5 x 109/L), RBC 5 (4.6-4.8 x 1012/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Microcytic anemia in a child: Iron deficiency: high RDW, low ferritin, reactive thrombocytosis, Mentzer index above 13 Thalassemia trait: normal RDW, high RBC count, Mentzer below 13, high HbA2 on electrophoresis Anemia
r: A preschool child with Hb 90 and MCV 68 has microcytic anemia. The high RDW (20%) shows variable red cell size typical of iron deficiency, and platelets 490 is reactive thrombocytosis, also typical of iron deficiency. Reticulocytes are not raised and the RBC count is only mildly high, which fits iro
wo: A. Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with normocytic or macrocytic cells and low reticulocytes; here WBC is normal and platelets are high. | B. Thalassemia minor gives marked microcytosis with a normal RDW and a clearly high RBC count (Mentzer index below 13), with mild or no anemia; here the RDW is high. | D. Hereditary spherocytosis is a hemolytic anemia with high reticulocytes, high MCHC, spherocytes, jaundice and splenomegaly; here MCHC is low and reticulocytes are normal.

q: 4-day-old preterm neonate presented with history of frequent apnea. he is found to have a continuous machinery-like murmur and wide pulse pressure. Chest X-ray: Wet lungs . What is the most appropriate initial management?
k: Preterm PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, pulmonary overload. Initial/supportive: fluid restriction, diuretic, respiratory support as needed Pharmacologic closure: indomethacin, ibup
r: A preterm neonate with a continuous machinery murmur and wide pulse pressure has a patent ductus arteriosus, and the wet lungs plus apnea show left to right shunt overload with pulmonary edema. The lead-in asks for the initial management, so this recall's key is supportive treatment of the overload
wo: A. Mechanical ventilation: for respiratory failure or apnea that does not respond to caffeine and non invasive support; it supports breathing but does not treat the shunt overload that is causing the wet lungs, and no failure of first line support is described. | B. Broad spectrum antibiotics: right for suspected neonatal sepsis (temperature instability, poor perfusion, lethargy); the murmur and wide pulse pressure point to a cardiac cause, not infection. | D. NSAIDs (indomethacin or ibuprofen): the drug treatment that closes a hemodynamically significant PDA in a preterm; the compiler accepts it as an alternative, but this key places supportive fluid management first.

q: Child with fever, rash and bilateral parotid gland enlargement What is the cause of?
k: Mumps: fever, malaise, then unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling (pain on chewing). Complications: orchitis (post pubertal), aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, deafness Prevention: MMR (live vaccine) Measles: 3 Cs + K
r: Bilateral parotid gland enlargement with fever in a child is the hallmark of mumps (paramyxovirus), especially in a child with incomplete immunization. Parotitis is the defining clue; none of the other common childhood exanthems causes bilateral parotid swelling as its main feature.
wo: A. Not recalled (EBV in the similar version): EBV gives fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical nodes and splenomegaly, with a rash mainly after amoxicillin; parotid swelling is not the typical picture. | B. Not recalled (CMV in the similar version): CMV gives a mononucleosis like illness or congenital infection, not bilateral parotitis. | D. Measles: fever with the 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots and a rash spreading from behind the ears downward; it does not cause parotitis.

q: 9 months old child unvaccinated want to vaccinate Which vaccine gives ?
o: DTaP, measles, BCG, Hep B, OPV
k: Unvaccinated child: give everything missed that is still age appropriate plus what is due now. Birth: BCG + hepatitis B Primary series: DTaP, polio, hepatitis B, Hib, PCV Around 9 to 12 months: measles containing vaccine
r: A 9 month old who has received no vaccines needs catch-up of everything missed plus what is due for his age. That means the birth vaccines he never had ( BCG and hepatitis B ), catch-up DTaP and polio, and measles containing vaccine now that he is 9 months. Option C is the only one that includes bot
wo: A. DTaP and BCG only: misses hepatitis B, polio and measles, so the catch-up is incomplete. | B. DTaP, BCG, IPV, OPV: giving IPV and OPV together is acceptable, but it omits hepatitis B and the measles vaccine that is due at 9 months, so the catch-up is incomplete. | D. DTaP, measles, MCV4, OPV: omits the birth vaccines BCG and hepatitis B; meningococcal conjugate is not the priority of a basic catch-up.

q: Child KC of asthma regular on medication the mother reported when he take pneumococcal or influenza ( i am not sure which one of them ) vaccine he developed urticaria, SOB and syncope What to do about vaccination?
o: give tha vaccine with steroids and anti histamine
k: Vaccine contraindications vs misconceptions. Absolute: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component Live vaccines: avoid in immunodeficiency and pregnancy DTaP: encephalopathy within 7 days of a prior dose Not c
r: Urticaria, shortness of breath and syncope after a vaccine is anaphylaxis. A serious allergic reaction to a previous dose is an absolute contraindication to further doses of that same vaccine, so he should not be given it again. The similar version words this as "don't give influenza vaccine": the b
wo: B. Intranasal (live) influenza vaccine: still the same antigen after an anaphylactic reaction, and it is also avoided in children with asthma or wheeze. | C. Give him the vaccine: only right for minor reactions (local swelling, fever, mild rash); anaphylaxis is an absolute contraindication. | D. Steroids and antihistamine premedication: does not reliably prevent anaphylaxis and is not an accepted way to re-vaccinate after a severe reaction.

q: Child KC of asthma came to ER with exacerbation he can complete full sentence his O2 saturation 95% on room air he has only mild wheezing ( it's written exactly mild ) his FEV 60% on his best , he takes to puf of salbutamol before comes What to do now ?
k: Acute asthma severity guides the step. Mild/moderate: talks in sentences or phrases, SpO2 ≥ 92%: SABA, reassess, add oral steroid Severe: words only, hunched, accessory muscles: O2, SABA + ipratropium, systemic steroid N
r: He talks in full sentences , has SpO2 95% on room air and only mild wheeze , so this is a mild to moderate exacerbation that did not settle with 2 puffs at home. The first step in the ER is a short acting beta agonist (salbutamol), then reassessment of the response to decide on discharge or escalati
wo: A. Intubation: reserved for life threatening asthma (exhaustion, silent chest, falling consciousness, rising CO2) failing maximal therapy including IV magnesium. | B. Oral steroid: is added for moderate exacerbations, but alone it does not relieve the bronchospasm now; the original version 'oral steroid and admit' is wrong because mild asthma is not admitted. | D. Discharge him: he came because home salbutamol did not help and FEV1 is only 60%; he needs treatment and reassessment before discharge.

q: 17 year old female KC of anorexia nervosa came to nutritional feeding on 3rd day her labs was Na 124, k 3, Ca 1.7, Mg .8, Phosphate .4
k: Refeeding syndrome: malnourished patient (anorexia, alcoholism, cachexia) started on rapid nutrition. Labs: hypophosphatemia (hallmark), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia Timing: first 2 to 5 days of feeding Risks: arrhythmia,
r: A 17 year old with anorexia nervosa on day 3 of nutritional feeding who develops low phosphate (0.4), low potassium, low magnesium and low calcium has refeeding syndrome. Starvation makes the body very sensitive to insulin, so feeding triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and ma
wo: A. False calculation (wrong protocol): an error in prescribing would not produce this classic, predictable pattern of intracellular shift electrolytes. | C. Labs error: right only when results are inconsistent with the clinical picture (e.g. hemolyzed sample with isolated high K); here several electrolytes fall together in a recognized pattern. | D. Malabsorption: causes gradual deficiencies with diarrhea and steatorrhea over weeks, not an acute fall in phosphate, potassium and magnesium on day 3 of feeding.

q: A 10-day-old male neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy and respiratory distress. On physical examination, the femoral pulses are absent . Coarctation of the aorta is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis ?
k: Coarctation of the aorta. Clues: weak or absent femoral pulses, radio femoral delay, upper limb BP higher than lower limb Neonate: shock when the duct closes; give prostaglandin E1 Confirm: echocardiography (CT/MRI for d
r: A 10 day old with lethargy, respiratory distress and absent femoral pulses has suspected critical coarctation presenting as the ductus closes. Echocardiography is the investigation that confirms the diagnosis: it is bedside, non invasive and shows the narrowed segment, gradient and associated lesion
wo: A. CT angiography: gives detailed anatomy of the aorta in older children and adults or for surgical planning, but needs contrast and radiation; it is not the first confirmatory test in a sick neonate. | B. MRI: excellent anatomy without radiation, used in older patients and follow up, but needs a long scan and sedation; not suitable for an unstable neonate. | D. Chest X-ray: may show cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion, and rib notching only in older children; it cannot confirm coarctation.

q: A 1-year-old boy presents with a history of recurrent episodes of pneumonia and persistent cough. He is known to have laryngomalacia , which has not resolved with age . What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Refer to ENT for surgical evaluation
k: Laryngomalacia: most common cause of stridor in infants. Inspiratory stridor, worse supine, crying and feeding; better prone Diagnosis: flexible laryngoscopy (omega shaped epiglottis) Mild: reassurance, resolves by 12 to
r: Laryngomalacia usually resolves on its own by 12 to 24 months, so most infants need only reassurance. This 1 year old has laryngomalacia that has not resolved and is complicated by recurrent pneumonia (likely aspiration) and persistent cough, which is a severe feature. Severe disease (failure to thr
wo: A. Observation and reassurance: correct for uncomplicated laryngomalacia with stridor but normal feeding and growth; not when there are complications like recurrent pneumonia. | C. Antibiotic therapy: treats an acute pneumonia episode but leaves the cause in place, so the pneumonias will recur. | D. Medical treatment and follow up: anti reflux therapy may help mild to moderate cases with reflux, but it does not address severe, complicated disease.

q: A case scenario describing a patient with measles . What is the mode of transmission ?
k: Airborne precautions: measles, varicella (and disseminated zoster), tuberculosis. Airborne: negative pressure room + N95 Droplet: surgical mask (influenza, meningococcus, mumps, rubella, pertussis) Contact: gown and glov
r: Measles spreads by the airborne route: small droplet nuclei stay suspended in the air and can infect people who enter a room after the patient has left. It is one of the most contagious infections, so patients need airborne isolation in a negative pressure room with N95 respirators.
wo: A. Droplet transmission: large droplets over short distance, typical of influenza, meningococcus, mumps, rubella and pertussis. | C. Contact transmission: direct or surface spread, typical of MRSA, C. difficile, scabies and RSV (also contact). | D. Fecal oral transmission: hepatitis A and E, rotavirus, polio, enteroviruses and typhoid.

q: A 6-month-old infant presents with a runny nose and fever . His mother brings him to the clinic for his routine 6-month vaccinations. She reports that he developed swelling in his arm after receiving a previous dose of DTaP. On examination, the infant is active and appears well . What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Postpone vaccination until the runny nose resolves.
Administer all scheduled vaccinations except DTaP, which should be postponed.
k: Vaccine contraindications vs misconceptions. True contraindication: anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component DTaP specific: encephalopathy within 7 days; defer in progressive neurologic disease Precaution: moderate to se
r: A runny nose with fever in an infant who is active and appears well is a minor illness, and minor illness is not a reason to delay vaccines. Local arm swelling after a previous DTaP is a common, expected reaction, not a contraindication. So all scheduled vaccinations should be given now to avoid lea
wo: B. Delay vaccination for 2 months: no indication to delay; delays leave the infant unprotected during the highest risk age. | C. Postpone until the runny nose resolves: postponement is right only for moderate to severe acute illness, not a mild URTI in a well, active infant. | D. Give all except DTaP: DTaP is withheld only after anaphylaxis to it, encephalopathy within 7 days of a dose, or a progressive neurologic disorder; local swelling is none of these.

q: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent otitis media and recurrent pneumonia . What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Recurrent infection pattern points to the defect. Sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria: antibody deficiency: immunoglobulin levels Viral, fungal, opportunistic infections, failure to thrive: T cell or comb
r: A 3 year old with recurrent otitis media and recurrent pneumonia has repeated sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria, the pattern of an antibody (humoral, B cell) deficiency. The first screening step is measuring serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM). This identifies conditions su
wo: A. C1 inhibitor testing: for hereditary angioedema (recurrent non itchy swelling of face, lips, airway or gut without urticaria), not recurrent infections. | C. Intestinal biopsy: for celiac disease or chronic diarrhea with malabsorption; it does not evaluate recurrent sinopulmonary infections. | D. Option not recalled (total hemolytic complement, CH50, in the lookalike): right for recurrent Neisseria infections in terminal complement deficiency.

q: A child was admitted to the PICU with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). His condition initially improved with treatment, but he suddenly developed confusion and neurological signs . What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Pediatric DKA cerebral edema. Timing: typically hours into treatment, often after initial improvement Signs: headache, confusion, falling GCS, bradycardia, hypertension, vomiting Risks: young age, new onset, rapid fluid
r: A child with DKA who initially improves on treatment and then suddenly develops confusion and neurological signs has cerebral edema, the leading cause of death in pediatric DKA. It is treated immediately on clinical grounds, without waiting for imaging, with an osmotic agent: IV mannitol (or hyperto
wo: A. Increase the insulin dose: a rapid fall in glucose and osmolality contributes to cerebral edema, so more insulin worsens it; insulin is kept at the standard rate. | C. Normal saline over 15 minutes: a bolus is for shock at presentation; in cerebral edema extra fluid worsens brain swelling, so fluids are restricted. | D. Option not recalled (stop insulin or give dextrose only in the lookalike): stopping insulin lets ketoacidosis return and does not treat the raised intracranial pressure.

q: A full-term baby girl is born with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). What is the most concerning complication in this newborn?
k: IUGR (small for gestational age) neonatal complications. Hypoglycemia: most important, low glycogen stores Hypothermia: little fat Polycythemia/hyperviscosity: chronic fetal hypoxia Hypocalcemia: usually mild Perinatal a
r: A term IUGR newborn has low glycogen stores and little fat, so after birth it cannot maintain glucose, making hypoglycemia the most common and most concerning metabolic complication. Untreated neonatal hypoglycemia can cause seizures and permanent brain injury, so these babies need early feeding and
wo: A. Hyperthermia: IUGR babies are at risk of the opposite, hypothermia, because they have little subcutaneous fat and a large surface area relative to weight. | C. Hypocalcemia: can occur (it was the answer in a version that lacked hypoglycemia), but it is usually mild and needs no specific intervention, so it is less concerning. | D. Option not recalled; polycythemia and hypothermia are other IUGR complications a student should know.

q: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother. She reports that 1–2 hours after falling asleep , he suddenly sits up in bed with his eyes wide open, appears distressed, and does not respond to her or seem aware of his surroundings. He then goes back to sleep. Upon waking in the morning, he has no memory of the episode . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Childhood parasomnias. Sleep terrors: non REM, first third of night, screaming/fear, unresponsive, no memory Sleepwalking: non REM, walks around, no memory Nightmares: REM, later in the night, wakes fully, consolable, re
r: A preschool child who 1 to 2 hours after falling asleep suddenly sits up, eyes open, distressed and unresponsive , then returns to sleep with no memory of the event has sleep terrors. They arise from deep non REM sleep in the first third of the night, which explains both the timing and the amnesia.
wo: A. Epilepsy: nocturnal seizures are brief, stereotyped, may show tonic clonic movements, incontinence or tongue biting and can occur at any time of night; EEG helps when episodes are atypical. | B. Nightmare: occurs in REM sleep in the second half of the night; the child wakes fully, is consolable and remembers the frightening dream. | C. Sleepwalking: also non REM with amnesia, but the child gets out of bed and walks around rather than sitting up terrified.

q: A 3-year-old asthmatic child's mother is concerned that they are not leaving the house much because they must use the nebulizer , which requires a power source . What advice should be given?
o: Advise her for a portable nebulizer
advice to (buy) inhalers and stop nebulizer
Stay at home as the priority is for asthma control
k: Spacer + MDI is equal or better than nebulizer for most children, at every age with the right interface. Under about 4 years: MDI + spacer + face mask Older children: MDI + spacer with mouthpiece Nebulizer: severe attack
r: The family's problem is that the nebulizer needs a power source and is keeping them at home. A metered dose inhaler with a spacer (and face mask at age 3) delivers salbutamol as effectively as a nebulizer and is portable, so the right advice is education on inhaler use and stopping the nebulizer. Wh
wo: A. Adding oral medication escalates treatment without any sign of poor control; the problem is the delivery device, not asthma severity. | B. A portable nebulizer solves the power issue but keeps an inferior, bulkier device; inhaler with spacer is preferred and equally effective. | D. Restricting the child's life is not needed and harms quality of life; good asthma control should allow normal activity.

q: A child presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of cough and shortness of breath. His mother administered inhaled salbutamol at home, but there was no clinical improvement . On physical examination, localized wheezing is heard over the right middle lung zone , with [additional examination finding]. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: (forgot; recaller noted it was clearly excluded)
k: Foreign body aspiration: sudden cough/choking, unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry, no bronchodilator response. Next step: CXR with expiratory or decubitus films (air trapping on affected side) Normal CXR does not exc
r: A child with acute cough and dyspnea, no response to salbutamol and localized wheeze over one lung zone suggests an inhaled foreign body rather than asthma (which gives diffuse wheeze that responds to bronchodilators). The lead-in asks for the next step: chest X-ray (ideally inspiratory and expirato
wo: A. Bronchoscopy is the best/definitive step and is done directly if suspicion is very high or the child is unstable; for 'next step' in a stable child imaging comes first. | B. Laryngoscopy looks at the larynx (laryngomalacia, laryngeal foreign body with stridor); localized lower zone wheeze points below the carina. | D. Option not recalled; the recaller noted it was clearly unlikely.

q: 11-month-old boy presents with right ulnar and radial fractures , 2 days after a reported fall on an outstretched hand . The parents delayed seeking medical care , stating that they did not notice any bruising and initially believed the injury was just a strain. The child is well-nourished, well-dressed, and has attended regular well-baby visits. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Believe the parents and treat the child
Admit the child for further evaluation and order a head CT
k: Suspected child abuse: protect, report, investigate. Red flags: delayed presentation, history inconsistent with development, fractures in non-ambulatory infants, injuries at different stages Report on reasonable suspicio
r: An 11-month-old with a radius and ulna fracture, a 2-day delay in seeking care and an explanation that may not match the child's mobility (falls on an outstretched hand with enough force to break both bones are unusual in infants) raises a reasonable suspicion of physical abuse. A well-dressed child
wo: B. Accepting the story ignores two red flags (infant age and delayed presentation); it would be right only for an ambulatory child with a consistent story and prompt presentation. | C. Admission for evaluation (skeletal survey, and neuroimaging in infants) is part of the work up and protects the child, but it does not replace reporting; it is the answer when the question asks how to keep the child safe or what investigation to do. | D. Police are involved by the child protection system when needed; the physician's duty is to report to child protection services, not to make a criminal accusation.

q: 11-month-old boy presents with right ulnar and radial fractures , 2 days after a reported fall on an outstretched hand. The parents delayed seeking medical care , stating that they did not notice any bruising and initially believed the injury was just a strain. The child is well-nourished, well-dressed, and has attended regular well-baby visits. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Believe the parents and treat the child
Admit the child for further evaluation and order a head CT
Report the police for child abuse
k: Suspected abuse: the report goes to the child protection authority, usually through the hospital child protection team or social worker. Threshold: reasonable suspicion, not proof Do not confront or accuse the parents Ke
wo: A. Believing the parents ignores the red flags (infant age, delayed presentation); fits only a consistent story with prompt presentation in a walking child. | B. Admission with work up (skeletal survey, head imaging in infants) is part of management and is the answer if the child's safety or the investigation is asked, but it does not fulfil the duty to report. | C. The hospital social worker or child protection team often helps file the report, but the duty is to report to the child protection authority itself; whether this wording counts is uncertain. | D. Police are not the first contact; child protection services decide whether law enforcement is involved.

q: Rooting reflex and when disappearin? A 2-week-old infant seen in the clinic. Rubbing side of his mouth with tip of the little finger is one of the primitive reflexes (see image). What is expected age (in months) for this reflex to disappear?
k: Primitive reflexes: approximate age of disappearance. Rooting and sucking: about 4 months Moro: by about 6 months Asymmetric tonic neck: about 3 to 6 months Palmar grasp: about 6 months; plantar grasp: about 12 months St
r: Stroking the side of the mouth makes the infant turn the head and open the mouth toward the stimulus: the rooting reflex . It is present from birth to help feeding and disappears at about 4 months as voluntary feeding control develops.
wo: A. 2 months is too early for rooting; the stepping reflex disappears around then. | C. 6 months matches the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes, not rooting. | D. 8 months is around when the parachute reflex appears; rooting is long gone.

q: A 2-week-old infant seen in the clinic. Rubbing side of the mouth with tip of the little finger is one of the primitive reflexes (see image). Which of the following is the name of this reflex ?
k: Primitive reflexes: approximate age of disappearance. Rooting and sucking: about 4 months Moro: by about 6 months Asymmetric tonic neck: about 3 to 6 months Palmar grasp: about 6 months; plantar grasp: about 12 months St
r: Touching the side of the mouth makes the newborn turn toward the stimulus and open the mouth: this is the rooting reflex, which helps the baby find the nipple. It is present at birth and fades at about 4 months.
wo: A. Moro is elicited by a sudden head drop or loud noise, producing arm extension and abduction then flexion. | C. Sucking is triggered by placing something inside the mouth (on the palate), not by stroking the cheek or corner of the mouth. | D. Parachute is a protective arm extension when the infant is tipped forward; it appears around 8 to 9 months, so it cannot be seen at 2 weeks.

q: A 2-week-old infant seen in the clinic. Rubbing side of his mouth with tip of the little finger is one of the primitive reflexes (see image). What is expected age (in months) for this reflex to disappear ?
k: Primitive reflexes: approximate age of disappearance. Rooting and sucking: about 4 months Moro: by about 6 months Asymmetric tonic neck: about 3 to 6 months Palmar grasp: about 6 months; plantar grasp: about 12 months St
r: The image shows the rooting reflex (stroking the side of the mouth, the infant turns toward it). It is present from birth and disappears at about 4 months .
kw: age (in months) for this reflex to disappear
wo: A. 2 months is when the stepping reflex fades, too early for rooting. | C. 6 months is the typical disappearance of the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes. | D. 8 months is when the parachute reflex appears.

q: A 3-year-old child seen in the clinic with fever and cough for 5 days following flu-like prodrome. On examination, he had decrease air entry and crackles over right lung middle zone . Chest X-ray is done (see image and lab results). Blood pressure 90/64 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Respiratory rate 20 /min, Temperature 36.6 C, Oxygen saturation 97 % . Hb 12 (normal 165-195 g/L newborn, 112-165 g/L child), Platelets count 328 (150-400 x 109/L), Neutrophils 80 (40-60%), WBC 22 (4.5-13.5 x 109/L 2-10 years; 4.5-11.1 x 109/L 11 years-older adult), Neutrophils 84% (2.4-7.3 x 109/L, 30%-77% 2-10 years; 2.7-6.5 x 109/L, 40%-75% 11 years-older adult), Lymphocytes 15% (2.8-9.3 x 109/L, 26%-56% birth; 3.7-10.7 x 109/L, 20%-64% 1-23 months). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Pediatric CAP: decide setting by severity. Stable, SpO2 normal, feeding: oral amoxicillin at home Admit: hypoxia, distress, grunting, dehydration, toxic, complications, under 3 to 6 months Atypical (older child, school a
r: Fever and cough with focal reduced air entry and crackles in the right middle zone, consolidation on X-ray, WBC 22 with neutrophilia point to bacterial community acquired pneumonia. The child is clinically stable: SpO2 97% , RR 20, normal BP, no distress and afebrile now, so he can be treated at hom
kw: crackles over right lung middle zone
wo: A. Reassurance would leave a bacterial pneumonia untreated; it fits a viral URTI with no focal chest signs. | B. Bronchodilators and steroids treat asthma or wheeze; there is no wheeze here, and steroids do not treat bacterial pneumonia. | C. Admission for IV antibiotics is for hypoxia (SpO2 below about 92%), respiratory distress, dehydration, inability to take oral medication, complications (effusion, empyema) or very young age.

q: Child Presented With Projectile Vomiting , non billous , palpable mass in ruq . What Is The initial step?
k: Pyloric stenosis workflow: 2 to 8 weeks, firstborn male, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hungry after Labs: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, paradoxical aciduria First investigation: ultrasound Stop feeds,
r: Projectile non-bilious vomiting with an RUQ palpable (olive) mass is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The compiler keys NPO as the initial step: feeding is withheld once the diagnosis is made, and stopping oral intake is immediate and effortless, before IV fluids are set up to correct the hypochloremi
wo: A. An NG tube is not routinely needed in pyloric stenosis; it is used when there is bilious vomiting or bowel obstruction requiring decompression. | C. Normal saline (with dextrose and potassium once urine output is confirmed) corrects the hypochloremic alkalosis and is the classic answer when the question asks for the fluid or the most important preoperative management.

q: Child Presented With Projectile Vomiting , Diagnosed With Pyloric Stenosis
k: Pyloric stenosis order: NPO, IV fluids and electrolytes, then pyloromyotomy. Fluid: normal saline, then add dextrose and potassium after urine output Never bicarbonate (patient is alkalotic) Surgery is definitive but ele
r: In a child diagnosed with pyloric stenosis , the compiler keys NPO: feeds are withheld immediately because oral intake only feeds further vomiting and worsens the alkalosis. Resuscitation with IV fluids and electrolyte correction then follows before surgery.
wo: B. Sodium bicarbonate is harmful: these infants already have a metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid. Bicarbonate is used for selected metabolic acidosis, not here. | C. IV sodium chloride (normal saline) is the correct fluid to correct the hypochloremic alkalosis and is the classic key when the question asks for fluid management; this card's compiler preferred NPO as the very first step. | D. Pyloromyotomy is the definitive treatment, but it is not an emergency and is done only after fluid and electrolyte correction to reduce anesthetic risk.

q: Sweet test positive What is most frequent complication :
k: Cystic fibrosis complications: Lung: bronchiectasis (most common), Pseudomonas and Staph infection, pneumothorax, hemoptysis GI: pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstruction Others
r: A positive sweat test means cystic fibrosis. Thick airway mucus causes recurrent infection and inflammation that permanently dilates the bronchi, so bronchiectasis is the most frequent complication and the main cause of morbidity and death. The fuller version adds recurrent chest infections and foul
wo: A. Malignancy (mainly GI tract cancers) is increased in long-term CF survivors but is far less frequent than lung disease. | C. This vague pulmonary option (emphysema in the fuller version) is not the typical CF lesion; CF damages the airways (bronchiectasis), whereas emphysema is the classic finding of smoking or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

q: A child brought by mother for development assessment. He can walk backwards , Follow simple commands . He started using a spoon and Pointing to things he is interested. What is the expected age for this child by months?
k: Toddler milestone anchors: 12 months: walks alone, pincer grasp, 1 to 2 words 15 months: walks well, tower of 2, follows simple command, points to show interest, begins spoon use 18 months: runs, tower of 4, spoon well,
r: Following simple commands and pointing to indicate interest are 15 month skills, and the child is only starting to use a spoon, which places him around 15 months. The compiler, following Nelson, keys all the versions of this recall (walks backward, stacks 2 blocks, follows a one step command) as 15
wo: A. 18 months: runs, walks up stairs with a hand held, tower of 4 cubes, uses a spoon well and has about 10 words; choose it when these more advanced skills are described. | C. 24 months: walks up and down stairs alone, kicks a ball, 2 word phrases, follows 2 step commands, tower of 6 to 7 cubes. | D. 48 months: hops on one foot, draws a cross or square, tells stories, plays cooperatively; far beyond this child.

q: A young patient presents complaining of recurrent urinary tract infections . What investigation should the doctor do in order to look for kidney scarring as a complication of recurrent UTIs. What's the investigation?
k: Pediatric UTI imaging by question: First febrile or recurrent UTI: renal and bladder ultrasound Hydronephrosis or suspected reflux: VCUG (MCUG) Renal scarring: DMSA scan Posterior urethral valves in boys: VCUG
r: The question asks specifically for kidney scarring . A DMSA scan (technetium labelled dimercaptosuccinic acid) is taken up by functioning cortical tubular cells, so scars appear as photopenic defects; it is the gold standard to detect renal scarring, ideally done months after the acute infection.
wo: A. Renal ultrasound is the first investigation after a febrile or recurrent UTI to look for hydronephrosis and structural anomalies, but it is insensitive for cortical scars. | B. Contrast voiding urosonography (or micturating cystography) detects vesicoureteral reflux, the cause of recurrent UTI, not the scarring itself. | D. Voiding cystourethrogram is the test for vesicoureteral reflux and posterior urethral valves; choose it when ultrasound shows hydronephrosis or the question asks for reflux.

q: A child's mother had TB a year ago . Her kid now presents with signs and symptoms of TB; chest X-ray is positive . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: INH, rifampin, and pyrazinamide for 6 months
INH, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, then continue INH and rifampin for 4 months.
k: Active TB: 2 months HRZE, then 4 months HR (2HRZE/4HR). Latent TB (positive test, normal CXR, no symptoms): isoniazid alone or a rifampin-based short regimen Exposed child with no infection yet: window prophylaxis with i
r: The child has active TB (symptoms and a positive chest X-ray) after household exposure, so the treatment is the standard 6-month regimen : an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then a continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months.
kw: mother had TB a year ago
wo: A. INH for 9 months: a latent TB regimen for a positive skin test with a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms; monotherapy in active disease breeds resistance. | B. INH and rifampin for 4 months: resembles a latent TB or continuation phase regimen; without the intensive phase it is inadequate for active disease. | C. INH, rifampin and pyrazinamide for 6 months: pyrazinamide belongs only to the 2-month intensive phase, and the fourth drug (ethambutol) is omitted.

q: 17-Child with difficulty swallowing and congested throat, febrile, no cough , she is ill and sitting silently in her mother's but with her neck extended ?
k: Epiglottitis: airway first, then antibiotics. Clinical: high fever, toxic, drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod or sniffing posture, no cough Do not examine the throat or distress the child Secure airway in the OR
r: A febrile, ill-looking child with dysphagia , no cough , sitting still with the neck extended (sniffing or tripod posture) has acute epiglottitis . The airway can obstruct suddenly, so the first priority is a controlled airway: intubation in the operating room by anesthesia with ENT ready for trache
wo: B. Steroids: a mainstay of croup (barking cough, stridor, low-grade fever); they do not secure the airway in epiglottitis. | C. IV ceftriaxone: needed in epiglottitis, but only after the airway is secured; placing an IV first can agitate the child and precipitate obstruction. | D. Epinephrine: nebulized epinephrine is for moderate to severe croup and IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis; it does not treat epiglottitis.

q: 3 years old boy came with fever, muffled sound , and drooling of saliva on exam he looks acutely ill, sit on his mother's lap with his neck extended . Fever 39 What is the next step?
k: Epiglottitis = airway emergency: secure the airway first, antibiotics second. Clues: high fever, toxic, drooling, dysphagia, muffled (hot potato) voice, tripod or neck extended, no cough Avoid throat exam, IV lines or ly
r: A 3-year-old with fever 39 , muffled voice , drooling , looking acutely ill and sitting on the mother's lap with the neck extended has acute epiglottitis. The airway can close suddenly, so the next step is controlled intubation in the OR (or PICU) by anesthesia with ENT ready for a surgical airway,
wo: A. Racemic epinephrine: treats moderate to severe croup (barking cough, stridor); it does not relieve supraglottic swelling of epiglottitis. | B. IM dexamethasone: the standard treatment of croup; it does not secure a threatened airway. | D. IV ceftriaxone: the correct antibiotic for epiglottitis, but given after the airway is secured, since inserting a line can upset the child and trigger obstruction.

q: two years old child came with generalized tonic clonic seizure that lasted for three minute then stopped. Patient is drowsy but responsive fever 38° with runny nose and cough, family history of febrile seizure . no focal neurological sign or symptoms no neck stiffness . what's the most appropriate next step?
o: parent salary, reassurance and assessment for the source of fever
k: Simple febrile seizure: 6 months to 6 years, generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, back to baseline. Management: reassure, educate, antipyretics, treat the fever source Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, or recu
r: A 2-year-old with a generalized seizure lasting 3 minutes , fever from a viral URTI, a family history of febrile seizure, and no focal signs or neck stiffness has a simple febrile seizure . Management is parental reassurance and education, fever control, and finding the source of fever; no investiga
wo: A. Urgent EEG: not indicated after a simple febrile seizure; considered for complex or recurrent afebrile seizures or suspected epilepsy. | B. Urgent CT brain: reserved for focal deficits, persistent reduced consciousness, signs of raised intracranial pressure or trauma; none are present. | C. Prophylactic antiepileptic medication: does not prevent later epilepsy and has side effects, so it is not given after simple febrile seizures.

q: A preterm delivered at 34 weeks of gestation with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) failed weaning from mechanical ventilation , what is the most appropriate next step ?
k: BPD: oxygen need at 36 weeks corrected age in a preterm baby; ventilator-dependent infants may get low-dose steroids. Failed extubation after 1 to 2 weeks: short tapering course of low-dose dexamethasone Avoid steroids i
r: A preterm infant with bronchopulmonary dysplasia who fails weaning from mechanical ventilation (beyond the first week) is given a short, tapering course of low-dose dexamethasone . It reduces lung inflammation and facilitates extubation, while the low dose limits the neurodevelopmental harm seen wit
wo: A. High-dose dexamethasone: higher and early dosing is linked to cerebral palsy, gastrointestinal perforation, hyperglycemia and hypertension, so it is avoided. | C. High tidal volume: causes volutrauma and worsens BPD; lung-protective ventilation is the rule. | D. Low (forgot): the option was not recalled; if it was a low tidal volume or ventilator change, lung-protective settings are routine care but do not answer failed weaning the way low-dose steroids do.

q: A previously healthy 4-month-old uncircumcised boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever. He has not had vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or nasal congestion. There has been no known contact with ill persons. He has continued to breastfeed and has not had a decrease in the number of wet diapers. He is mildly ill-appearing but alert and interactive . Examination shows no focus of infection. Urinary catheterization is performed. Temperature 39.1 C. Urinalysis shows: pH 7.5 (normal 4.3-8), specific gravity 1010 (normal 1001-1030), protein absent, glucose absent, ketones absent, nitrite positive (absent normally), leukocytes 30-40 (normal 0-3 per high power field), erythrocytes 5-10 (normal 0-2 per high power field). Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical therapy?
k: Febrile UTI in infants: route depends on how sick the child is. Well-appearing, feeding, older than 2 months: oral cephalosporin (e.g. cephalexin) Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated, or under 2 months: admit, IV antibiotics Dia
r: Fever with a catheter sample showing positive nitrite and pyuria in a 4-month-old uncircumcised boy is a febrile UTI. He is older than 2 to 3 months , only mildly ill, alert , still breastfeeding with normal wet diapers, so he can take oral antibiotics, which are as effective as IV therapy in well-a
wo: B. Oral azithromycin does not reliably cover the Gram-negative uropathogens (E. coli) that cause UTI; it is used for atypical respiratory infections or pertussis. | C. IV ceftriaxone is right when the infant is toxic or ill-appearing, vomiting or unable to feed, dehydrated, or under about 2 months; none apply here. | D. IV cefuroxime is also a parenteral option for infants who cannot take oral therapy; this child tolerates feeds and is well enough for oral treatment.

q: A pediatric patient has fatigue and weakness that worsen by the end of the day ; his parents report evening difficulty keeping his eyes open with bilateral ptosis , with no muscle wasting, normal reflexes, and intact sensation; what is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
k: Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, ocular first, reflexes and sensation preserved. Diagnosis: AChR antibodies (anti-MuSK if negative) Electrophysiology: decremental response on repetitive stimulation, single-fiber EM
r: Fatigable weakness that worsens by the end of the day with bilateral ptosis , and normal reflexes, normal sensation and no wasting , is the picture of myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disorder. The most appropriate diagnostic test is serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies , which are spe
kw: worsen by the end of the day
wo: A. Muscle biopsy is used for myopathies (e.g. muscular dystrophy, myositis) with fixed weakness, often wasting and raised CK; it is not used to diagnose MG. | B. A standard nerve conduction study evaluates neuropathies such as GBS (areflexia, sensory loss); it is typically normal in MG unless repetitive stimulation is specifically performed. | D. Creatine kinase is raised in muscle diseases (dystrophies, myositis); it is normal in MG.

q: 5y/o child came in pre school clinic just to check for pre school, you found the right ? eye misaligned what to do NEXT / initial?
o: Refer to pediatric optha next day
Gather Detailed History That Point Out history that point out for possible perinatal
k: Strabismus in a child: assess, confirm, refer. History: onset, perinatal/birth history, family history, diplopia, head posture Exam: Hirschberg (corneal light reflex), cover/uncover test, red reflex Any strabismus persis
r: This recall's key is to gather a detailed history first, looking for perinatal events (e.g. birth trauma) that could explain the squint. The compiler's reasoning: the stem says 'you found' the eye misaligned at a routine preschool check, so this may be a long-standing deviation that was never notice
wo: A. Referral to pediatric ophthalmology is required for any persistent strabismus at this age, but it follows the initial assessment; it is not the first thing done in clinic. | B. Glasses are prescribed by ophthalmology after cycloplegic refraction (e.g. accommodative esotropia); they are never started before the cause is assessed. | C. The Hirschberg corneal light reflex test is the bedside screening/confirmation test for strabismus; it is the examination step after history, and in many keys it is the answer when the question asks how to screen or confirm.

q: A newborn has not passed meconium within 48 hours and develops abdominal distension. Rectal examination causes explosive passage of stool and temporarily relieves the symptoms. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
k: Hirschsprung disease: delayed meconium, distension, explosive stool on DRE. Initial imaging: abdominal x-ray, contrast enema (transition zone) Confirmation: rectal suction biopsy (no ganglion cells) Anorectal manometry:
r: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours , abdominal distension, and an explosive passage of stool after rectal examination (squirt sign) is classic Hirschsprung disease. The definitive diagnostic step is a rectal suction biopsy , which shows absent ganglion cells (with hypertrophied nerve fibers).
wo: A. An oral probiotic has no role in diagnosing or treating a mechanical/aganglionic obstruction. | B. Abdominal ultrasound is used for pyloric stenosis or intussusception; it does not diagnose Hirschsprung disease. | D. A glycerin suppository may relieve simple functional constipation but would only temporarily decompress the bowel here and gives no diagnosis.

q: A 7-year-old child presents with 12 days of persistent purulent nasal discharge , daytime cough, and low-grade fever; there is frontal bone tenderness but no periorbital swelling and normal eye exam; what is the appropriate next step in management?
k: Acute bacterial sinusitis in children (clinical diagnosis). Persistent: nasal discharge or daytime cough over 10 days without improvement Severe: fever 39 or higher with purulent discharge for 3 days or more Worsening: n
r: Purulent nasal discharge with daytime cough lasting 12 days (beyond 10 days without improvement), low-grade fever and frontal tenderness meets the definition of acute bacterial sinusitis with persistent symptoms. With a normal eye exam and no periorbital swelling (no complication), the treatment is
wo: A. Supportive care alone is right for a viral URTI with symptoms under 10 days and improving; persistent symptoms beyond 10 days justify antibiotics. | C. Intranasal corticosteroids may be an adjunct, mainly in allergic rhinitis or chronic sinusitis; they do not treat bacterial infection. | D. Sinus x-ray is not needed for uncomplicated sinusitis (clinical diagnosis); CT is reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial complications or surgical planning.

q: A 10-year-old child presents with a tender, warm, red swelling on the left leg that has gradually increased in size. There is no history of trauma or insect bite . The child has a low-grade fever but is otherwise normal . What is the initial step in management?
k: Pediatric cellulitis: indications for IV antibiotics. Fever or systemic features Face, perineum, hand or foot involvement Rapid progression Toxic appearance or oral intolerance Otherwise: oral antibiotics and follow-up
r: This recall's key is IV antibiotics because, following the compiler's table of pediatric cellulitis IV indications, fever (even if low grade) is listed alongside facial, perineal, hand or foot involvement, rapid progression, toxicity and oral intolerance. The child has a tender, warm, red swelling t
kw: no history of trauma or insect bite
low-grade fever but is otherwise normal
wo: A. Oral antibiotics with follow-up are used for mild, afebrile cellulitis in a well child without high-risk sites; in this key the presence of fever moves treatment to IV. | B. Warm compresses and observation suit a superficial abscess that is pointing or a minor localized reaction, not spreading cellulitis with fever. | C. X-ray is used when osteomyelitis, a foreign body or gas is suspected (e.g. bone pain, trauma, crepitus); it does not change initial management of simple cellulitis.

q: A 12-year-old presents with diarrhea, vomiting, miosis , bronchoconstriction , sweating, and excessive secretions . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Toxidromes by pupils and secretions. Cholinergic (organophosphate): miosis, wet (sweating, salivation, bronchorrhea), bradycardia Anticholinergic: mydriasis, dry, hot, flushed, retention Sympathomimetic (cocaine): mydria
r: Diarrhea, vomiting, miosis , bronchoconstriction , sweating and excessive secretions form the cholinergic (muscarinic) toxidrome (DUMBBELSS), caused by acetylcholinesterase inhibition. In a child this is most likely organophosphate (insecticide) poisoning; a garlic odor on the breath in the original
wo: B. DKA causes vomiting and abdominal pain with Kussmaul breathing, dehydration and fruity breath, not miosis, bronchorrhea and sweating. | C. Cyanide causes rapid collapse, seizures, severe lactic acidosis and a bitter almond odor, without a cholinergic secretion pattern. | D. Cocaine is sympathomimetic: mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia and agitation, the opposite of miosis and secretions.

q: A child presents with symptoms of celiac disease and has positive anti-tTG IgA and positive anti-endomysial antibody (EMA) . Which of the following is considered the confirmatory test ?
k: Celiac disease diagnosis. Screen: anti-tTG IgA with total IgA (IgG-based tests if IgA deficient) Confirm: duodenal biopsy on a gluten diet HLA-DQ2/DQ8: rules out when negative Follow-up: tTG falls on a gluten-free diet;
r: In suspected celiac disease, serology (anti-tTG IgA, EMA) is the screening step and duodenal biopsy (multiple samples while on a gluten-containing diet) is the confirmatory test, showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. The lead-in asks for the confirmatory test,
wo: A. Skipping further testing relies on the no-biopsy pathway (very high tTG with positive EMA on a separate sample), which is not universally accepted; the standard confirmatory step is biopsy. | C. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value and is used to exclude celiac disease, not to confirm it. | D.
