Repeating serology is used to monitor adherence to a gluten-free diet after diagnosis, not to confirm the diagnosis.

q: Name of the reflex ?
k: Primitive reflexes, stimulus and disappearance: Rooting: stroke cheek, mouth turns to stimulus; gone by about 4 months Stepping: soles on surface, walking movements; gone by about 2 months ATNR (fencing): head turned, fa
r: The picture shows a finger stroking the cheek and the infant's mouth turning toward the finger. A tactile stimulus at the side of the mouth that makes the infant turn and seek the stimulus is the rooting reflex, present from birth to help locate the nipple for feeding.
wo: B. Stepping reflex: the infant is held upright with the soles touching a surface and makes alternating walking movements; it involves the legs, not the mouth.

q: (Recall context from the page: a picture of the rooting reflex.) Time of disappearance ?
k: Match the reflex to its disappearance age: Stepping: about 2 months ATNR: about 3 months (2 accepted in recalls) Rooting, Galant: about 4 months Moro, palmar grasp: about 6 months Babinski: 12 to 18 months Parachute: app
r: The picture is the rooting reflex (stroking the cheek, mouth turns toward it). It is present from birth and disappears by about 4 months , as voluntary head control and feeding behaviour take over.
wo: A. By 2 months: the age usually quoted for disappearance of the stepping reflex, and the age the ATNR (fencing) question accepts; too early for rooting. | C. By 6 months: disappearance age of the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes, not rooting.

q: 14girl come with Amenorrhea , no secondary sexual character FSH and LH was low
k: No puberty: FSH and LH split central from gonadal causes. High FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic): ovarian failure, think Turner; next karyotype Low FSH/LH (hypogonadotropic): constitutional delay, Kallmann, CNS tumor, chronic i

q: A 24-month-old baby is brought in with a right sided red inflamed hemiscrotum. On exploration, the right tests is viable however; the cord is thick and oedematous . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Acute scrotum in children: Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex; explore immediately Appendage torsion: upper-pole tenderness, blue dot, cremasteric reflex present; analge
r: At exploration the testis was viable (not twisted or ischemic) and the cord was thick and edematous . Inflammation that thickens the cord and epididymis with a healthy testis is epididymo-orchitis; the red, inflamed hemiscrotum fits the inflammatory process.
wo: A. Testicular torsion: exploration would show a twisted cord and a dusky or necrotic testis; a viable, untwisted testis excludes it. | C. Incarcerated inguinal hernia: there would be bowel or omentum in a hernial sac extending up into the groin, not just an edematous cord. | D. Torsion of a testicular appendage: shows a small infarcted appendage at the upper pole (blue dot sign) with a normal cord, usually in boys aged 7 to 12.

q: 6 year Child fully vaccinated came with injury from rusty nail What the propriate mangement additional to ab
k: Tetanus prophylaxis in wounds: Clean minor wound: vaccine if last dose >10 years or unknown Dirty or tetanus-prone wound: vaccine if last dose >5 years Unknown or fewer than 3 doses: vaccine, plus tetanus immunoglobulin
r: A fully vaccinated 6-year-old has just completed (or recently received) the DTaP booster at 4 to 6 years, so the last dose is well within 5 years even for a tetanus-prone rusty-nail wound. No vaccine or immunoglobulin is needed; what every wound still needs is thorough cleaning and irrigation (with
wo: A. Td: the booster for children 7 years and older and adults; it would be given for a dirty wound if more than 5 years have passed since the last dose. | B. DTaP: the formulation for children under 7, given for a dirty wound only if the series is incomplete or the last dose was more than 5 years ago. | C. Nothing: wrong because wound cleaning and irrigation are always required, even when no tetanus prophylaxis is needed.

q: 1-week-old infant presents with a history of conjunctivitis associated with white eye discharge . Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
k: Ophthalmia neonatorum by onset: Within 24 hours: chemical (prophylaxis drops) 2 to 5 days: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, hyperpurulent, risk of corneal perforation; IV/IM ceftriaxone 5 to 14 days: Chlamydia trachomatis; oral er
r: Neonatal conjunctivitis appearing at 1 week (typical window 5 to 14 days) with watery to mucoid discharge fits Chlamydia trachomatis acquired from the birth canal. The timing is the key: gonococcal infection starts earlier (2 to 5 days) with profuse purulent discharge, and chemical conjunctivitis ap
wo: A. Haemophilus influenzae: causes bacterial conjunctivitis in older infants and children (often with otitis media); not the classic organism at 1 week. | B. Adenovirus: causes viral conjunctivitis with fever, pharyngitis or diarrhea in older children; uncommon in the first week of life.

q: Which of the following cerebral palsy type is associated with Kernicterus ?
k: Cerebral palsy type by lesion site: Spastic (pyramidal tract): diplegia in prematurity/PVL, hemiplegia after stroke, quadriplegia after severe HIE Dyskinetic (basal ganglia): kernicterus, HIE at term Ataxic (cerebellum)
r: Kernicterus is deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) and brainstem nuclei. Basal ganglia injury produces dyskinetic (athetoid or choreoathetoid) cerebral palsy, often with sensorineural hearing loss and upward gaze palsy.
wo: A. Spastic: the most common type, from upper motor neuron (pyramidal) injury such as periventricular leukomalacia in preterm infants (diplegia) or stroke (hemiplegia). | B. Ataxic: results from cerebellar damage, giving wide-based gait and intention tremor. | C. Hypotonic: a nonspecific early or atonic picture, not the classic consequence of kernicterus.

q: Child diagnosed with meningococcal , contact with brother and sister. What is the most appropriate chemoprophylaxis for household members ?
k: Meningococcal chemoprophylaxis for close contacts: Rifampicin twice daily for 2 days (common choice in children) Ciprofloxacin single oral dose Ceftriaxone single IM dose (preferred in pregnancy) Hib contacts: rifampicin
r: Household contacts of a meningococcal case need chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible, regardless of vaccination. Accepted regimens are rifampicin for 2 days, a single IM dose of ceftriaxone, or a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin ; of the listed options only ciprofloxacin is given with the correct r
wo: A. Penicillin and rifampicin for 1 week: penicillin does not eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage, and rifampicin prophylaxis is a 2 day course, not a week. | C. Ceftriaxone IM 3 doses: ceftriaxone is effective but given as a single IM dose (useful in pregnancy); multiple doses are not needed.

q: picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia , the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue , CBC shows microcytic hypochromic RBC , What is the treatment ?
k: Microcytic + koilonychia = iron deficiency, treat with oral iron. Clues: pallor, pica, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, thrombocytosis Labs: low MCV, low ferritin, high RDW Common cause in children: excess cow's milk, poo
r: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic film is iron deficiency anaemia. First line treatment in a child is oral ferrous sulfate , continued for about 3 months after Hb normalises to refill stores.
wo: A. Parenteral iron is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance or non-adherence to oral iron, or failure of oral therapy; it is not first line. | C. Folic acid treats folate deficiency, which causes a macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia, not a microcytic one. | D. B12 treats megaloblastic anaemia with high MCV and possible neurological signs; it does not correct a microcytic picture.

q: Young boy under 10 with fatigue dsypnea and palpitations during physical activity . His physical examination is normal. His older brother has a history of sudden cardiac death . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Family history of sudden death in the young = exclude HCM (echo + ECG). Autosomal dominant sarcomere mutation Murmur: ejection systolic at left sternal edge, louder with Valsalva/standing Symptoms: exertional syncope, ch
r: Exertional fatigue, dyspnoea and palpitations in a child with an older brother who had sudden cardiac death point to an inherited cardiomyopathy, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in the young. A normal examination does not exclude it, since many have no mu
kw: older brother has a history of sudden cardiac death
wo: A. PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur and bounding pulses; it is not familial and is not linked to sibling sudden death. | B. AVSD is usually detected in infancy (often with Down syndrome) with a murmur and heart failure; the exam would not be normal. | C. VSD produces a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge; a normal exam and family sudden death argue against it.

q: -5m infant is brought by his mother, who has noticed decreased activity and that he no longer smiles . He has repeated crusts of sudden brief flexion-extension spasms , each lasting 1-2 seconds, with about 20 spasms per cluster . An EEG is ordered. Which finding is expected?
k: West syndrome triad: spasms + hypsarrhythmia + developmental arrest. Onset: usually 3 to 12 months Spasms in clusters, often on waking Causes: tuberous sclerosis, hypoxic injury, metabolic, idiopathic Treatment: ACTH or
r: A 5 month old with clusters of brief flexion extension spasms (1 to 2 seconds, about 20 per cluster) and developmental regression (stopped smiling, less active) has infantile spasms (West syndrome). The characteristic EEG is hypsarrhythmia : chaotic, high voltage, disorganised background with multif
wo: B. Centrotemporal spikes are seen in benign rolandic epilepsy of school-age children with nocturnal facial or oropharyngeal seizures. | C. Slow spike and wave below 3 Hz is the EEG of Lennox Gastaut syndrome, which begins later in early childhood with multiple seizure types; infantile spasms may evolve into it. | D. Generalised 3 Hz spike and wave is the pattern of childhood absence epilepsy with staring spells in school-age children.

q: mother brought her 2month baby with squint next assessment ?didn't mention sudden or hx of truma
k: Infant squint: confirm with the corneal light reflex first. Reflex displaced temporally = esotropia; displaced nasally = exotropia Intermittent squint can be normal up to about 4 months Constant squint at any age or any
r: The first assessment of an infant with a squint is the corneal light reflex (Hirschberg test) : a penlight at both eyes should give symmetrical, centred reflections, and a displaced reflex in one eye confirms a true deviation and separates it from pseudostrabismus (broad epicanthal folds). It needs
wo: B. The cover test (cover/uncover) needs the child to fixate on a target and is the test for older infants and toddlers, roughly from 6 months; a 2 month old cannot cooperate. | C. Referral to ophthalmology is right when the squint is confirmed and constant, persists beyond about 4 months, or the red reflex is abnormal (leukocoria); first you confirm the deviation with the corneal reflex.

q: An 8-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 75/50 mmHg and a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. His ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: SVT: stability decides the first step. Unstable (hypotension, shock, altered consciousness, heart failure): synchronized cardioversion Stable: vagal manoeuvre, then adenosine (rapid IV push with flush) Child minimum syst
r: The ECG is a regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT), and the first decision is stability. A BP of 75/50 in an 8 year old is hypotension (below the lower limit of about 70 + 2 × age = 86 mmHg systolic), so he is haemodynamically unstable even though he is alert. Unstable SVT with a pulse is treated
wo: A. Adenosine is the drug for stable SVT after vagal manoeuvres fail (or can be given quickly if IV access is ready), but hypotension calls for cardioversion. | B. Amiodarone is for stable wide complex tachycardia or refractory SVT under expert advice; it is slower and can worsen hypotension. | C. Vagal stimulation (ice to the face in infants, Valsalva in older children) is first line only for a stable child with SVT.

q: A 9 year old girl in contact with her maid who is has confirmed active tuberculosis TB and lives with them at the same house The child is asymptomatic . Doesn't complain from any physical symptoms. After testing, IGRA is +ve and chest x-ray pic is provided What is the most definitive treatment?
o: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid, and rifampin for 4 months
k: Latent TB (positive TST/IGRA, no symptoms, normal CXR): preventive therapy. Preferred: 3 months weekly isoniazid + rifapentine (3HP), 4 months rifampin (4R), 3 months daily isoniazid + rifampin (3HR) Alternative: isoniaz
r: An asymptomatic child with a positive IGRA after household contact and a normal chest X ray has latent TB infection, not active disease, so she needs preventive therapy, not full treatment. Rifamycin based short regimens are preferred because they have higher completion rates and similar efficacy to
wo: A. Isoniazid alone for 6 (or 9) months treats latent TB too, but it is the older, longer alternative with poorer completion and more hepatotoxicity; short rifamycin regimens are preferred. | C. A three drug regimen with pyrazinamide is not a latent TB regimen; pyrazinamide belongs to active TB treatment (or old rifampin-pyrazinamide courses abandoned for liver toxicity). | D. Four drugs for 2 months then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months is the standard regimen for active TB, right only if she had symptoms or an abnormal chest X ray.

q: A 10 years old patient came with mother with eye puffiness for one week and had history of flu like illness No lower limb edema or any remarkable findings in abdomen/chest Protein was low Urine protein was 4+ What's the dx
k: Nephrotic vs nephritic in children: Nephrotic: proteinuria > 3.5 g/day (> 40 mg/m²/h), albumin < 25 g/L, oedema, hyperlipidaemia Child: minimal change disease, steroid responsive, first line prednisolone Nephritic: haema
r: Periorbital puffiness (worse in the morning) in a child, with low protein and urine protein 4+ , is nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, with hyperlipidaemia. The preceding flu like illness is a common trigger, and normal BP without haematuria fits minimal change disea
wo: A. Nephritic syndrome gives haematuria (cola urine, RBC casts), hypertension, oliguria and only mild proteinuria, typically 1 to 3 weeks after streptococcal throat or skin infection. | C. Hereditary angioedema causes recurrent non pitting swelling of face, limbs, gut or larynx with low C4, without proteinuria or hypoalbuminaemia. | D. Protein losing enteropathy causes low albumin and oedema through the gut, often with diarrhoea, but urine protein is negative.

q: Pediatric pt have symptoms of ( encephalitis or meningitis ) Hot to prevent risk to his family ?
k: Meningitis contacts: prophylaxis depends on the organism. Neisseria meningitidis: prophylaxis for household and close contacts (rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone in pregnancy) Hib: rifampicin for household with u

q: A 65-year-old female presented with progressive loss of recent memory , can't remember place, time or person, can't remember names. Family noted a Day-to-day deterioration. Loss of skilled motor skills. No change in personality or social behavior. Lack of insight . What's the diagnosis?
k: Dementia type by the first and dominant feature. Recent memory first, personality preserved: Alzheimer Fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism: Lewy body Early personality/behavior change, younger age: frontote
r: A 65-year-old with gradually progressive loss of recent memory , disorientation, naming difficulty and loss of skilled motor tasks (apraxia), with preserved personality and social behavior and lack of insight, is the classic picture of Alzheimer disease. It is the most common dementia and starts wit
wo: B. Prion disease (CJD) causes a rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months with myoclonus and ataxia, not a slow memory first decline. | C. Lewy body dementia shows fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism, none of which are described. | D. Multi-infarct dementia progresses stepwise with focal neurological signs and vascular risk factors, not a smooth decline.

q: A 26-year-old woman presented with insomnia, fatigue, and sadness. She delivered her first child 5 days ago . Examination reveals a tearful and depressed appearance . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Postpartum mood disorders. Blues: days 2 to 5, lasts under 2 weeks, mild, no impairment: reassure and follow up Depression: symptoms 2 weeks or more, within weeks to months, impaired function: SSRI with or without psycho
r: This recall's key reads the tearful, depressed appearance with insomnia, fatigue and sadness after delivery as postpartum depression rather than simple blues. For postpartum depression an SSRI (for example sertraline, compatible with breastfeeding) is the first line drug treatment, with psychotherap
kw: delivered her first child 5 days ago
wo: B. Benzodiazepines do not treat depression, risk dependence and sedate the infant via breast milk; not appropriate. | C. Follow up in about 1 week is the management of postpartum blues (onset days 2 to 3, mild, resolves within 2 weeks); the key treats this presentation as depression that needs treatment. | D. Multivitamins have no role in treating postpartum mood disorders.

q: Seventeen-year-old female presents with decreased concentration for past 6 months; spends around 9 hours daily on social media and compares herself frequently with others. Symptoms suggestive of anxiety and depression but no prior medical treatment . What is the best course of action?
o: Force her to leave social media
k: Adolescent depression and anxiety ladder: Mild to moderate: psychotherapy (CBT) first Moderate to severe or no response: add SSRI (fluoxetine first line) Always screen for suicide risk Lifestyle measures (sleep, screen t
r: A 17-year-old with anxiety and depressive symptoms linked to heavy social media use and constant comparison with others , and no prior treatment , should start with psychotherapy. CBT is first line for mild to moderate depression and anxiety in adolescents; it targets the negative thought patterns b
wo: A. Antidepressants (fluoxetine first line in adolescents) are added for moderate to severe depression or when psychotherapy fails, with monitoring for suicidal thoughts; they are not the first step in an untreated teenager with this picture. | B. Forcing her off social media is coercive, damages the therapeutic alliance and does not treat the underlying anxiety and depression. | C. Limiting screen time is a sensible supportive measure, but on its own it does not treat established anxiety and depressive symptoms; it is better built into CBT as a behavioral goal.

q: An 82-year-old man hospitalized for a severe urinary tract infection develops acute confusion, agitation, and fluctuating consciousness . He is diagnosed with delirium . In addition to treating the infection, what is the most appropriate supportive measure ?
o: Frequently reorient him to time and place
Keep him in a dark, isolated room
k: Delirium: treat the cause, then non-drug measures first. Reorientation, clocks, calendars, family presence Daylight by day, quiet dark sleep at night Glasses, hearing aids, hydration, mobilization Avoid restraints, antic
r: Delirium is managed by treating the cause (here the UTI) plus non-pharmacological supportive measures , the first line of which is frequent reorientation (clocks, calendars, familiar faces), together with a calm lit environment, sleep hygiene, glasses and hearing aids. Antipsychotics are reserved fo
wo: A. Routine haloperidol is not recommended; low-dose antipsychotic is used only for severe agitation or distress endangering the patient or others, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. | C. Routine physical restraints worsen agitation, cause injury and prolong delirium; they are a last resort. | D. A dark, isolated room removes orientation cues and worsens delirium; patients need a well-lit room with day/night cues and familiar people.

q: A 28-year-old [gender not recalled] known case of asthma and alcohol consumption presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident . [Number of days not specified] days after the accident, he starts to have tremors, sweating , and (additional symptoms consistent with alcohol withdrawal). What is the most appropriate initial treatment ?
k: Alcohol withdrawal timeline and treatment: 6 to 24 h: tremor, sweating, anxiety, tachycardia 12 to 48 h: withdrawal seizures 48 to 96 h: delirium tremens (confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability) Treatment: benz
r: A drinker who develops tremors and sweating a few days after admission (alcohol cut off by hospitalization after the MVA) is in alcohol withdrawal. Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice to control withdrawal and prevent seizures and delirium tremens, and thiamine must be given alongside (ideal
wo: B. Chlordiazepoxide: a correct benzodiazepine for withdrawal, but alone it omits thiamine; the combined option is more complete and safer. | C. IV fluid: supportive and often needed for sweating and poor intake, but it does not treat withdrawal; giving dextrose fluids before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. | D. Not recalled: cannot be assessed.

q: 17 years old male, with 6 months of recurrent episodes of muscle cramps and fatigue, presented with muscle weakness since the morning. His father was diagnosed with HTN when he was 30 years old. BP 162/102, HR 70. Na 142, K 2.7 , bicarb 34, renin serum low , aldosterone serum low . Genetic testing requested SCNN1B and SCNN1G . Whats the most likely diagnosis?
k: Hypertension + hypokalaemia: look at renin and aldosterone. High renin, high aldosterone: renal artery stenosis, renin secreting tumour Low renin, high aldosterone: Conn syndrome Low renin, low aldosterone: Liddle, appar
r: A young man with hypertension , hypokalaemia (K 2.7) and metabolic alkalosis (bicarbonate 34) with low renin AND low aldosterone has mineralocorticoid excess that is not due to aldosterone. A father with early hypertension suggests autosomal dominant inheritance, and SCNN1B and SCNN1G encode subunit
wo: A. Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) shares hypertension and hypokalaemia but has HIGH aldosterone with suppressed renin (high aldosterone to renin ratio). | C. Bartter syndrome gives hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis but with NORMAL or LOW blood pressure and high renin and aldosterone, because it is a salt wasting defect of the loop of Henle. | D. Cushing syndrome can cause hypertension and hypokalaemia (especially ectopic ACTH) but comes with cushingoid features and raised cortisol, not an ENaC gene defect.

q: Woman on 15 mg methotrexate for RA in remission. 4 months ago LFTs were normal. This visit they were mildly elevated: AST 90 , ALT 84 . Like above reference range but less that x2 the upper normal limit . Whats the most appropriate management
k: Methotrexate with raised ALT: grade it against the ULN. ALT <2-3x ULN, asymptomatic: continue, repeat LFTs, avoid alcohol DILI criterion 1: ALT ≥3x ULN plus symptoms or high bilirubin: stop DILI criterion 2: ALT ≥5x ULN
kw: less that x2 the upper normal limit
wo: A. Liver US: not needed for a mild, asymptomatic, isolated transaminase rise; imaging is for persistent elevation, cholestatic pattern, or features of chronic liver disease. | B. Liver biopsy: invasive and reserved for persistent unexplained abnormalities or suspected methotrexate fibrosis after repeated rises, not a first mild abnormality. | C. Stop methotrexate: right when ALT is >3x ULN with symptoms or high bilirubin, or >5x ULN without symptoms (the lookalike with AST 300, ALT 280); here it would needlessly risk an RA flare. | D. (forgot): recalled as possibly 'Reassure & follow up'; if it carries the meaning of observe or repeat LFTs, it is the answer.

q: A 35-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis who maintained on methotrexate 15 mg weekly . She is currently on remission. 4 months ago, her liver function tests were normal but the most recent liver function tests are shown (see lab results). Aspartate aminotransferase 300 (12-40 IU/L), Alanine aminotransferase 280 (5-40 IU/L), Albumin 30 (34-56 g/L). What is the most appropriate action to be done for her abnormal liver function tests?
k: Methotrexate hepatotoxicity: thresholds decide stop versus observe. ALT ≥5x ULN without symptoms: stop ALT ≥3x ULN with symptoms or high bilirubin: stop Below criteria and asymptomatic: observe and repeat LFTs Monitor LF
r: Her LFTs were normal 4 months ago and now ALT 280 with ULN 40 is about 7x ULN, above the 5x ULN threshold (5 x 40 = 200) that defines drug induced liver injury even without symptoms. Methotrexate is the likely culprit, so the most appropriate action is to stop methotrexate, then repeat LFTs and look
wo: A. Do ultrasound for the liver: may be part of later workup, but it does not address the injury; removing the offending drug comes first. | B. Start glucocorticoids: used for autoimmune hepatitis (positive ANA, high IgG, interface hepatitis); drug injury is managed by withdrawing the drug, not steroids. | D. Order liver biopsy: reserved for persistent unexplained abnormalities or suspected methotrexate fibrosis; not the first action for an acute rise.

q: Patient undergoing CRC screening . The found a sigmoid polyp that was completely resected Histopath :Sigmoid Tubular adenoma 1.5 cm resected When should the Next colonoscopy be preformed ?
k: Post polypectomy surveillance: Normal colonoscopy: 10 years 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years 3-4 small adenomas: 3-5 years Advanced adenoma (≥10 mm, villous, high grade dysplasia) or 5-10 adenomas: 3 years Pieceme
r: A completely resected tubular adenoma of 1.5 cm is an advanced adenoma because its size is ≥10 mm. Surveillance colonoscopy after an advanced adenoma is recommended at 3 years , provided the bowel prep was adequate and resection complete.
wo: A. 3-6 months: for piecemeal resection of a large polyp (≥20 mm) to check the site for residual tissue, or an incomplete resection; this was completely resected. | C. 10 years: the interval after a normal colonoscopy or small hyperplastic polyps only. | D. No follow up colonoscopy: adenomas need surveillance; stopping applies only around age 75 or with limited life expectancy.

q: 23 wemone with SLE come to clinc with 3 month history of lower extremity swelling, SOB, no chest pain fever or palpitations, on examination Jagular venous destination, enogorge with inspiration , clear breath sound, heart sound were distant with early diastolic sound without gallops or murmur, abdominal shifting dullness , lower limp edema to the level of ankle were noted. Pb 110/70, HR 96, RR 22 OR 25, T 36.6, O2 90. LABS: Hb 8 or 10, Ceriat 150, Albumin 28, Low c3 and c4, WBC 3, Platlate 450, AST 100, ALT 94, No urea. Which of the following SLE associations conditions explain her presentation?
k: Constrictive pericarditis signature: Raised JVP with Kussmaul sign Pericardial knock (early diastolic sound) Right sided failure: ascites, hepatomegaly, edema; lungs clear Causes: TB, viral, post radiation, post surgery,
r: In a woman with SLE, the JVP engorging with inspiration is Kussmaul sign, the early diastolic sound without gallop or murmur is a pericardial knock, and distant heart sounds with ascites and leg edema reflect right sided failure from a restricted heart. Clear lungs make left heart failure unlikely.
kw: heart sound were distant with early diastolic sound
wo: B. Renal failure: lupus nephritis causes edema, but it would not produce Kussmaul sign or a pericardial knock; no urea rise is reported. | C. Liver failure: ascites and mild transaminase rise can occur, but it does not cause raised JVP; here hepatic congestion is secondary to the heart. | D. MI: there is no chest pain, and MI gives gallops or murmurs and pulmonary congestion rather than a pericardial knock.

q: 30 y/o male complaining of 4 months upper abdominal pain after eating , no medication, no family history of gastric or esophagus cancer, unremarkable examination . Vitally stable. BMI 35, Hb 15, Platlate 250, WBC 8 (NOT SURE). Which of the following most appropriate next step?
k: Dyspepsia without alarm features: test and treat H. pylori. Tests: urea breath test or stool antigen Positive: eradication therapy; negative: PPI trial Alarm features: age ≥60, weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding or anemia,
r: A 30 year old with 4 months of postprandial upper abdominal pain, no family history of upper GI cancer, normal examination and a normal Hb has uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features. The recommended approach is test and treat for H. pylori (urea breath test or stool antigen), with endoscopy
wo: B. Upper endoscopy: indicated with alarm features (age ≥60, weight loss, dysphagia, GI bleeding or anemia, persistent vomiting, mass, family history of cancer) or failure of empirical therapy. | C. Abdominal CT: for suspected pancreatic or other structural disease or complications; not part of routine dyspepsia workup. | D. Barium esophagogram: for dysphagia or suspected hiatal hernia, achalasia or stricture; not for simple dyspepsia.

q: A 20-year-old woman, recently married , presents with burning micturition for one week. Physical examination reveals suprapubic tenderness (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic?
k: Uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant woman: short oral first-line course. First line: nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX (if local resistance allows), fosfomycin Fluoroquinolones: keep for pyelonephritis Fever, flank pain, CVA
r: A young, recently married (sexually active) woman with burning micturition and suprapubic tenderness , no fever or flank pain, has acute uncomplicated cystitis. Oral nitrofurantoin is a first-line agent for uncomplicated lower UTI because it concentrates in the bladder and keeps resistance low.
wo: B. Oral fluoroquinolone: effective but reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line agents cannot be used, because of resistance and adverse effects. | C. IV gentamicin: parenteral therapy is for severe or complicated infection such as septic pyelonephritis; not needed for simple cystitis. | D. Oral beta-lactam: less effective than first-line agents for cystitis; used when others are unsuitable or in pregnancy (e.g. amoxicillin late in pregnancy).

q: 76-year-old man, known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, presented to the clinic with exertional shortness of breath for 1 year. He has to slow down his walk and stop after 10 meters. He denied any history of syncope, chest pain, or palpitation. Precordium examination revealed a forceful apex beat and a crescendo- decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids = aortic stenosis. Classic triad: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope Signs: slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, heaving apex Elderly: degenerative calcification;
r: An elderly man with vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia), progressive exertional dyspnea , a forceful (heaving) apex from LV pressure overload and a crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids has calcific aortic stenosis.
wo: A. Mitral stenosis: mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with opening snap, tapping apex; typically rheumatic, not a systolic murmur to the carotids. | C. Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge, louder on inspiration, does not radiate to the carotids; usually congenital in the young. | D. Aortic regurgitation: early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge with collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure.

q: An adult woman presents with high fever and urinary symptoms. Her temperature is 39.1 C and the white cell count is high. Urinalysis shows significant pyuria . Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
k: Febrile UTI = pyelonephritis: choose an agent with renal tissue penetration. Systemically unwell or cannot take oral: IV ceftriaxone Mild, tolerating oral: oral fluoroquinolone outpatient Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin: c
r: High fever (39.1 C) , raised white cell count and significant pyuria point to an upper or systemic urinary infection (acute pyelonephritis), not simple cystitis. A systemically unwell patient needs parenteral therapy, and IV ceftriaxone is a standard empiric choice.
wo: B. Oral cephalosporin: an option for mild pyelonephritis managed as an outpatient, but a high fever with leukocytosis favours initial IV therapy. | C. Oral nitrofurantoin: does not reach adequate tissue levels in the kidney; only for lower UTI (cystitis). | D. Oral amoxicillin: high E. coli resistance; not a reliable empiric choice for febrile UTI in adults.

q: A young woman with acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis is evaluated in the Emergency Department. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit to start ceftriaxone and vancomycin
k: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: outpatient oral therapy if tolerating oral and stable. Options: oral fluoroquinolone, or ceftriaxone Admit if: sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, obstruction, failed outpatient therapy Get urine c
r: A young woman with acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis (no sepsis, obstruction, pregnancy or inability to take oral) can be managed as an outpatient with an oral fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin. Ceftriaxone is also acceptable, but it is not offered alone in the options.
wo: B. Clarithromycin: a macrolide for respiratory or atypical infections; no useful activity against E. coli in the urinary tract. | C. Admit and start a carbapenem: reserved for severe or complicated infection, sepsis or known ESBL organisms; overtreatment for an uncomplicated case. | D. Admit for ceftriaxone plus vancomycin: vancomycin covers gram-positives such as MRSA, not the gram-negatives that cause pyelonephritis; admission is unnecessary when uncomplicated.

q: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with cola-coloured urine , a persistent headache and light-headedness for the past day. He had an episode of severe sore throat and fever 4.5 -5 days ago , for which he did not seek medical care. Which of the following laboratory findings would best support the provisional diagnosis?
k: PSGN vs IgA nephropathy: latency and complement. PSGN: 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis (3 to 6 after skin), low C3, raised ASO IgA nephropathy: hematuria within 1 to 2 days of URTI (synpharyngitic), normal C3 Nephritic: h
r: Cola-coloured urine with headache and light-headedness (hypertension and fluid overload) days after a severe sore throat with fever is a nephritic picture keyed as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. PSGN activates the alternative complement pathway, so a low C3 (with normal C4) is the laboratory
wo: A. High ANA titre: supports lupus nephritis (multisystem features, usually low C3 and C4), not a post-infectious nephritis in a young man. | B. Normal ASO titre: would argue against a recent streptococcal infection; PSGN is supported by a raised ASO (or anti-DNase B). | C. Normal serum creatinine: does not support any diagnosis; PSGN often shows a raised creatinine from reduced GFR.

q: Ptn with non-hodgkin lymphoma and he passed away before going through chemotherapy by 1 week wil he died before his chemotherapy session and he is known case of uncontrolled DM2 for 20 years and HTN. Labs: high uric acid, high potassium What's the cause of his death?
k: Tumor lysis syndrome: release of intracellular contents. High: potassium, phosphate, uric acid; low: calcium (binds phosphate) AKI from uric acid and calcium phosphate deposition High risk: Burkitt and other high-grade l
r: A patient with non-Hodgkin lymphoma , a high cell-turnover tumour, who dies before chemotherapy with high uric acid and high potassium (and, per the compiler, raised creatinine) fits spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome. TLS can occur before treatment in bulky, rapidly growing lymphomas, and hyperkalemi
wo: A. Drug induced nephropathy: possible with nephrotoxins or chemotherapy, but he had not started chemotherapy and it does not explain hyperuricemia. | C. Undiscovered renal failure: 20 years of diabetes and hypertension can cause CKD, which can raise both potassium and uric acid, but an acute fatal picture just before chemotherapy in a high-turnover lymphoma is best explained by spontaneous TLS, and the stem gives no history of renal impairment. | D. Renal tubular acidosis: type 4 RTA in diabetics causes mild hyperkalemia with normal anion gap acidosis, not a high uric acid or sudden death.

q: Which of the following diagnostic tools is the best option for screening for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhotic patients ?
k: HCC surveillance ladder in cirrhosis. Screen: ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months Nodule under 1 cm: repeat ultrasound in 3 months Nodule over 1 cm: triphasic CT or contrast MRI Typical HCC: arterial enhancement with venous
r: HCC screening in cirrhosis is done with abdominal ultrasound every 6 months , with or without AFP. When only one tool is chosen, ultrasound is preferred because it is safe, cheap and detects lesions AFP misses.
wo: A. Liver function test: assesses synthetic function and injury; it cannot detect a tumour. | B. Alpha fetoprotein: poor sensitivity alone (many HCCs do not secrete it); used together with ultrasound, not as the single screening test. | D. Triphasic CT: the diagnostic test after ultrasound finds a nodule over 1 cm (arterial enhancement with washout); too costly and radiation-heavy for routine screening.

q: A 25-year-old college student comes for a routine check-up with no active complaints. Examination reveals a diastolic murmur at the base of the heart that increases when he leans forward in full expiration . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: First decide systolic or diastolic, then the location and maneuver. Diastolic at base, sitting forward in expiration: aortic regurgitation Mid-diastolic at apex, left lateral position: mitral stenosis Right-sided murmurs
kw: diastolic murmur at the base of the heart

q: A 28-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of lower back pain associated with morning stiffness for almost 1 hour , as well as joint pain affecting both knees and ankles bilaterally. He denied any history of skin rash or mucosal ulcerations. Clinical examination reveals limited lumbar spine movements, a positive modified Schober test , and active arthritis in both knees bilaterally. He also has tenderness over the Achilles tendon . Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
k: Ankylosing spondylitis: inflammatory back pain in a young man. Stiffness improves with activity, worse with rest Signs: reduced Schober, enthesitis (Achilles), uveitis Plain pelvic X-ray: initial test; MRI SI joints: mos
r: A young man with over 3 months of inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness "almost 1 hour"), reduced lumbar movement with a "positive modified Schober test", peripheral arthritis and Achilles enthesitis = axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis). The diagnosis is established by imaging sacr
wo: A. HLA-B27 analysis: supportive only; many healthy people are positive and some patients are negative, so it cannot establish the diagnosis. | C. Knee joint aspiration: for an acute effusion to exclude septic or crystal arthritis; it does not diagnose spondyloarthritis. | D. CT scan of sacroiliac joint: shows erosions and structural change but misses early inflammation and gives high radiation; MRI is preferred.

q: A 60-year-old man with liver cirrhosis presents to the Emergency Room with increasing ascites. He has no history of fever or decreased level of consciousness. His medications include spironolactone 50 mg/day and furosemide 40 mg/day . His physical examination confirms the presence of large ascites (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Cirrhotic ascites ladder. Sodium restriction (under 2 g/day) Spironolactone, add furosemide (ratio 100:40) Large/tense or refractory: large-volume paracentesis + albumin Repeated need: TIPS or liver transplant Fever, pai
r: He already takes spironolactone and furosemide yet presents with "increasing" and "large ascites" (grade 3). Large, tense or diuretic-refractory ascites is treated with large-volume therapeutic paracentesis (with albumin replacement for large volumes), which relieves symptoms quickly; there is no fe
wo: A. Intravenous diuretics: no benefit over oral in cirrhosis and raise risk of renal failure and electrolyte disturbance. | C. Increase the dose of furosemide: dose titration (keeping the 100:40 spironolactone:furosemide ratio) suits moderate ascites; large ascites needs paracentesis first. | D. TIPS: for truly refractory ascites needing frequent paracenteses, in selected patients; not the next step.

q: A 38-year-old woman, mother of three, presents with fatigue and weight loss for the last few months. She was unable to breastfeed her last child and her menses did not return after giving birth . She has cold intolerance and loss of appetite. Examination reveals a croaky voice with delayed relaxation phase of her ankle jerks (see lab results). What is the next step in management?
o: Treat with levothyroxine 50 mcg per day
k: Sheehan syndrome: severe PPH leads to pituitary necrosis. Earliest sign: failure of lactation (prolactin) Amenorrhea (LH/FSH), hypothyroidism (TSH), adrenal insufficiency (ACTH) Labs: low/normal TSH with low free T4, hyp
r: Failure of lactation and no return of menses after delivery suggest Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary infarction), and the cold intolerance, croaky voice and "delayed relaxation phase of her ankle jerks" show hypothyroidism. The next step is to confirm with thyroid function tests: TSH together
kw: unable to breastfeed her last child
menses did not return after giving birth
delayed relaxation phase of her ankle jerks
wo: A. Give conjugated estrogen: hormone replacement for hypogonadism comes later, after the diagnosis is confirmed and more urgent axes are treated. | C. Correct hyponatremia with hypertonic saline: only for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma); she is not described this way. | D. Treat with levothyroxine 50 mcg per day: needs a confirmed diagnosis first; in hypopituitarism, cortisol must be replaced BEFORE thyroxine to avoid an adrenal crisis.

q: A 42-year-old homeless man was recently released from prison . He presented to the Emergency Room with a fever, productive cough, weight loss, and night sweats over the past 3 months (see report). Chest X-ray: Left lung apical infiltration . Sputum sample was collected and sent to the lab. Which of the following tests has the highest diagnostic value?
k: Suspected pulmonary TB workup. Risk groups: prisoners, homeless, HIV, contacts, migrants CXR: upper lobe infiltrate or cavity Sputum x3: Ziehl-Neelsen for AFB, NAAT (GeneXpert) for rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistan
r: "Homeless", "recently released from prison", 3 months of fever, productive cough, weight loss and night sweats with "left lung apical infiltration" = pulmonary tuberculosis. On the sputum sample, the Ziehl-Neelsen stain detects acid-fast bacilli and is the most useful listed test; culture (or NAAT/G
wo: A. Thin blood film: identifies the malaria species (and blood cell morphology); not used on sputum. | B. Congo red stain: detects amyloid (apple-green birefringence under polarised light); not for infection. | C. Thick blood film: the most sensitive test to detect malaria parasites; irrelevant to a chronic cough with apical infiltrate.

q: A 38-year-old woman who is not known to have any medical illness is referred to the clinic because of a chest x-ray that showed prominent hilar structures bilaterally. She is having on- and-off cough but denies any history of shortness of breath, sputum production, chest pain, skin lesions, weight loss, fever, or contact with sick people. She is not a smoker. Examination reveals clear chest bilaterally (see lab results and reports). CT chest: Confirmed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy , otherwise lung parenchyma was clear . CT-guided biopsy: Showed noncaseating granuloma . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Sarcoidosis: treat according to severity, not according to the diagnosis alone. Hilar nodes only, mild symptoms, normal exam: observe Progressive dyspnea, parenchymal infiltrates, crackles: glucocorticoids Noncaseating g
r: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with noncaseating granuloma on biopsy in a young non-smoking woman is sarcoidosis. Her disease is mild: only an "on-and-off cough", a clear chest, and CT shows the lung parenchyma was clear (hilar nodes only, stage I). Stage I sarcoidosis with minimal symptoms usually
wo: B. Prednisone: reserved for progressive or symptomatic disease (worsening dyspnea, parenchymal infiltrates, falling lung function) or serious extrapulmonary involvement (eye, heart, nervous system, hypercalcemia); none is present here. | C. Azithromycin: treats atypical pneumonia or chlamydia; there is no fever, sputum or infiltrate, and granulomas are not an infection to cover. | D. Anti-tuberculosis therapy: TB gives caseating granulomas with fever, weight loss or sick contacts, all denied here.

q: A 65-year-old man, a heavy smoker, known to have hypertension and COPD on Ventolin, Anoro Ellipta (Umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol) , and lisinopril, presents with worsening shortness of breath for 4 months. There has been no change in his sputum amount or purulence , and he has had no fever, PND, or orthopnea. He was not admitted to the hospital for more than a year. Examination reveals decreased breath sounds without added sounds (see lab results and report). Chest CT 6 months ago: Diffuse emphysematous changes . Which of the following is the best intervention to improve his shortness of breath?
k: COPD: only smoking cessation and long-term oxygen (in hypoxemic patients) improve survival. Persistent dyspnea on LAMA/LABA: check oxygenation, refer to pulmonary rehabilitation Long-term oxygen if resting hypoxemia or c
r: He has severe emphysematous COPD with 4 months of worsening dyspnea but no exacerbation (no change in sputum, no fever, no admission for over a year), and he is already on a LAMA/LABA (Anoro) plus Ventolin. Inhaler therapy is already maximised for his phenotype, so the keyed answer is home oxygen ,
kw: no change in his sputum amount or purulence
wo: B. Add LABA: he already takes vilanterol, a LABA, inside Anoro Ellipta; adding a second LABA adds nothing. | C. Volume reduction surgery: for selected patients with upper lobe predominant emphysema after pulmonary rehabilitation; this is diffuse emphysema and he still smokes. | D. Add inhaled corticosteroid: added for frequent exacerbations or high eosinophils; he has had no exacerbation or admission for over a year.

q: A 44-year-old man complains of dyspnea on exertion. Heart auscultation reveals an early diastolic murmur at the base of the heart. The intensity and duration of the murmur increase during inspiration . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
k: Timing and site pick the valve, the respiratory change picks the side. Early diastolic at base: AR or PR Louder on inspiration: right-sided (PR, TR) Louder on expiration: left-sided (AR, MR); leaning forward accentuates
r: An early diastolic murmur at the base comes from a semilunar valve: aortic or pulmonary regurgitation. The decisive clue is that it increases during inspiration : inspiration raises venous return to the right heart, and right-sided murmurs get louder, so this is pulmonary regurgitation.
kw: early diastolic murmur at the base
wo: A. Mitral regurgitation: holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, louder on expiration; not diastolic. | B. Aortic regurgitation: also an early diastolic murmur at the base, but left-sided, so it is louder in expiration with the patient leaning forward. | C. Tricuspid regurgitation: increases with inspiration but is holosystolic at the left lower sternal border, not diastolic at the base.

q: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for a 2-day history of dysuria and urethral discharge . He had recent sexual activity with a new female partner . He is afebrile, and his examination is unremarkable (see report) . Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Urethritis in a young man after a new partner = STI until proven otherwise. Chlamydia: azithromycin single dose or doxycycline 7 days Gonorrhea: ceftriaxone IM (plus chlamydia cover if not excluded) Cystitis in a woman:
r: A young sexually active man with dysuria and urethral discharge after a new partner , afebrile, has urethritis; the recall (report) points to Chlamydia trachomatis, the commonest cause of non-gonococcal urethritis. The key treats chlamydia with azithromycin (single dose); doxycycline is the alternat
wo: A. Gentamycin: an aminoglycoside used in pyelonephritis or sepsis combinations; not a urethritis treatment. | C. Ceftriaxone: right for gonococcal urethritis (gram-negative intracellular diplococci, purulent discharge), usually with chlamydia cover; alone it misses chlamydia. | D. Nitrofurantoin: for uncomplicated cystitis, mostly in women; it does not treat sexually transmitted urethritis.

q: A 33-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital after a road traffic accident that resulted in multiple fractures and had undergone multiple orthopedic surgical procedures. She has a positive urinary culture for Candida albicans . She denies any history of fever or urinary symptoms . She had an indwelling urinary catheter . Her examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Treat candiduria only if: symptomatic, neutropenic, or undergoing a urologic procedure. Asymptomatic + catheter: remove or change catheter, no antifungal Treatment of choice when needed: fluconazole Candidemia: echinocan
r: This is asymptomatic candiduria in a catheterised inpatient: she "denies any history of fever or urinary symptoms" and the exam is unremarkable. Candida in the urine of a catheterised patient is usually colonisation, so no antifungal is given; the catheter is removed or changed.
kw: positive urinary culture for Candida albicans
denies any history of fever or urinary symptoms
wo: A. Fluconazole: first line when candiduria needs treatment: symptomatic, neutropenic, or before a urologic procedure; none applies. | B. Caspofungin: an echinocandin for invasive candidiasis or candidemia; it also concentrates poorly in urine. | C. Amphotericin B: for severe invasive fungal infection or fluconazole-resistant species; far too toxic for colonisation.

q: A 55-year-old man with diabetes mellitus for 10 years was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with severe pneumonia that required intubation and ventilation. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, and his vital signs, including his blood pressure, were maintained within the normal range. However, last night, he developed hypotension that required two inotrope agents (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Very high transaminases right after shock = ischemic hepatitis. AST/ALT often >1000, LDH high, rapid fall after recovery Risk: hypotension, heart failure, sepsis Viral or toxic (paracetamol) are the other causes of level
r: A previously stable ICU patient developed sudden hypotension needing two inotropes last night; the labs (not shown) would show a sharp rise in liver enzymes. Hypoperfusion of the liver causes ischemic hepatitis (shock liver), with AST and ALT rising quickly, often above 1000, then falling over days
kw: developed hypotension that required two inotrope agents
wo: A. Acute cholangitis: fever, RUQ pain and jaundice (Charcot triad) with a cholestatic pattern from biliary obstruction; nothing points to the biliary tree here. | C. Acute viral hepatitis: develops over days to weeks with prodrome and exposure history, not overnight after a hypotensive episode. | D. Drug-induced hepatitis: possible with antibiotics, but the timing tied to the hypotension and inotrope need points to ischemia.

q: A 45-year-old man was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with fever. He required a vasopressor to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of more than 65 mm Hg . He is receiving adequate IV fluid resuscitation (see lab result). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Sepsis continuum: SIRS, sepsis, severe sepsis, septic shock. SIRS: ≥2 of temp <36 or >38, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12 or <4 Sepsis: SIRS + infection Severe sepsis: + organ dysfunction Septic shock: hypotension needing vasopr
r: He has fever (infection) and needs a vasopressor to keep MAP above 65 mm Hg despite adequate IV fluid resuscitation . That is the definition of septic shock: sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors (Sepsis-3 also adds lactate above 2 mmol/L).
wo: A. Sepsis: infection with organ dysfunction; it becomes septic shock once vasopressors are needed despite fluids. | B. Septicemia: an old term for bacteria in the blood with systemic illness; it is not a defined stage and does not describe refractory hypotension. | D. SIRS: two or more of temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate or WBC criteria without necessarily an infection or hypotension; the earliest stage.

q: A 70-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of confusion and irritability . He was well until 5 days ago, when he injured his right leg and has been bed-bound since the accident . He is hypertensive and well-controlled on medication. He has no fever (see reports). Chest X-ray: Normal . ECG: Sinus tachycardia . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Immobilization + sudden cardiorespiratory or mental change = think PE. Risks: surgery, trauma, immobility, long travel, malignancy ECG: sinus tachycardia most common; S1Q3T3 and RBBB less common CXR usually normal Diagno
r: He has been bed-bound for 5 days after a leg injury , a major DVT risk, and now has sudden confusion with sinus tachycardia and a normal chest x-ray , without fever. Acute confusion in the elderly can be the presenting sign of hypoxia from pulmonary embolism; sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG f
wo: A. Arrhythmia: the ECG shows only sinus tachycardia, which is a response, not a primary arrhythmia like AF or VT. | B. Cerebral infarction: gives focal deficits (weakness, aphasia) rather than isolated confusion and irritability, and does not explain tachycardia after immobilization. | C. Brain hemorrhage: sudden headache, vomiting, focal signs and severe hypertension; his BP is well controlled and there is no head trauma.

q: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus was recently diagnosed with hypertension . Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive medication?
k: Diabetes or CKD with hypertension: ACE inhibitor or ARB first. Age <55 or diabetic: ACEi/ARB Age ≥55 or African descent (non-diabetic): calcium channel blocker Pregnancy: labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine; ACEi contraind
r: In a patient with type 2 diabetes and new hypertension, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is first line because it lowers intraglomerular pressure and protects against diabetic nephropathy. Ramipril is the ACE inhibitor among the options.
wo: A. Hydralazine: a direct vasodilator kept for hypertension in pregnancy (IV) or resistant heart failure combinations, not first line. | B. Amlodipine: first line in non-diabetic patients of African descent or older than 55, or as add-on; no renal protection. | C. Metoprolol: beta blockers are for compelling indications (post MI, heart failure, rate control), not first line in uncomplicated hypertension, and may mask hypoglycemia.

q: A 31-year-old woman known to have rheumatic mitral stenosis recently developed atrial fibrillation , for which she was placed on warfarin therapy. What is the most appropriate target of the international normalized ratio (INR) range?
k: Warfarin targets: most indications 2 to 3, mechanical mitral valve higher. AF (with or without MS), DVT, PE: 2.0 to 3.0 Mechanical aortic valve without risk factors: 2.0 to 3.0 Mechanical mitral valve or extra risk facto
r: She has rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation , a very high embolic risk lesion that needs warfarin whatever her stroke score (DOACs are not used in moderate to severe rheumatic MS). The standard therapeutic INR target for AF, including AF with mitral stenosis, is 2.0 to 3.0 .
wo: A. <1.0: this is below a normal untreated INR (about 1.0) and means no anticoagulation at all. | B. 1.0-1.5: a near normal, subtherapeutic INR that gives no protection against thromboembolism. | D. >3.0: higher targets (2.5 to 3.5) are used for some mechanical valves, especially mitral; above 3 in AF mainly raises bleeding risk.

q: 60 years old male present with jaundice for 2 months (he was asymptomatic no added info just us finding it was very short Q) Us showed liver cirrhosis with 2 lesions What is the cause of his condition?
k: Liver lesions in a cirrhotic liver = HCC until proven otherwise. A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Hepatitis B infection. Commonest HCC risk worldwide: hepatitis B (can cause HCC even without cirr

q: A patient presents with Cushingoid features . Laboratory results show elevated cortisol(4pm around 800, 8pm around 500) and elevated ACTH ( 17 and the reference was 15 ). What is the most likely cause?
k: High cortisol: check ACTH to decide where the lesion is. Low ACTH: adrenal tumour or exogenous steroids Normal to mildly high ACTH: pituitary adenoma Very high ACTH: ectopic (carcinoid, small cell lung cancer) High dose

q: An elderly patient with end-stage metastatic cancer receiving palliative care becomes aggressive and confused , and the staff cannot calm her. What is the best drug to give?
k: Delirium: treat the cause, non-drug measures first, then an antipsychotic. Search reversible causes: drugs (opioids), infection, hypercalcemia, retention, hypoxia First-line drug: haloperidol Benzodiazepine first: alcoho
r: An end-stage cancer patient who becomes acutely confused and aggressive has delirium (terminal agitation). When non-drug measures fail, haloperidol is the first-line drug for delirium in palliative care because it controls agitation and psychotic features without worsening confusion.
wo: B. Lorazepam: benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and confusion; they are used for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, seizures, or added to an antipsychotic for refractory terminal agitation.

q: Elderly diabetic, black toe , dorsalis absent/not palpable , next or initial management :
k: Diabetic foot: first decide if it is ischemic, infective or neuropathic. Absent pulses, gangrene: ABI first, then duplex or angiography ABI <0.9: PAD; >1.3: non-compressible calcified vessels Probe to bone or deep ulcer:
r: An elderly diabetic with a black toe (dry gangrene) and an absent dorsalis pedis pulse has suspected peripheral arterial disease with critical limb ischemia. The initial bedside test is the ankle brachial index ; arterial calcification in diabetics can falsely raise it, so toe pressures or duplex fo
wo: A. Tissue Biopsy: for a chronic non-healing ulcer suspicious of malignant change (Marjolin ulcer), not for ischemic gangrene. | C. MRI: the best imaging for suspected osteomyelitis under a diabetic foot ulcer; the problem here is arterial supply, not bone infection.

q: 45 years old female with no significant past medical history presents with red eye pain for 2 days associated with blurry vision , increased sensitivity to light and watery discharge. Examination revealed conjunctival injection. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Red eye + any red flag = refer to ophthalmology before treating. Red flags: reduced vision, photophobia, severe pain, ciliary flush, abnormal or fixed pupil, corneal opacity Conjunctivitis: normal vision, gritty, dischar
r: A red eye with blurry vision and photophobia is not simple conjunctivitis: these are red flags for sight threatening disease such as anterior uveitis (iritis), keratitis or acute angle closure glaucoma. The correct next step is urgent ophthalmological examination (slit lamp, visual acuity, intraocul
wo: A. Artificial tears: for dry eye or mild irritation with normal vision; they would only delay diagnosis of a vision threatening cause here. | B. Antiviral drops: for confirmed herpes simplex keratitis (dendritic ulcer on fluorescein); you need slit lamp examination first, and starting drops blindly is wrong. | C. Topical antibiotics: for bacterial conjunctivitis with purulent discharge and normal vision; the watery discharge plus visual loss and photophobia point away from it.

q: 65 YO male coming to the GP for a checkup. Heavy smoker . Otherwise healthy with no complaints. What is the first screening he should undergo
k: Screening triggers to memorise: AAA: men 65-75 who ever smoked: one time ultrasound Colorectal: 45 to 75 (choose 50 if 45 not offered) Osteoporosis: women ≥65 DXA Lung cancer: 50-80 with heavy smoking history: low dose C
r: A 65 year old male who is a heavy smoker meets the classic criteria for one time abdominal aortic aneurysm screening with abdominal ultrasound (men 65 to 75 who have ever smoked). This screening is triggered specifically by his age, sex and smoking, which is exactly the combination highlighted in th
wo: A. Colorectal cancer: average risk screening runs from 45 to 75, so he is due, but it is not specific to his profile; the stem's clues (65, male, smoker) point to AAA. | C. Diabetes: screening is aimed at overweight or obese adults about 35 to 70 or those with risk factors; nothing here makes it the first priority. | D. Osteoporosis: routine DXA screening is for women ≥65; men are screened only with risk factors, and the classic exam answer is women.

q: You have a patient with severe multiple sclerosis that is advanced and progressive who now develops renal failure secondary to diabetes. The patient is alert and has elected to put the DNR (Do-Not-Resuscitate) order in place at her own discretion. The patient's potassium level is now markedly elevated at 8 meq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
o: Dialysis cannot be done because of the DNR order.
You can do the dialysis if the DNR is reversed for the procedure.
Go ahead with the dialysis; ignore the DNR order.
Give kayexalate until the DNR status is discussed with the family.
k: DNR = do not resuscitate, not do not treat. Covers: CPR, defibrillation, intubation at arrest Does not cover: dialysis, antibiotics, transfusion, surgery Competent patient decides; family does not override Urgent dialysi
r: A DNR order means no CPR or intubation in the event of cardiopulmonary arrest ; it does not mean withholding other treatment. This alert , capacitated patient has life-threatening hyperkalemia ( K 8 meq/L ) from renal failure, which is an indication for urgent dialysis, so dialysis proceeds and the
kw: potassium level is now markedly elevated
wo: A. Dialysis cannot be done because of the DNR: wrong; DNR restricts only resuscitation after arrest, not indicated treatments such as dialysis, antibiotics or surgery. It would be right only if the patient herself refused dialysis. | B. Dialysis only if the DNR is reversed: no reversal is needed because the DNR does not cover dialysis; DNR is suspended only for procedures with a high risk of arrest (e.g. anesthesia), after discussion with the patient. | D. Kayexalate until the family is consulted: too slow for K 8, and the decision belongs to the alert, competent patient, not the family.

q: A new study was conducted to investigate the effect of HIV on mortality . The target group was recruited from hospitals and followed for 10 years to compare mortality between negative and positive HIV patients. What does ethics impose on this research ?
o: To have in its center the rights of the target group
To have in its center the achievement of the hypothesis
k: Participant interests come before those of science and society (Declaration of Helsinki). Informed voluntary consent, right to withdraw Confidentiality, especially for stigmatised conditions like HIV Independent ethics c
r: A long cohort study following HIV positive and negative patients involves a vulnerable group with sensitive data. Research ethics require that the rights, safety, welfare and confidentiality of participants come first (informed consent, privacy, freedom to withdraw), above the interests of science,
kw: What does ethics impose on this research
wo: A. A considerable profit: financial gain is a conflict of interest to declare and limit, never an ethical goal of research. | B. Frequent appearances on social media: publicity is irrelevant and may threaten participant confidentiality, especially with HIV status. | D. To have in its center the achievement of the hypothesis: research must remain objective; prioritising proving the hypothesis invites bias and harms participants.

q: A female underwent caesarean section and consent was obtained. Patient later developed massive bleeding that was not being controlled by medical management and hence a decision for hysterectomy was made by the two consultants . However, no consent for hysterectomy has been obtained. What will the surgeon do?
k: Emergency exception: act to save life without consent, then document and inform. Competent adult: she signs her own consent Non-emergency, lacks capacity: legal guardian or next of kin Emergency: proceed, documented by t
r: This is a life-threatening emergency : massive bleeding not controlled by medical management, with two consultants agreeing hysterectomy is needed. When delay would endanger life and the patient cannot consent, the doctrine of implied consent in emergencies allows the surgeon to proceed without writ
wo: A. Obtain consent from the husband: when a patient lacks capacity in a non-urgent situation the family may be asked, but with uncontrolled massive bleeding waiting for consent delays lifesaving surgery and is not required. | C. Consult the ethics committee: for non-urgent ethical disputes; it cannot be convened in time for an exsanguinating patient. | D. Do not perform the hysterectomy: withholding lifesaving surgery would let the patient die and is not respecting autonomy, since she has expressed no refusal.

q: A patient with a "Do Not Resuscitate" ( DNR ) order was transferred to another hospital . What is the most accurate statement?
o: DNR from another institution is valid for 6 months
DNR from another institution is valid for 24 hours
DNR from another institution is not valid
DNR from another institution is valid
k: Saudi DNR rules (exam points). DNR decision: made by a team of three treating physicians, not by the family Transferred DNR order: valid 24 hours, then the receiving team reissues DNR does not mean stopping other treatme
r: Under the Saudi DNR guidelines, when a patient is transferred to or received from another national or international health institution, a signed DNR order from the other facility is valid for 24 hours . During that time the receiving team must reassess the patient and issue its own DNR order if stil
wo: A. Valid for 6 months: no such period exists; DNR status must be reconfirmed by the receiving facility promptly. | C. Not valid: ignoring it would expose the patient to unwanted resuscitation during the handover period; the guideline honours it temporarily. | D. Valid: it is not valid indefinitely; it lapses after 24 hours unless renewed by the receiving institution.

q: Researcher wants to apply for a grant but the ethics authority may have concerns and reject it. He will collect data on patients who undergo cervical cancer screening. He won't tell them the results and it'll be blind . What will get his application accepted?
o: Hand reports over the phone to the patients
Tell the negative cases about their results
Tell the positive cases about their results and instruct them where to go after that
k: Research cannot withhold clinically actionable findings from participants. Positive or incidental significant findings: disclose and refer Participant welfare comes before study design convenience Blinding is acceptable
r: The design is unethical as written because withholding results means women with an abnormal cervical screen would miss treatment of a precancerous or cancerous lesion. Beneficence requires that participants with clinically important findings are informed and referred, so telling the positive cases a
wo: A. Nothing, it will be accepted: an ethics committee will not approve a study that knowingly withholds a positive cancer screening result from participants. | B. Hand reports over the phone to the patients: the method of delivery is not the problem, and giving reports by phone without a referral plan can breach confidentiality and leave positives without care. | C. Tell the negative cases about their results: informing only negatives protects no one; the participants at risk of harm are the positive ones.

q: 47 years old Female came to preventive clinic , no family history, medical history positive for HTN for 5 years , BMI 37 what is the appropriate screening test:
k: Preventive clinic questions: match the screening test to the stated risk factor. Obesity or hypertension: screen for diabetes (FBG, HbA1c, OGTT) Heavy smoker 50 to 80: low-dose CT Sexually active woman 21 to 65: Pap or H
r: She has a BMI of 37 (obesity) and has hypertension , both strong risk factors for type 2 diabetes. Adults who are overweight or obese, especially with another cardiovascular risk factor, should be screened for diabetes, so fasting blood glucose is the test the vignette points to.
wo: A. Fecal occult blood: colorectal cancer screening for average risk adults; the vignette's risk factors (obesity, hypertension) target diabetes instead. | C. pap smear: routine cervical screening (21 to 65 years) depends on when she was last screened; nothing in the stem makes it the targeted test. | D. Low-dose CT for lung cancer: only for older heavy smokers (age about 50 to 80 with a significant pack-year history); she has no smoking history.

q: Parents bring 7 YO to Gp with concerns of not going to school . No other symptoms mentioned. Developmentally and growth are tracking well . Next step in management
k: School refusal: treat with behavioral support and early return, not avoidance or drugs. Rule out organic causes, bullying, learning difficulty first Gradual exposure and gentle separation from parents Coordinate with sch
r: A 7 year old who refuses school with normal growth and development and no other symptoms fits school refusal driven by separation anxiety. First line management is behavioral: reassure the parents, avoid reinforcing avoidance, and promote gradual, gentle separation with an early return to school, wo
kw: Developmentally and growth are tracking well
wo: A. Defer school 1 more year: avoidance reinforces the anxiety and harms learning and socialization; deferral is only considered for true developmental unreadiness, which is excluded here. | B. Start home schooling: also rewards avoidance; the goal is the earliest possible return to regular school. | D. Anti anxiety medication: reserved for severe or persistent anxiety disorder that fails behavioral therapy (CBT), not as the first step.

q: 16 y/o Male come to ER with acute onset chest pain , fever, SOB, had similar episodes several times , clear cardiopulmonary examination, PB 110/70, HR 100, T: 37.8, RR 22, O2: 90 or 93. Labs: Hb 8 or 10, Reticulocyte 2.5 , Platlet 250, WBC 12, ESR 10. Which of the following most helpful to establish the diagnosis
k: Sickle cell disease diagnosis and crises: Confirm: hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC Screen: sickle solubility test Acute chest syndrome: chest pain, fever, hypoxia, new infiltrate Aplastic crisis: low reticulocytes (pa
r: A 16 year old with acute chest pain, fever, dyspnea and hypoxia (SpO2 about 90%), recurrent similar episodes, anemia and raised reticulocytes is typical of sickle cell disease presenting with acute chest syndrome or vaso occlusive crises. Hemoglobin electrophoresis (or HPLC) confirms the diagnosis b
wo: A. Coombs test: for autoimmune or immune hemolytic anemia (positive DAT); it does not explain recurrent pain crises. | B. Bone marrow aspiration: for suspected leukemia or marrow failure (pancytopenia or blasts); counts here do not suggest it. | C. Blood film: may show sickle cells and supports the diagnosis, but it cannot confirm the genotype; electrophoresis is definitive.

q: A 16-year-old boy came to the Emergency Department complaining of exertional dyspnea and easy fatiguability for the past few weeks. His parents admitted that he used to be a sick child requiring multiple hospital admissions and frequent blood transfusions . His parents are related . He was found to be pale, jaundiced, and have hepatosplenomegaly , with a scar from laparoscopic cholecystectomy (see lab results). Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
k: Hemoglobinopathy workup: Clues: consanguinity, transfusions, hemolysis, gallstones young, hepatosplenomegaly Diagnostic: hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC Screen: solubility test (HbS only) Film: target cells, sickle ce
r: Consanguineous parents , frequent transfusions since childhood, pallor, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and a prior cholecystectomy (pigment stones from chronic hemolysis) indicate an inherited hemoglobinopathy such as thalassemia or sickle cell disease. Hemoglobin electrophoresis identifies the abnorm
wo: A. Peripheral blood film: shows target cells, microcytosis or sickle cells and suggests the diagnosis, but it does not quantify or confirm the hemoglobin type. | B. Sickle cell saturation (the sickling or solubility screen): detects HbS only; it cannot distinguish trait from disease and misses thalassemia, so it is a screen, not the confirmatory test. | C. Bone marrow biopsy: for marrow failure, leukemia or infiltration; not needed for hemoglobinopathies.

q: 3 y/o boy brought to the ER by his mother, he ate unknown number of tablet. His irritable with abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, hematemisis, Melena , admitted for further evaluation, few hour later he seems stable , but after 6 h he become drowsy with high liver enzymes What is the type of tablet?
k: Iron poisoning stages: Stage 1 (0-6 h): GI toxicity, vomiting, hematemesis, melena Stage 2 (6-24 h): latent, apparent improvement Stage 3: shock, metabolic acidosis, lethargy Stage 4 (2-5 days): hepatotoxicity Stage 5 (w
r: Iron poisoning follows a staged course: an early GI phase from direct corrosive injury (abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hematemesis and melena ), then a latent phase where the child seems stable , followed by shock, metabolic acidosis, altered consciousness and hepatotoxicity . A toddler with GI
kw: few hour later he seems stable
wo: B. Paracetamol: causes delayed hepatotoxicity after 24 to 72 hours, but early symptoms are mild nausea and vomiting, not hematemesis and melena. | C. Digoxin: causes vomiting, arrhythmias, bradycardia, heart block, hyperkalemia and visual changes (yellow vision), not GI bleeding with liver injury. | D. Aspirin: causes vomiting, tinnitus, hyperventilation with mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, and fever; liver failure is not its signature.

q: 6 day preterm baby at 34 weeks of gestation with poor feeding, bilirubin 380 , mainly unconjicated . Instited phototherpay but failed Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: High loading IV fluid or hydration
k: Severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia: Intensive phototherapy first, thresholds lower for preterm babies Rising despite phototherapy or signs of encephalopathy: exchange transfusion IVIG for isoimmune hemolysis
r: A 34 week preterm baby on day 6 with mainly unconjugated bilirubin 380 µmol/L (about 22 mg/dL) and failed phototherapy is at risk of bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus), and preterm babies have lower treatment thresholds. The next step is to remove bilirubin directly by exchange transfusion, whic
wo: A. Phenobarbital: induces hepatic glucuronyl transferase but acts too slowly for acute severe hyperbilirubinemia; used in Crigler Najjar type II, not as rescue therapy. | C. High IV fluids: correct dehydration that worsens jaundice, but hydration alone cannot lower dangerous bilirubin levels after phototherapy failure; it is the answer for neonatal polycythemia. | D. Antibiotics: for suspected sepsis (temperature instability, lethargy, raised markers); poor feeding alone does not make it the next step for failed phototherapy.

q: A full-term infant of a diabetic mother has a hematocrit of 71% and appears plethoric . What is the appropriate management?
k: Neonatal polycythemia (venous Hct >65%): Causes: infant of diabetic mother, IUGR, delayed cord clamping, twin to twin transfusion Features: plethora, hypoglycemia, jaundice, lethargy, respiratory distress Asymptomatic or
r: An infant of a diabetic mother is prone to polycythemia (chronic fetal hypoxia drives erythropoietin). A hematocrit of 71% with plethora but no stated symptoms is managed with hydration, enterally or with IV fluids, and close monitoring. Partial exchange transfusion is reserved for very high hematoc
wo: A. Reassurance: Hct 71% is above the polycythemia threshold of 65%, so the infant needs hydration and monitoring, not reassurance alone. | B. Partial exchange transfusion if symptomatic: kept for symptomatic infants with Hct ≥70-75% whose symptoms worsen despite IV hydration; benefit is unclear and NEC risk rises, so it is not the appropriate first management. | C. Phototherapy: treats hyperbilirubinemia, which may follow polycythemia, but does nothing for the high hematocrit.

q: 8-year-old girl with an 8-week history of rash, weight loss, and weakness. She has a heliotrope rash over the eyelids , rash over the elbows , and truncal weakness . CK 850 , LDH 650. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Juvenile dermatomyositis: Skin: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules over knuckles, elbows, knees Symmetrical proximal weakness Raised CK, LDH, AST, aldolase Calcinosis is a later complication in children Treatment: steroids
r: A heliotrope rash on the eyelids, a rash over the elbows (extensor surfaces, like Gottron papules), proximal and truncal weakness and raised muscle enzymes ( CK 850, LDH 650 ) in a child are classic for juvenile dermatomyositis. It is the most common childhood idiopathic inflammatory myopathy and is
wo: A. SLE: malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, renal disease; a heliotrope rash and high CK point to myositis. | B.
