Scleroderma: skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly; not a heliotrope rash with myositis. | C. Muscular dystrophy: progressive weakness with Gower sign and very high CK, but no rash; Duchenne mainly affects boys.

q: A 6 year old presented to the emergency department due to palpitations and being pale for 30 minutes . He was now stable. They didn't mention any interventions. BP: 95/80, HR: 220 , RR: 25. What is the initial step :
k: Pediatric tachycardia approach: Stable: 12 lead ECG first Narrow QRS SVT (infants often >220, children >180, no P waves): vagal maneuvers, then adenosine Unstable (shock, altered consciousness): synchronized cardioversio
r: A 6 year old with sudden palpitations and pallor and a HR of 220 has a tachyarrhythmia, most likely SVT, and he is currently stable . The initial step is a 12 lead ECG (during the tachycardia) to confirm the rhythm and QRS width, which decides treatment: vagal maneuvers then adenosine for narrow com
wo: A. Electrolytes: useful later to find triggers (potassium, magnesium), but they do not identify the rhythm or guide immediate treatment. | C. Echo: assesses structural heart disease or cardiomyopathy after the rhythm is managed; not the first step. | D. ABG: for shock, respiratory failure or metabolic derangement; it does not diagnose the arrhythmia.

q: 11-month-old boy presents with right ulnar and radial fractures , 2 days after a reported fall on an outstretched hand. The parents delayed seeking medical care , stating that they did not notice any bruising and initially believed the injury was just a strain. The child is well-nourished, well-dressed, and has attended regular well-baby visits. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Believe the parents and treat the child
Admit the child for further evaluation and order a head CT
Report the police for child abuse
k: Suspected non-accidental injury: suspicion is enough, report to child protection. Red flags: delay in seeking care, mechanism not matching development, changing story Long-bone fractures in a non-ambulant infant are susp
wo: A. Believe the parents and treat: wrong because the history (delay, implausible mechanism for age) is inconsistent with the injury; treating the fracture alone misses the duty to protect. Right only when the mechanism fits the child's development and there is no delay or other red flag. | B. Admit and order a head CT: admission for safety plus a skeletal survey and head imaging is the recommended workup of suspected physical abuse in a child under 1 year, so this is a strong listed alternative (see concern). The compiler, however, keys the reporting step, which is the action this recall is built around. | C. Report to the social worker: the wording candidates debated; social work is often the hospital route to child protection, but the classic keyed action is reporting to the child protection authority. Right if the options list no authority/child protection choice and the exam treats the social worker as the reporting channel. | D. Report to the police: police involvement is the role of the child protection system after a report, not the physician's first action. Right only if there is immediate danger or the exam explicitly frames police as the reporting authority.

q: A child presents with signs and symptoms of rheumatic fever and a heart murmur . What is the most appropriate investigation ?
k: Rheumatic fever = Jones criteria + proof of recent strep infection. 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus strep evidence Strep evidence: raised or rising ASO, anti-DNase B, positive throat culture or rapid antigen Echo: de
r: Diagnosing rheumatic fever needs Jones criteria plus evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection . With the clinical signs already present, the ASO titer supplies that evidence and confirms the diagnosis. Echocardiography is not offered here.
wo: A. ECG: shows a prolonged PR interval, which is only a minor Jones criterion and is not diagnostic; useful for monitoring, not for confirming rheumatic fever.

q: A child presents with fatigue and weight gain. On examination, the growth velocity is reduced , with delayed growth on the growth chart. Thyroid function tests reveal markedly elevated TSH and low T4 levels. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Short stature with weight gain = endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing). High TSH, low T4: primary hypothyroidism, give levothyroxine Low or normal TSH, low T4: central cause Short with weight loss or t
r: Markedly elevated TSH with low T4 is primary hypothyroidism, which explains the fatigue, weight gain and reduced growth velocity . Treatment is thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, which also allows catch-up growth.
kw: markedly elevated TSH and low T4
wo: B. Growth hormone therapy: for confirmed growth hormone deficiency or specific syndromes; growth failure here is due to hypothyroidism and corrects with levothyroxine. Hypothyroidism must be treated first.

q: A child with type 1 diabetes experiences recurrent hypoglycemia at night , on basal- bolus insulin regimen:
o: Reduce basal insulin dose at night
Add a meal at 3 at night
k: Match the low to the insulin acting at that time. Night or fasting lows: reduce basal (long-acting) insulin Postprandial lows: reduce mealtime (rapid-acting) bolus Lows with exercise: reduce the pre-exercise bolus Recurr
r: On a basal-bolus regimen, recurrent nocturnal hypoglycemia (overnight and fasting) reflects too much basal insulin acting at night, so the fix is to reduce the night basal dose. Adjust the insulin that is acting at the time of the lows.
wo: A. Drink juice at bedtime: a temporary fix that treats the symptom and raises glucose but leaves excess basal insulin in place. | C. Reduce bolus before meal: corrects hypoglycemia occurring a few hours after meals (postprandial), not overnight. | D. Add a meal at 3 at night: disrupts sleep and adds calories instead of correcting the dose; not recommended practice.

q: Newborn in 3rd percentile , family poor was diluting formula milk , what is next most appropriate?
o: Advice family how to make formula
k: Failure to thrive: hospitalize when unsafe at home or severe. Admit: severe malnutrition, dehydration or electrolyte abnormality, failed outpatient management, suspected neglect or unsafe home Diluted formula: risk of hy
r: A newborn at the 3rd percentile whose poor family is diluting formula has failure to thrive from inadequate intake with a risk of hyponatremia and water intoxication from over-dilute feeds. The keyed step is hospitalization to correct the nutritional deficit safely, monitor electrolytes and weight g
wo: B. High calorie formula: does not solve the cause (dilution due to poverty) and a poor family may not afford or prepare it correctly; used for children with increased needs (e.g. heart disease). | C. Advise family how to make formula: education is essential and would be enough for mild growth faltering in a family able to comply, but at the 3rd percentile with ongoing dilution and poverty, outpatient advice alone is unsafe.

q: 9-month-old baby mainly breastfed , mother slowly introducing solid foods . Best nutritional advice?
o: Advise mother to introduce solid foods more rapidly
k: Breastfed infants: iron and vitamin D. Vitamin D: from the first days of life for breastfed infants Iron: stores deplete at 4 to 6 months; give iron-rich foods or supplements Complementary foods from about 6 months, one
r: A mainly breastfed 9-month-old whose mother is introducing solids slowly is at risk of iron deficiency: fetal iron stores run out around 4 to 6 months and breast milk is low in iron, so iron must come from foods or supplements. With iron-rich foods not yet established, iron supplementation is the be
wo: B. Give vitamin D supplements: breastfed infants should already receive vitamin D from birth; the gap this stem highlights (slow solids at 9 months) is iron. | C. Add formula milk: unnecessary; breastfeeding should continue, and formula does not replace the need for complementary foods. | D. Introduce solid foods more rapidly: complementary foods should progress, but forcing faster introduction does not quickly correct the iron gap, and new foods are still introduced a few days apart.

q: A child presents with signs and symptoms of rheumatic fever and a heart murmur . What is the most appropriate investigation ?
k: Rheumatic fever = evidence of strep + Jones criteria. Major: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules Minor: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR Strep evidence: raised or ris
r: Diagnosing acute rheumatic fever by the Jones criteria needs evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection plus 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, criteria. With echocardiography not among the options (the recaller confirmed no ECHO), the ASO titre is the investigation that proves recent str
wo: A. ECG: shows a prolonged PR interval, which is only a minor criterion and is not specific; it cannot confirm rheumatic fever.

q: family brought their kid who has a fever, cough, and runny nose. Symptoms started after hx of choking after he ingested some seed . Chest exam: dec RT side breathing sound X ray pictures was shown What is the next thing to do?
o: Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid
k: Suspected airway foreign body in a child: x-ray first, rigid bronchoscopy for diagnosis and removal. Clues: choking episode, sudden cough, unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds CXR: hyperinflation on the obstructed
r: A choking episode after eating a seed followed by decreased breath sounds on the right is foreign body aspiration (the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical). The fever, cough and runny nose reflect post-obstructive infection. The chest x-ray, the initial test, is already done, so the next
kw: choking after he ingested some seed
wo: A. Epinephrine subcutaneous: used in anaphylaxis (urticaria, stridor, hypotension after an allergen); it does not remove an airway foreign body. | C. Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid: right for a simple viral URTI, but the choking history and unilateral reduced air entry make missing a foreign body dangerous. | D. IV: fluids or antibiotics may be supportive for secondary pneumonia, but they do not treat the cause, which is the retained seed.

q: A 1-week-old infant seen in screening clinic (see image). Which of the following is the name of this primitive reflex ?
k: Name the reflex by its stimulus and response. Stepping: upright, feet on surface, walking steps; gone about 2 months Rooting: cheek stroke, turns to stimulus; gone about 4 months Moro: sudden head drop, arms abduct then
r: The image shows a newborn held upright with the soles touching a surface , making alternating walking movements; this is the stepping (walking) reflex, a primitive reflex present at birth.
wo: A. Rooting: stroking the cheek or side of the mouth makes the baby turn the head and open the mouth toward the stimulus. | C. Parachute: a postural reflex appearing around 8 to 9 months; when tipped forward the infant extends the arms to break the fall, so it cannot be seen at 1 week. | D. Lateral neck: the asymmetric tonic neck (fencing) reflex: head turned to one side, arm on that side extended and opposite arm flexed.

q: A 2-week-old infant seen in screening clinic (see image). What is expected age (in months) for this reflexto disappear ?
k: Primitive reflexes disappear on a schedule; persistence suggests neurological disease. Stepping: about 2 months Rooting: about 4 months Moro, ATNR: about 4 to 6 months Palmar grasp: about 6 months; plantar grasp about 12
r: The image shows the stepping reflex (infant held upright making walking movements). It is present from birth and disappears early, by about 2 months , which is the earliest age among the options.
kw: age (in months) for this reflexto disappear
wo: B. 4: the age at which rooting (and sucking) disappears, not stepping. | C. 6: around when Moro and the asymmetric tonic neck reflex are gone; persistence of these beyond 6 months suggests a CNS problem. | D. 8: around when the parachute reflex appears; it is not a disappearance age for stepping.

q: Pediatric 4 yrs c/o fatigue fever pruritic and changes of sclera on exam splenomegaly . Hb 87, Mcv low, Plt 200, + combs test . He brought a picture close to this picture
k: Spherocytes + hemolysis: the Coombs test separates immune from hereditary. Coombs positive: autoimmune (warm) hemolytic anemia Coombs negative + family history: hereditary spherocytosis Bite cells, Heinz bodies, trigger:
r: The child has hemolysis: fatigue, scleral changes (jaundice) and splenomegaly with anemia (Hb 87). The decisive clue is the positive Coombs test , which shows antibody or complement on the red cells, so this is autoimmune hemolytic anemia, often triggered by a recent infection in young children; the
wo: A. IDA: microcytic anemia with high RDW and often reactive thrombocytosis, but no jaundice, splenomegaly or positive Coombs test. | B. Spherocytosis: hereditary spherocytosis also gives spherocytes, jaundice and splenomegaly, but the Coombs test is negative and there is often a family history. | D. G6PD anemia: acute hemolysis after fava beans, infection or oxidant drugs with bite cells and Heinz bodies; Coombs negative.

q: A baby is observed walking independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance . At approximately what age is a child typically expected to walk independently this way?
k: Gross motor ladder for walking. 9 months: pulls to stand, cruises 12 months: walks alone, wide-based, arms up 15 months: walks well, may walk backwards 18 months: runs stiffly, climbs stairs with help Not walking by 18 m
r: A wide-based gait with arms raised for balance (high guard) is how a child walks when independent walking has just been achieved. Independent walking is expected at about 12 months (normal range roughly 9 to 18 months).
wo: A. 9 months: the age to pull to stand and cruise holding furniture, not to walk alone. | C. 15 months: by now most children walk well with a narrower gait and arms lowered; the typical age for first independent, wide-based walking is earlier (red flag only if not walking by 18 months).

q: 12 months old Saudi boy and came for vaccination . Which vaccines should be given
k: Saudi schedule at 12 months: OPV + MMR + MCV4 + PCV13. 2, 4, 6 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV (+ rotavirus at 2 and 4 months) 9 months: measles 12 months: OPV, MMR, MCV4, PCV School entry: OPV, DTaP, MMR, varicella
r: At 12 months the Saudi national schedule gives OPV, MMR, the meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MCV4) and the PCV booster. Option B is the only one containing all four.
wo: A. IPV, MCV, PCV, MMR: IPV belongs to the 2, 4 and 6 month doses (with DTaP and Hib); at 12 months the polio dose is OPV. | C. Varicella, OPV, MCV, PCV: misses MMR, which is mandatory at 12 months; varicella is given with the 18 month or school entry doses in the current schedule. | D. Hib, MCV, OPV, MMR: Hib is given in the infant series and its booster at 18 months, not at 12 months, and PCV is missing.

q: A child can walk steadily without support , say 6-10 words , point to 2 body parts . What is the most likely age?
k: Language milestones are the most precise age markers in toddlers. 12 months: 2 to 3 words 18 months: 6 to 10 words, points to body parts 24 months: about 50 words, 2-word sentences 36 months: about 100 words, 3-word sent
r: Saying 6 to 10 words and pointing to body parts are milestones reached by about 18 months, and walking steadily is expected by 15 months. The child has none of the 24 month skills (about 50 words, 2-word phrases), so the keyed age is 17 months , a toddler who has just reached the 18 month language m
wo: A. 24 months: expect about 50 words, 2-word phrases, running well and kicking a ball; 6 to 10 words is too few. | B. 19 months: also near the 18 month milestones, but by then vocabulary is usually growing past 10 words toward 2-word phrases; the source keys the younger age.

q: A child came with his mother to a well-baby clinic for a general check-up. The child can skip , draw a rectangle , count from 1-10 , and knows opposites . How old is he?
k: Preschool ladder (gross motor and drawing). 2 years: runs, kicks ball, copies line 3 years: tricycle, copies circle 4 years: hops on one foot, copies cross/square 5 years: skips, copies triangle, counts to 10, opposites
r: Skipping , counting to 10 and knowing opposites are 5 year milestones; drawing a rectangle (square) is a 4 to 5 year skill. Taken together, the highest milestones set the age at 5 years .
wo: B. 4: hops on one foot, copies a cross or square, tells a story; skipping and counting to 10 are not yet expected. | C. 3: rides a tricycle, copies a circle, knows name, age and gender, 3-word sentences. | D. 2: runs, kicks a ball, copies a line, 2-word phrases, about 50 words.

q: A neonate with meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS) is on maximum oxygenation mechanical ventilation but is still hypoxic . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Refractory hypoxemia in MAS = think PPHN. Clue: preductal saturation higher than postductal Management: optimise ventilation, surfactant, inhaled nitric oxide Failure of iNO: ECMO Exclude pneumothorax when a ventilated b
r: Meconium aspiration is often complicated by persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn , causing right to left shunting, so hypoxia persists despite maximum mechanical ventilation . Inhaled nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator that reduces the shunt and improves oxygenation; it is
wo: A. Increase tidal volume: higher volumes on already maximal settings cause barotrauma, air leak and pneumothorax, a known risk in MAS, so avoiding further lung injury takes priority. | B. Give systemic steroid: steroids are not recommended routinely in MAS and do not reverse pulmonary hypertension.

q: 36 week G3P4 singleton pregnancy with frank breech . All previous normal vaginal. Would like to have a vaginal delivery. Which week should ECV be preformed
k: ECV timing: 36 weeks nullipara, 37 weeks multipara. Frank breech: hips flexed, knees extended Contraindications: placenta previa or APH, ruptured membranes, abnormal CTG, need for CS anyway, major uterine anomaly, multip
r: External cephalic version is offered from 36 weeks in nulliparous women and from 37 weeks in multiparous women. This woman is G3P4 with previous normal vaginal deliveries, so she is multiparous and ECV should be performed at 37 weeks. Before then spontaneous version is still likely in a multipara, a
kw: Which week should ECV be preformed
wo: A. 36 weeks: the timing for a nulliparous woman; in a multipara spontaneous turning is still common, so waiting to 37 weeks is preferred. | C. 38 weeks: later than recommended; less amniotic fluid and a larger baby lower success, and labor may start before the attempt. | D. 39 weeks: too late as the planned time; it delays the attempt with a growing risk of spontaneous labor in breech.

q: 32 YO (G2P3) undergoing repeat elective C section . Previous C section was uncomplicated. What is the most evidence based method to reduce the risk of post operative endometritis
k: Cesarean infection prevention: antibiotics before incision. Cefazolin within 60 minutes before skin incision Add azithromycin for CS in labor or after ruptured membranes Vaginal cleansing: adjunct, mainly in labor Endome
r: The single most evidence based measure to reduce post cesarean endometritis and wound infection is prophylactic antibiotics given before the skin incision (typically a first generation cephalosporin), which substantially cuts infectious morbidity in both elective and emergency cesarean sections. The
wo: A. Vaginal iodine prep: also lowers endometritis, mainly in women in labor or with ruptured membranes, but it is an adjunct with weaker evidence than antibiotic prophylaxis. | C. Daily wound checking: detects wound infection after it happens; it does not prevent endometritis. | D. Monitoring for post operative fever: a detection strategy for infection that has already occurred, not prevention.

q: To reduce the occurrence of adhesions in pregnant women undergoing elective Cesarean sections , which of the following strategies can be employed?
o: Add an adhesion barrier before closing the wound
k: Match the measure to the complication asked at CS: Adhesions: meticulous hemostasis, gentle handling Endometritis and wound infection: antibiotics before incision Elective CS timing: ≥39 weeks Routine drains: not recomme
r: Adhesions form where there is tissue trauma, ischemia, blood and fibrin left in the peritoneal cavity. Careful surgical technique with meticulous hemostasis (gentle tissue handling, removing clots, avoiding excess dry packing) is the simplest well accepted measure to reduce adhesions at cesarean sec
wo: A. Perform the C section preterm: delivering early adds neonatal prematurity risks and does nothing to reduce adhesions; elective CS is timed at ≥39 weeks. | B. Using drains: routine drains do not reduce adhesions or infection after CS and are a foreign body; they are kept for specific bleeding concerns. | C. Adhesion barrier: evidence that barriers reduce clinically significant adhesions after cesarean is limited and inconsistent, so they are not the recommended standard measure.

q: What is the appropriate method to prevent adhesions in a pregnant woman with a history of previous difficult cesarean sections and scheduled for elective cesarean section?
o: Perform Cesarean section before going into labor
k: Cesarean adhesion and infection prevention: Adhesions: meticulous hemostasis, gentle tissue handling, irrigation of clots Infection (endometritis, SSI): antibiotics before skin incision Adhesion barriers: limited evidenc
r: This recall's key is preoperative antibiotics, on the reasoning that postoperative infection (endometritis, peritonitis) causes inflammation that promotes adhesion formation, so preventing infection indirectly reduces adhesions in a woman with previous difficult cesarean sections . The compiler chos
wo: A. Maintain hemostasis: the measure most directly linked to fewer adhesions (blood and fibrin in the field are the substrate for adhesions); many would choose it, as in the companion recall. | B. Insert drain: drains do not prevent adhesions and may promote them as a foreign body; not recommended routinely. | C. CS before labor: scheduling before labor avoids an emergency procedure but does not change adhesion formation.

q: 20 y/o wemon complaining of worsening menstrual cramping , resulting of absence of the university frequent, tried NSIDs with patrial relief . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start oral combined oral contraceptive pills
k: Dysmenorrhea ladder: Step 1: NSAIDs Step 2: hormonal therapy (COCP, progestin, LNG IUS) Step 3: failure of both: laparoscopy for endometriosis Secondary signs: onset after years of painless periods, dyspareunia, abnormal
r: A 20 year old with worsening menstrual cramps causing missed university and only partial relief from NSAIDs has dysmenorrhea that has failed first line therapy. The next step is hormonal therapy, usually combined oral contraceptive pills, which suppress ovulation and endometrial prostaglandins; lapa
wo: B. Diagnostic laparoscopy: for suspected endometriosis after failure of NSAIDs plus hormonal therapy (3-6 months), or with abnormal findings. | C. Refer to pain clinic: for chronic pain refractory to medical and surgical management, not after one partly effective drug. | D. Pelvic MRI: for a suspected structural cause such as adenomyosis or a mass after abnormal examination or US; not the next step here.

q: 35 y/o wemon diagnosed with left tube ectopic pregnancy, managed with MTX , she remined asymptomatic with plautuing on day 4,7 b-hcg Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Methotrexate monitoring for ectopic pregnancy: Measure β hCG on day 4 and day 7 Fall ≥15%: weekly β hCG until negative Fall <15% or plateau: second dose methotrexate Rupture, instability, or failure of second dose: surge
r: After single dose methotrexate, β hCG is measured on day 4 and day 7, and it should fall by at least 15% between them. A plateau between days 4 and 7 in an asymptomatic , stable woman means inadequate response, so the next step is a second dose of methotrexate, with repeat monitoring.
wo: A. Laparoscopic salpingectomy: for rupture, hemodynamic instability, severe pain, or failure after a second methotrexate dose; she is asymptomatic. | B. Repeat β hCG in 48 h: serial 48 hour testing is for a pregnancy of unknown location before diagnosis, not the protocol after methotrexate. | C. Repeat β hCG in 1 week: correct only if the day 4 to 7 fall is ≥15% (weekly follow up until negative).

q: A 44-year-old woman presented with heavy vaginal bleeding ( PB 95/47 , HR 107, Hb 68 , B-hch 3). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Acute AUB management: Stable: IV conjugated estrogen first line; COCP, oral progestin or tranexamic acid Severe, unstable or refractory: D&C (or balloon tamponade) Age ≥45 or risk factors: endometrial sampling Definitive
r: A 44 year old with heavy bleeding, hypotension (95/47) and tachycardia (107) , and Hb 68 has severe acute abnormal uterine bleeding with hemodynamic compromise; β hCG 3 excludes pregnancy. After resuscitation, D&C rapidly stops bleeding that is too severe for medical therapy and gives endometrial ti
wo: A. Hysterectomy: definitive for refractory bleeding or structural disease (adenomyosis, fibroids) once she is stabilised and the cause is known, not as the first emergency step. | B. Mefenamic acid: an NSAID for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding or dysmenorrhea; too weak for unstable acute bleeding. | C. Insert hormonal IUD: excellent for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding, but it acts over months and cannot control acute hemorrhage.

q: 45-year-old pregnant woman at 36 weeks, planned C-section . BMI 32 , no previous DVT/ PE, no significant PMH, and no DVT signs. What is the appropriate prophylaxis?
k: Peripartum VTE prophylaxis: Risk factors: age >35, BMI ≥30, parity ≥3, smoking, CS, immobility, preeclampsia, previous VTE, thrombophilia Agent of choice: LMWH (safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding) Add mechanical: compre
r: Pregnancy and the puerperium are prothrombotic, and cesarean section is a major added VTE risk. This woman has several risk factors: age 45 (>35), BMI 32 (≥30) and a planned C section . That combination warrants pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH (enoxaparin) after delivery, with graduated compre
wo: B. Warfarin: teratogenic in pregnancy and not used for routine peripartum prophylaxis; it can be used postpartum for longer term anticoagulation, including in breastfeeding, but LMWH is the standard. | C. No prophylaxis: right only for a low risk woman with no or minimal risk factors; age >35 and obesity plus CS put her at increased risk.

q: A 32-year-old woman with twin pregnancy , presented at 38 weeks of gestation in active labor. Examination revealed twin A is in vertex presentation , and twin B is also in vertex presentation . Both fetal heart rates are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Twin delivery by presentation: Vertex vertex: vaginal delivery Vertex non vertex: vaginal delivery possible (breech extraction or ECV of twin B) or CS Twin A non vertex: cesarean section Monochorionic monoamniotic: cesar
r: Twins at 38 weeks in active labor with twin A vertex and twin B vertex and normal fetal heart rates have the most favourable twin presentation. Vertex vertex twins are delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery, with continuous monitoring and readiness for intervention for the second twin.
kw: twin A is in vertex presentation
twin B is also in vertex presentation
wo: A. Forceps delivery: only for specific second stage indications (prolonged second stage, fetal distress with a low head); there is no indication here. | B. Cesarean section: right when twin A is non vertex, in monoamniotic twins, or with usual obstetric indications such as fetal distress. | C. Ventouse delivery: an assisted delivery needing an indication in the second stage; none is present.

q: 30 weeks pregnant all normal came for prenatal visit what vaccine I can give ?
k: Vaccines in pregnancy: Recommended: Tdap at 27-36 weeks each pregnancy; inactivated influenza any trimester If at risk: hepatitis A, hepatitis B Contraindicated (live): MMR, varicella, BCG, live intranasal influenza DTaP
r: At 30 weeks a healthy pregnant woman should receive the inactivated Tdap vaccine (printed here as 'dtap'), ideally between 27 and 36 weeks in every pregnancy. Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn against pertussis before the infant's own vaccines start at 2 months.
wo: A. MMR: a live attenuated vaccine, contraindicated in pregnancy; give it postpartum to rubella non immune women. | C. Hepatitis A: inactivated and can be given in pregnancy if at risk (travel, exposure, liver disease), but it is not routine for a healthy woman. | D. Varicella: live attenuated, contraindicated in pregnancy; offer postpartum if non immune.

q: A 40-year-old woman came in labor with her seventh child . Following delivery, she developed postpartum hemorrhage due to failure to deliver the placenta (retained placenta). What is the type of postpartum hemorrhage ?
k: PPH classification is by TIME, not cause. Primary: within 24 hours of delivery (atony, trauma, retained placenta, coagulopathy) Secondary: 24 hours to 12 weeks (retained products, endometritis) Grand multiparity and age
r: This recall's key is secondary PPH, reasoning that retained products of conception are a classic cause of secondary (late) PPH. However, PPH type is defined by timing, not cause: bleeding following delivery because the placenta has failed to deliver happens within 24 hours, which is primary PPH. The
wo: A. Primary: bleeding within 24 hours of delivery; a retained placenta right after birth fits this timing, so many sources would key it here (see concern). | C. Tertiary: not a standard PPH category; PPH is only primary (within 24 hours) or secondary (24 hours to 12 weeks).

q: 45-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days . Now she is feeling drowsy and easily fatigued and sometimes faints . Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
k: Heavy bleeding with symptoms of anemia: assess severity first (CBC), exclude pregnancy (hCG). Then stabilize: transfusion if Hb low and symptomatic Then imaging (pelvic US) and endometrial sampling if age ≥45 or risk fac
r: A 45-year-old still in reproductive age with 15 days of bleeding who is now drowsy, fatigued and fainting has symptomatic anemia. The first step is to measure the hemoglobin (CBC) to judge need for transfusion and to exclude pregnancy with beta-hCG, since pregnancy-related bleeding changes the whole
kw: period has not stopped for the past 15 days
wo: A. Ultrasound: needed to look for structural causes (fibroids, endometrial thickness) but comes after stabilization and excluding pregnancy. | B. Urine pregnancy test: excludes pregnancy but ignores the anemia that is causing her symptoms; CBC plus hCG covers both. | C. Dilatation and curettage: used for acute uncontrolled bleeding or tissue sampling after initial assessment; not the first step before labs.

q: A pregnant woman attending antenatal care has pre-existing type 1 diabetes mellitus with a HbA1c of 12% . What is the most common complication in this case?
k: Pregestational diabetes: high HbA1c at conception = congenital anomalies. HbA1c is the best predictor of fetal anomaly risk in early pregnancy Typical anomalies: cardiac defects, neural tube defects, caudal regression La
r: In pre-existing type 1 diabetes with a very high HbA1c of 12% , hyperglycemia during organogenesis in the first trimester markedly raises the risk of congenital malformations (cardiac, neural tube, caudal regression). The recaller notes she was at 12 weeks, so the early-pregnancy complication is key
wo: B. Polyhydramnios: a common complication of diabetes later in pregnancy (fetal polyuria from hyperglycemia); it is the answer when the stem is in the second or third trimester or describes a large-for-dates uterus.

q: A woman required oxytocin for augmentation of labor . Physicians were discussing how to prevent PPH in her case.
o: Monitor for signs of uterine atony
Active management of 3rd stage of labor
k: PPH prevention = active management of the third stage for every birth. Uterotonic: oxytocin is first line Controlled cord traction Uterine tone check after placental delivery Atony risks: augmentation, prolonged labor, o
r: Oxytocin augmentation of labor is a risk factor for uterine atony, the most common cause of PPH. The proven measure to prevent PPH is active management of the third stage of labor : a prophylactic uterotonic (oxytocin) after delivery, controlled cord traction and uterine assessment.
wo: A. Monitor for signs of uterine atony: surveillance detects PPH after it starts but does not prevent it. | C. Delayed cord clamping: benefits the newborn (iron stores, preterm outcomes); it does not prevent maternal PPH and is compatible with active management.

q: A 34-year-old G2P1 has a fetus with a single umbilical artery .
k: Single umbilical artery: normal cord has 2 arteries and 1 vein. Associations: multiple pregnancy, maternal diabetes Fetal: renal and cardiac anomalies, aneuploidy, growth restriction Management: detailed anatomy scan, co
r: The stem asks what is associated with a single umbilical artery . Multiple pregnancy is a recognized risk factor (more common in twins), so it is the keyed association among these options. At 34 years she is not of advanced maternal age, and parity is not a risk factor.
wo: A. Age: advanced maternal age has been linked in some studies, but 34 years is below the usual threshold and age is not the classic association here. | B. Parity: G2P1 is not a recognized risk factor for single umbilical artery. | D. Hypothyroidism: not an established association; the classic maternal disease associated is diabetes.

q: A 12-week pregnant woman presents with exertional dyspnea. She is otherwise healthy, and systemic examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound shows monochorionic twin pregnancy with evidence of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Laser photocoagulation of placental vascular anastomoses
k: TTTS occurs in monochorionic twins (shared placenta with vascular anastomoses). Donor: oligohydramnios, growth restriction; recipient: polyhydramnios, heart failure Staging by Quintero About 16 to 26 weeks, stage II or m
r: This recall's key is amnioreduction , following the compiler's reasoning that fetoscopic laser ablation is performed only from about 16 weeks , so at 12 weeks it is not yet an option. Removing excess amniotic fluid from the recipient sac relieves the maternal symptom ( exertional dyspnea from uterin
wo: A. Termination of pregnancy: may be discussed in severe early TTTS with poor prognosis, but it is not the default first step in a healthy mother. | B. Expectant management with observation only: appropriate for mild disease (Quintero stage I) with no maternal symptoms; here the mother is symptomatic. | C. Laser photocoagulation: the definitive treatment for moderate to severe TTTS between about 16 and 26 weeks; another candidate chose it regardless of gestation, but at 12 weeks it is too early.

q: A 24-year-old woman primigravida undergoes an uneventful vaginal delivery at term. After placental delivery, she has 1000 cc of vaginal bleeding . She is alert, and her vital signs are stable, with the uterus noted to be firm . Which of the following is the most common cause?
k: PPH causes: the 4 Ts. Tone (atony): most common, soft boggy uterus Trauma: lacerations with a firm uterus Tissue: retained placenta or products Thrombin: coagulopathy Firm uterus with bleeding: inspect cervix, vagina, pe
r: 1000 cc of bleeding after placental delivery is PPH. The decisive clue is a firm uterus , which means normal tone and excludes atony; with an uneventful delivery and stable patient, the next most common cause is genital tract laceration (cervical, vaginal, perineal).
wo: A. Uterine atony: the most common cause of PPH overall, but the uterus would be soft and boggy; a firm uterus excludes it. | B. Coagulopathy: suspected with oozing from puncture sites, abruption, preeclampsia/HELLP, amniotic fluid embolism or massive transfusion; none here. | D. Retained products of conception: suggested by an incomplete placenta and a uterus that does not stay contracted; usually atony coexists.

q: 30-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism is taking levothyroxine 125 µg daily. Her thyroid function tests are within the normal range. She is newly diagnosed with pregnancy . What is the most appropriate management of her levothyroxine dose?
o: Continue the same dose without any change
k: Hypothyroidism in pregnancy: increase the dose on confirmation. Typical step: about 25 to 30% increase (e.g. two extra doses per week) Check TSH every 4 weeks in the first half of pregnancy Return to pre-pregnancy dose a
r: Pregnancy raises thyroxine requirements (higher thyroid-binding globulin, placental deiodination, fetal dependence on maternal T4 in the first trimester). A woman with known hypothyroidism should therefore increase her levothyroxine as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even with normal pre-pregnancy t
wo: B. Decrease the dose: requirements rise, not fall, in pregnancy; decreasing risks maternal hypothyroidism and impaired fetal neurodevelopment. | C. Continue the same dose: would be acceptable only with close TSH monitoring showing she stays on target; standard advice is to increase pre-emptively. | D. Stop levothyroxine: levothyroxine is safe in pregnancy and stopping it harms the fetus.

q: A 29-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room with a very heavy period. She is morbidly obese and diabetic . Her periods are irregular, occurring every 3-4 months . She had her period 2 weeks ago and it has not stopped, with heavy clots. Pregnancy test is negative . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Irregular, infrequent cycles + heavy prolonged bleeding = anovulatory AUB (unopposed estrogen). Risk: obesity, diabetes/insulin resistance, PCOS Regular heavy periods: think fibroids, adenomyosis, coagulopathy Always exc
r: The decisive clues are "morbidly obese and diabetic" (insulin resistance, PCOS picture), periods "every 3-4 months" (oligomenorrhea = anovulation) and a negative pregnancy test. Without ovulation there is no progesterone, so the endometrium keeps building under unopposed estrogen until it sheds irre
wo: A. Fibroids: cause heavy but REGULAR cyclical periods (menorrhagia), often with a bulky irregular uterus; they do not explain cycles every 3-4 months. | B. Bleeding disorder: suspect in an adolescent with heavy bleeding since menarche or a personal/family history of bruising and mucosal bleeding; nothing here suggests it. | C. Incomplete abortion: needs a positive pregnancy test, open os and passage of tissue; the pregnancy test here is negative.

q: A 46-year-old woman is complaining of heavy menstruation lasting for 14 days every period. She is morbidly obese and has type 2 diabetes mellitus (see lab results and report). Ultrasound: Endometrial thickness of 18 mm . Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
k: AUB over 45, or under 45 with unopposed estrogen risk / failed treatment = endometrial biopsy. Office (pipelle) sample is first line Hysteroscopy-guided biopsy if sample inadequate or bleeding persists TVUS assesses thic
r: She has abnormal uterine bleeding at "46" (over 45) with strong unopposed estrogen risk factors ("morbidly obese", "type 2 diabetes") and a thickened endometrium of 18 mm. Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma must be excluded, and the next step is tissue: an office (pipelle) endometrial sample, whic
wo: A. Pelvic CT: used for staging once cancer is confirmed, not for diagnosing the cause of AUB; it cannot give histology. | B. Pelvic MRI: helps characterise adenomyosis or fibroids or stage a known endometrial cancer; it does not replace tissue diagnosis. | C. Hysteroscopy: chosen when office sampling fails, is non-diagnostic or bleeding persists despite a benign sample, or for a focal lesion such as a polyp; it is not the first step here.

q: A 27-year-old G4P3 woman is seen in labor at 39 weeks of gestation. Examination revealed the cervix is 5 cm dilated with clear amniotic fluid draining. Cardiotocography shows that the baseline is 140 beats per minute, no accelerations, good variability, and no decelerations . The uterine contractions are regular and strong, occurring at a rate of 3 to 4 in 10 minutes . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Reassurance and reassessment in 30 to 60 minutes
k: Normal active labor + reassuring CTG + adequate contractions = continue and reassess. Adequate contractions: 3-5 in 10 minutes Not in labor + indication: induction In labor, weak contractions, slow progress: augmentation
r: At "5 cm dilated" with regular strong contractions she is in the active first stage of labor. The CTG is reassuring (baseline 140, good variability, no decelerations; absent accelerations alone in labor is not worrying) and contractions are adequate at "3 to 4 in 10 minutes". Labor is progressing no
wo: A. Induction of labor: starts labor in a woman who is NOT in labor (e.g. post-term, unripe cervix); she is already in active labor. | B. Augmentation of labor: for slow progress with inadequate contractions (fewer than 3 in 10 min); her contractions are adequate. | C. Emergency cesarean section: for fetal distress (bradycardia, reduced variability, late decelerations) or obstructed labor; the CTG here is reassuring.

q: A newly married woman is presented to the gynecology clinic for a routine examination and checkup. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value ?
k: Bimanual pelvic exam = highest-yield component of the gynecological examination. Assesses uterus (size, position, mobility) and adnexa Detects cervical motion and adnexal tenderness Virgin patient: avoid digital vaginal
r: In a routine gynecological check the bimanual (digital pelvic) examination gives the most diagnostic information: uterine size, shape, position and mobility, adnexal masses and cervical or adnexal tenderness. A "newly married" woman is sexually active, so a digital pelvic exam is acceptable.
wo: A. Vaginal inspection: shows only the external genitalia and vaginal walls (discharge, lesions); it cannot assess the uterus or adnexa. | B. General appearance: part of every exam but nonspecific for pelvic pathology. | C. Abdominal examination: detects only large pelvic masses rising out of the pelvis; small uterine or adnexal pathology is missed.

q: A 27-year-old woman delivered 2 weeks ago and presented with a painful, hard mass in the right breast. She received a 4-day course of antibiotics with no improvement . Examination revealed she is febrile, and a breast abscess is suspected . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Mastitis that fails antibiotics, or a fluctuant/hard mass = think abscess: ultrasound + drainage. Mastitis: antistaphylococcal antibiotic (e.g. flucloxacillin, cephalexin), continue breastfeeding Abscess: US-guided aspir
r: Two weeks postpartum with a "painful, hard mass", fever and "no improvement" after 4 days of antibiotics = mastitis that has progressed to a suspected abscess. Antibiotics cannot sterilise a pus collection, so ultrasound is needed to confirm it and a surgical review for drainage (needle aspiration o
kw: 4-day course of antibiotics with no improvement
wo: A. Change antibiotics: changing the drug does not treat a collection; it only fits mastitis with no abscess (or a resistant organism such as MRSA) once an abscess is excluded. | B. Stop breastfeeding: not needed for mastitis or abscess; continued emptying helps resolution (feeding from the other side or expressing if drainage is near the nipple). | C. Encourage breastfeeding: correct supportive advice, but it does not address a suspected abscess, so it is not the most appropriate management.

q: A 30-year-old woman at 6 weeks gestation is receiving methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy. The first dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM was administered one week ago. The human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels on days 1, 4, and 7 were as follows: Day 1: 1000 mIU/mL Day 4: 1200 mIU/mL Day 7: 2100 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
k: Methotrexate monitoring: compare day 4 vs day 7 hCG. Fall ≥15%: weekly hCG until negative Fall <15% or plateau: second MTX dose Clearly rising hCG or failure after repeat dosing: surgery Unstable / rupture signs: immedia
r: After single-dose methotrexate, hCG is compared between day 4 and day 7. Here it RISES from 1200 to 2100 (about 75%), which means treatment failure with an actively growing ectopic and rising rupture risk. This recall's key is that a clearly rising hCG after methotrexate = failed medical treatment,
wo: A. Repeat beta-hCG in 1 week: correct only when hCG falls by ≥15% between day 4 and day 7 (successful response, weekly follow-up until negative). | C. Administer a second dose of methotrexate: the response to a plateau or fall of less than 15% between day 4 and day 7; a marked rise suggests failure of medical treatment. | D. Admit for multiple methotrexate regimen: a different protocol chosen from the start, not the response to a sharply rising hCG on single-dose therapy.

q: A 31-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 had an uneventful pregnancy and a spontaneous vaginal delivery after 2 hours of labor , just making it to the hospital . She delivered a healthy boy weighing 3000 g . After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage?
k: PPH causes = 4 Ts: Tone (most common), Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin. Atony risks: overdistension (macrosomia, twins, polyhydramnios) Labor: precipitous OR prolonged, oxytocin use Grand multiparity, chorioamnionitis Precipito
r: Delivery "after 2 hours of labor, just making it to the hospital" is precipitous labor (less than 3 hours). Very rapid labor predisposes to uterine atony (and genital tract trauma), the commonest cause of PPH. She is only para 1 and the baby is 3000 g, so the other options do not apply.
kw: just making it to the hospital
wo: A. Grand parity: requires high parity (around 5 or more deliveries); she is G2 P1. | B. Prolonged labor: also a risk for atony, but her labor was very short, not prolonged. | C. Macrosomic baby: means about 4000 g or more (uterine overdistension); 3000 g is a normal weight.

q: A 30-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 presented to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with profuse vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain . CTG showed a normal heart rate with regular contractions . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Antepartum hemorrhage: classify by pain. Painful bleeding + tender/hard uterus: abruption Painless bright red bleeding: placenta previa Painless bleeding at membrane rupture + fetal distress: vasa previa Previa suspected
r: Third-trimester bleeding with "abdominal pain" is PAINFUL antepartum hemorrhage = placental abruption. Bleeding from the separating placenta irritates the uterus, causing regular (often frequent) contractions; the fetal heart may still be normal when the separation is small.
kw: profuse vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain
wo: A. Labor: at 30 weeks this would be preterm, and labor gives only a show (mucus with streaks of blood), not profuse bleeding. | B. Preterm labor: contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks; it does not explain profuse bleeding, which here comes from the abruption. | C. Placenta previa: bleeding is classically PAINLESS with a soft, non-tender uterus; this patient has pain.

q: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her 8th week presented to the Emergency Room with bleeding and reported passing vesicles . After assessing, her uterine size appears larger than the date . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Bleeding + uterus larger than dates + vesicles = molar pregnancy. Very high hCG: hyperemesis, early preeclampsia (<20 weeks), hyperthyroidism, theca lutein cysts US: snowstorm, no fetus (complete mole) Treatment: suction
r: First-trimester bleeding with "passing vesicles" (grape-like hydropic villi) and a uterus "larger than date" is the classic triad of a hydatidiform (complete) mole. Confirm with very high hCG and the snowstorm pattern on ultrasound, then suction evacuation and hCG follow-up.
kw: uterine size appears larger than the date
wo: B. Missed abortion: non-viable pregnancy with a closed os; the uterus is SMALLER than dates and there is no vesicle passage. | C. Ectopic pregnancy: pain and spotting with an empty uterus; the uterus is not larger than dates and vesicles are not passed. | D. Threatened abortion: bleeding with a closed os and a viable fetus; uterine size matches dates.

q: A 25-year-old G1 P0 woman presented to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with abdominal pain. There was no leaking or bleeding. The CTG shows a normal heart rate with regular contractions 4 in 10 minutes . Which of the following is the most appropriate way to diagnose if she has preterm labor ?
o: History only is enough to diagnose
CTG showing regular contractions is diagnostic
If there is no leaking, then she isn't in preterm labor
k: Preterm labor = regular contractions + cervical change, at 20-37 weeks. Digital exam only after previa excluded and membranes intact PPROM suspected: sterile speculum, avoid digital exam Confirmed under 34 weeks: steroid
r: Preterm labor is regular contractions PLUS cervical change (dilation and/or effacement) before 37 weeks. She has contractions "4 in 10 minutes" and no bleeding or leaking (so no contraindication to a digital exam), and the missing piece is cervical change, which a digital exam for dilation provides.
kw: diagnose if she has preterm labor
wo: B. History only is enough: history cannot separate true preterm labor from false (Braxton Hicks) contractions; objective cervical change is required. | C. CTG showing regular contractions is diagnostic: contractions alone are not enough; without cervical change it may be false labor. | D. No leaking means not in preterm labor: wrong, preterm labor can occur with intact membranes; leaking relates to PPROM, a separate diagnosis.

q: A 45-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days and now she is feeling drowsy and easily fatigued (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Manage the bleeding and send her home
k: Acute heavy AUB: ABC and stabilise first, then stop bleeding, then find the cause. Transfuse: Hb below 7 g/dL, or higher if symptomatic or unstable Medical: IV estrogen, COCP or high-dose progestin, tranexamic acid D&C:
r: Fifteen days of continuous bleeding at "45" with "drowsy and easily fatigued" means symptomatic anemia; the labs (not shown in the recall) are keyed as a low hemoglobin. A symptomatic, drowsy patient must be stabilised first, so the next step is blood transfusion, then control of the bleeding and en
kw: not stopped for the past 15 days
wo: A. Ultrasound: part of the AUB workup (structural causes, endometrial thickness) but done after the patient is stabilised, not before treating symptomatic anemia. | B. Dilatation and curettage: for severe bleeding that fails medical therapy or in an unstable patient after resuscitation; it is not the first step and does not correct anemia. | D. Manage the bleeding and send her home: unsafe in a drowsy woman with symptomatic anemia; it fits only a stable patient with mild bleeding and acceptable hemoglobin.

q: A 28-year-old woman presented with mild pelvic pain and spotting. She was diagnosed with an ectopic pregnancy and offered medical management . Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to treat this patient?
k: Methotrexate for ectopic: needs ALL of the following. Hemodynamically stable, no rupture No fetal cardiac activity, small mass Low hCG (lower levels = higher success) Reliable follow-up; no liver, renal or blood disease,
r: "Mild pelvic pain and spotting" describes a stable, unruptured ectopic, and she was "offered medical management". The medical treatment of ectopic pregnancy is methotrexate, a folate antagonist that stops the rapidly dividing trophoblast; it is usually given as single-dose IM with hCG checks on days
wo: A. Oxytocin: a uterotonic used for induction/augmentation of labor and for PPH; it has no effect on a tubal pregnancy. | B. Carboprost: a PGF2-alpha used for PPH due to atony (avoid in asthma); not a treatment for ectopic pregnancy. | C. Misoprostol: used for medical management of missed or incomplete miscarriage and for induction; it empties the uterus, not the tube.

q: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy. She is 20 weeks pregnant and known to have SLE . She has been symptom-free for the past 2 years. She is taking Plaquenil daily . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer to Rheumatology to stop the medication
k: Well-controlled chronic disease on a pregnancy-safe drug = continue it. SLE safe: hydroxychloroquine, low-dose steroids, azathioprine SLE avoid: methotrexate, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide Epilepsy controlled: continue
r: Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) is safe in pregnancy and is recommended to be continued in SLE. She is in remission ("symptom-free for the past 2 years") ON it; stopping it raises the risk of a lupus flare, which is far more dangerous for mother and fetus than the drug.
wo: A. Stop Plaquenil: withdrawal increases flare risk in pregnancy; the drug is not teratogenic. | B. Switch it to steroids: steroids are for active flares; switching a well-controlled patient adds risks (diabetes, hypertension, PPROM) with no benefit. | D. Refer to Rheumatology to stop the medication: co-management is reasonable, but the plan to STOP is wrong.

q: A 29-year-old woman presented to the clinic unsure of her gestational age. She missed her period 3 months ago but her periods are irregular (see report). Ultrasound: Determined gestational age as 11 weeks . Which of the following was measured in the ultrasound to determine gestational age?
k: Ultrasound dating by trimester. Up to 13+6 weeks: CRL (most accurate) From 14 weeks: HC/BPD, with FL Growth and fetal weight: AC (most sensitive) Earliest scans: gestational sac / yolk sac
r: Her dates are unreliable ("irregular" periods) and the scan gives "11 weeks", which is first trimester. Crown-rump length is the most accurate dating parameter in the first trimester (up to 13+6 weeks), with an error of only about 5-7 days.
wo: A. Femur length: a second and third trimester biometry measure used with BPD, HC and AC; not for first-trimester dating. | C. Abdominal circumference: used after the first trimester; it is the most sensitive parameter for fetal growth and weight (IUGR, macrosomia), not for dating. | D. Biparietal diameter and head circumference: used for dating from about 14 weeks onwards, when CRL is no longer valid.

q: A 45-year-old woman P6 is complaining of chronic pelvic pain and heavy menstruation (see report). Pelvic MRI: Diffuse thickened myometrium . Which of the following is the most definitive treatment for her condition?
k: Adenomyosis = endometrial glands within the myometrium. Typical: multiparous, 40s, dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia Exam: diffusely enlarged, boggy, tender, symmetric uterus Imaging: TVUS then MRI (thickened junctional zone) S
r: Chronic pelvic pain, heavy menstruation and a "diffuse thickened myometrium" on MRI in a multiparous woman ("P6") at 45 = adenomyosis. Medical options only control symptoms; the only definitive cure is hysterectomy, appropriate here because her family is complete.
wo: B. Hormonal IUD: effective first-line SYMPTOM control (reduces bleeding and pain) and fertility-sparing, but not definitive. | C. Oral contraceptive pills: symptomatic control of bleeding and dysmenorrhea only; disease persists. | D. Dilatation and curettage: removes endometrium for diagnosis or acute bleeding; it cannot reach adenomyosis, which lies within the myometrium.

q: A 43-year-old woman presented with intermenstrual bleeding in the last 3 months (see report). Ultrasound: A 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
o: Hysteroscopy and removal of the structure
k: Endometrial polyp: intermenstrual bleeding + focal echogenic lesion. Best test to confirm: saline sonography or hysteroscopy Symptomatic or 1 cm or more: hysteroscopic polypectomy Small and asymptomatic (premenopausal):
r: "Intermenstrual bleeding" with a discrete "13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium" is an endometrial polyp. It is symptomatic and over 1 cm, so it should be removed; hysteroscopic polypectomy both treats the bleeding and provides tissue for histology.
wo: A. Endometrial sample: a blind pipelle sample can miss a focal lesion; it suits diffuse thickening (e.g. AUB over 45), not a discrete polyp. | B. Repeat the ultrasound in 6 weeks: observation fits only small (under 1 cm), asymptomatic polyps; she is symptomatic. | C. Cyclic progesterone for 3 months: a treatment for anovulatory bleeding or hyperplasia without atypia; it does not remove a polyp.

q: A 30-year-old woman is complaining of yellowish , fishy-smelling vaginal discharge and itching . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Vaginal discharge by its key feature. Fishy odor, thin gray, clue cells, pH over 4.5: BV (metronidazole, no partner treatment) White curdy, itchy, odorless, pH normal: Candida (azoles) Frothy yellow-green, strawberry cer
r: The decisive clue is "fishy-smelling": a fishy (amine) odor, worse after intercourse and positive on the whiff test with KOH, is the defining feature of bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella and anaerobes, clue cells, pH over 4.5). This recall's key treats the odor as decisive over the color and the itch
wo: A. Candida vaginitis: thick white cottage-cheese, ODORLESS discharge with marked itching and normal pH (under 4.5). | C. Vaginal gonorrhea: mainly causes cervicitis (mucopurulent cervical discharge, often asymptomatic); no fishy odor. | D. Vaginal trichomoniasis: frothy yellow-green discharge with itching, dyspareunia and strawberry cervix; motile flagellates on wet mount, treat partners too.

q: A 25-year-old pregnant woman with 7 weeks' amenorrhea presented to the clinic with a history of passing tissue at home and vaginal bleeding. Examination revealed mild vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix . Which of the following is the most likely abortion type?
k: Abortion types by cervix and tissue passage. Closed, no tissue: threatened (or missed if non-viable) Open, no tissue: inevitable Open, tissue passed: incomplete Closed, tissue passed: complete Missed: non-viable fetus re
r: Use the 2x2 rule: tissue passed? cervix open or closed? She "passed tissue at home" and now has only "mild" bleeding with a "closed cervix" = all products expelled = complete abortion. Confirm an empty uterus on ultrasound; no evacuation is needed.
wo: B. Inevitable: OPEN cervix but NO tissue passed yet. | C. Threatened: closed cervix with bleeding but no tissue passed and a viable pregnancy. | D. Incomplete: tissue passed but the cervix is still OPEN with retained products and often heavier bleeding.

q: A 37-year-old G3 P1011 at 28 weeks ' gestation had vaginal spotting 2 weeks ago but no abdominal cramping or passing any clots or tissue. Examination reveals fundal height equivalent to 18 weeks ' size. Ultrasound confirms lack of fetal heart activity and no fetal movement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Fetal death is named by gestational age. Under 20 weeks: missed abortion 20 weeks or more: IUFD / fetal demise Retained IUFD: risk of DIC, check coagulation Management: induction of labor (misoprostol) or expectant
r: The key word is "28 weeks". Absent fetal heart activity and movement on ultrasound at 20 weeks or more (or fetal weight above about 350-500 g) is intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD), not an abortion. The fundal height of only 18 weeks shows the fetus stopped growing weeks ago, and the earlier spotting
wo: B. Missed abortion: the same picture (non-viable, retained, closed os, small for dates) but BEFORE 20 weeks. | C. Incomplete abortion: requires passage of tissue with an open cervix; she passed no tissue. | D. Gestational trophoblastic disease: uterus LARGER than dates, very high hCG and snowstorm ultrasound; here the uterus is small and a fetus is seen.

q: A 24-year-old primigravida presents at 12 weeks gestation to an antenatal visit. Blood electrolytes and renal function tests were requested 3 days earlier. Which of the following is the most expected finding on her blood tests?
o: A fall in serum creatinine level
An increase of plasma sodium level
Increased plasma blood urea nitrogen level
Unaffected serum blood urea nitrogen level
k: Renal physiology in pregnancy: GFR up about 50%. Creatinine and BUN: decrease Sodium and osmolality: slight decrease Uric acid: falls early (rise suggests preeclampsia) Glycosuria and mild proteinuria can be physiologica
r: Renal plasma flow and GFR rise by up to about 50% from early pregnancy, so creatinine is cleared faster and serum creatinine FALLS (and so does BUN). By "12 weeks" this fall is already measurable; a "normal" nonpregnant creatinine may actually indicate renal impairment in pregnancy.
wo: B. An increase of plasma sodium level: plasma sodium falls slightly in pregnancy (hemodilution and a reset osmostat). | C. Increased plasma blood urea nitrogen level: BUN falls with the higher GFR; a rise suggests renal impairment or dehydration. | D. Unaffected serum blood urea nitrogen level: BUN does change; it decreases from the first trimester.

q: A 35-year-old G9 P6026 at 8 weeks' gestation presents to the hospital with vaginal spotting associated with very mild lower abdominal pain. She has noticed some dark brown clots. Examination reveals she is comfortable in bed with no abdominal tenderness appreciated. Pelvic examination reveals minimal dark-red clots in the introitus and cervical os closed (see report). Transvaginal ultrasound: 5-week gestational size with no fetal heart . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step of management plan?
k: Missed abortion (closed os, non-viable, small for dates). Stable, under 13 weeks: expectant management Medical: misoprostol (up to about 20 weeks) Surgical (suction evacuation): heavy bleeding, instability, infection, fa
r: At "8 weeks" by dates the scan shows a "5-week gestational size with no fetal heart" and the "cervical os closed": a non-viable pregnancy retained in the uterus = missed abortion (early pregnancy loss). She is stable, "comfortable", non-tender with only minimal bleeding and no infection, and under 1
kw: 5-week gestational size with no fetal heart
wo: A. Suction curettage: chosen for heavy bleeding, instability, infection, failed expectant/medical management or patient preference; none is present here. | B. Prostaglandin E2: used for cervical ripening before induction of labor at term; for medical management of miscarriage the agent is misoprostol (PGE1). | D. Abortifacient agent with antibiotic: implies septic abortion (fever, foul discharge, tenderness); she has no signs of infection.

q: A 34-year-old healthy woman presents with recurrent symptoms, including headache, anxiety, and mastalgia , that start 8-10 days before menstruation and improve afterward . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: PMS = cyclic symptoms in the luteal phase, gone soon after menses begin. Symptom-free week after menses is required Diagnosis: clinical, prospective diary for 2 cycles Severe mood symptoms impairing function: PMDD Treatm
r: Physical (headache, mastalgia) and emotional (anxiety) symptoms that "start 8-10 days before menstruation and improve afterward", recurring each cycle in a healthy 34-year-old, are luteal-phase symptoms = premenstrual (tension) syndrome. It is a clinical diagnosis, best confirmed with a prospective
wo: A. Endometriosis: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain and subfertility; it does not cause cyclic anxiety and mastalgia that resolve with menses. | B. Perimenopausal symptoms: hot flushes, night sweats and irregular cycles, usually after 45; not tied to the week before each period. | C. Pelvic congestion syndrome: dull pelvic aching from pelvic varices, worse on standing and after intercourse, usually in multiparous women; no breast or mood symptoms.

q: A 36-year-old G4 P3003 is admitted in preterm labor at 36+5 weeks with polyhydramnios . Fetal bradycardia is noted after spontaneous rupture of membranes . Which of the following needs to be excluded by a prompt vaginal examination?
k: Cord prolapse: sudden bradycardia or variable decelerations right after ROM. Risks: polyhydramnios, malpresentation, prematurity, high head, multiple pregnancy Confirm: vaginal exam (cord felt/seen) Act: call for help, e
r: "Fetal bradycardia" immediately "after spontaneous rupture of membranes" in a woman with "polyhydramnios" (gush of fluid sweeps the cord down) and a preterm, possibly high presenting part is cord prolapse until proven otherwise. A prompt vaginal exam confirms it by feeling the cord below the present
wo: B. Breech presentation: a risk factor for cord prolapse but not itself a cause of sudden bradycardia; it is not what the urgent exam needs to exclude. | C. Placental abruption: painful bleeding with a tender hard uterus; a digital exam does not diagnose it. | D. Shoulder/arm prolapse: occurs with transverse lie; it does not cause sudden bradycardia after membrane rupture the way cord compression does.

q: A 32-year-old G2 Pi AO at 12 weeks of gestation . She is a known case of IDDM for 12 years and attended the Antenatal Clinic. Which of the following will most likely increase markedly in this patient?
k: Pregestational DM vs gestational DM. Pregestational: congenital anomalies (cardiac, NTD, caudal regression), miscarriage Both: macrosomia, polyhydramnios, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia GDM begins after organog
r: She has long-standing pregestational diabetes ("IDDM for 12 years"). Hyperglycemia during organogenesis in the first trimester markedly raises the risk of congenital malformations (cardiac defects, neural tube defects, caudal regression), and this is the complication most strongly increased compared
wo: A. Preeclampsia: increased in pregestational diabetes (especially with vasculopathy or nephropathy), but the marked, organogenesis-related increase is in malformations. | B. Polyhydramnios: also more common in diabetes (fetal polyuria), but it is a later, less specific complication. | C. Postpartum hemorrhage: may rise slightly through macrosomia and overdistension, but it is not the markedly increased risk.

q: A 22-year-old pregnant woman at 40 weeks of gestation was diagnosed with DVT and started on a therapeutic dose of heparin. The patient had a normal vaginal delivery. Shortly after a heparin injection , she sustained postpartum hemorrhage. The uterus was contracted and examination revealed no lacerations . Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: PPH 4 Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin. Heparin (UFH, partly LMWH) reversal: protamine sulfate Warfarin reversal: vitamin K + PCC or FFP DIC: FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets ITP with bleeding: platelets + steroids/IVIG
r: The uterus is "contracted" (not tone) and there are "no lacerations" (not trauma), leaving thrombin as the cause, and the bleeding started "shortly after a heparin injection" at a therapeutic dose. Heparin-related hemorrhage is reversed with its specific antidote, protamine sulfate.
wo: A. Vitamin K: reverses warfarin (vitamin K antagonists), not heparin; it also acts slowly. | B. Tranexamic acid: an antifibrinolytic recommended early in PPH generally, but it does not neutralise heparin; the targeted treatment is protamine. | D. Fresh frozen plasma: replaces clotting factors in DIC or warfarin reversal; it does not reverse heparin effect.

q: A 22-year-old PG at 33 weeks of gestation newly diagnosed with gestational diabetes . Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy ?
k: GDM treatment ladder. 1st: diet + exercise + self-monitoring 2nd: insulin (preferred drug, does not cross placenta) Alternative: metformin (or glyburide in some settings) Screening: OGTT at 24-28 weeks
r: She is "newly diagnosed" with gestational diabetes. First-line therapy is medical nutrition therapy (diet) with exercise and glucose self-monitoring; most women reach targets this way. Medication is added only if targets are not met within about 1-2 weeks.
wo: B. Metformin: an alternative or add-on when diet fails (or insulin is declined); not first-line at diagnosis. | C. Intravenous insulin: for DKA or intrapartum glucose control on a sliding scale; not for routine GDM. | D. Subcutaneous insulin: the preferred drug if diet and exercise fail to control glucose, but not the first step.

q: postpartum woman had DIC whats the commonest cause
k: Commonest cause of PPH and commonest cause of obstetric DIC are different questions. PPH: tone (atony) > trauma > tissue > thrombin Obstetric DIC: abruption most common Others: amniotic fluid embolism, severe preeclampsi

q: Pregnant came and asked about what vaccine to take in first trimester . Best answer
k: Pregnancy vaccines: inactivated yes, live no. Influenza (inactivated): any trimester Tdap: 27 to 36 weeks of every pregnancy Contraindicated: MMR, varicella, live intranasal influenza Live vaccines: avoid pregnancy for a
r: The decisive phrase is "first trimester" : the inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended for every pregnant woman at any gestational age, including the first trimester. It protects the mother from severe influenza and the newborn through transferred antibodies.
wo: A. MMR: a live attenuated vaccine, contraindicated in pregnancy; given postpartum to rubella non-immune women. | B. Varicella: also live attenuated and contraindicated in pregnancy; give after delivery if non-immune. | C. DTAP: DTaP is the paediatric formulation; pregnant women receive Tdap, and it is timed at 27 to 36 weeks, not the first trimester.

q: Pregnant lady in labor her bishop score is 3 , what would you do?
k: Bishop score decides the induction method. Low score (unfavourable): ripen first with prostaglandin or a balloon catheter High score (≥8, favourable): amniotomy and oxytocin Components: dilation, effacement, station, con
r: A Bishop score of 3 means an unfavourable cervix (score below 6 to 8). Before oxytocin or amniotomy can work, the cervix must be ripened, and prostaglandin (E2 dinoprostone or E1 misoprostol) is the agent used for cervical ripening.
wo: A. Oxytocin: used to induce or augment labour once the cervix is favourable (Bishop ≥8) or after ripening; on a closed cervix it usually fails. | B. Amniotomy: needs a dilated, accessible cervix with an engaged head; not possible or effective with a low Bishop score. | C. Progestrone: used to prevent preterm birth (short cervix, prior preterm birth); it maintains pregnancy rather than ripening the cervix.

q: Pregnant with previous history of hydrocephalus . What is the dose of folic acid you will give her at this time? No GA Mentioned
k: Folic acid dose depends on NTD risk and timing. Low risk: 400 micrograms from before conception to 12 weeks High risk (previous NTD, antiepileptics, sickle cell): 4 to 5 mg Neural tube closes by about 4 weeks after conce
r: A previous history of hydrocephalus (often linked with a neural tube defect) raises NTD risk, and no gestational age is given , so the compiler treats her as being in early pregnancy, when the neural tube is still forming. Following his rule (<12 weeks: 1000 micrograms, >12 weeks: 400 micrograms), t
wo: A. 400 micrograms: the routine low risk dose, and the keyed answer in the lookalike that states 16 weeks, after neural tube closure. | C. 2 mg: not a standard folic acid regimen in any guideline. | D. 5 mg: the high dose for high risk women (previous NTD-affected pregnancy, antiepileptic drugs, sickle cell disease, diabetes, obesity), ideally started before conception.

q: A 39-year-old primigravida a ended her routine prenatal visit at 39 weeks ' gestation. She denied any headache, visual changes, nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain. Urinalysis Was Negative for protein (see lab results). Vital signs at this visit: Blood pressure 160/90 mmHg, Heart rate 84 /min. Vitals signs at all other visits: Blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, Heart rate 68 /min. Labs: HCT 0.34 (0.7t-0.48), Platelets count 165 (150-400 x10^9/L), Alanine aminotransferase 12 (5-40 IU/L), Aspartate aminotransferase 22 (12-40 IU/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Hypertension in pregnancy is defined by timing and end-organ signs. Before 20 weeks or pre-pregnancy: chronic hypertension After 20 weeks, no proteinuria or organ damage: gestational hypertension After 20 weeks + protein
r: Her BP was 120/70 at all previous visits and is now 160/90 at 39 weeks, so the hypertension is new and after 20 weeks. There is no proteinuria , no symptoms, and normal platelets and liver enzymes, so there is no end-organ involvement: this is gestational hypertension.
wo: A. Eclampsia: requires new onset seizures in a woman with hypertensive disease of pregnancy; she has no seizures. | B. Chronic hypertension: BP elevated before pregnancy or before 20 weeks; her earlier readings were normal. | D. Superimposed preeclampsia: needs pre-existing chronic hypertension plus new proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; she has neither.

q: 38 M brought by ambulance following an MVA. He has abdominal distention with signs of hemorrhage (echmosis i think) and a suspected pelvic fracture . He is orientated and appears in distress and pain. Vitals: BP 60/40 , HR 120 , RR 20 with O2 sat 92%, temp a febrile. Whats the nect appropriate step in management
k: Hemorrhagic shock in trauma: stop the bleeding and restore volume. Class III: HR 120-140, low BP, confused or anxious Class IV: HR >140, very low BP, lethargic Two large bore IV lines, warm crystalloid bolus, early blood
r: BP 60/40, HR 120 after an MVA with abdominal distension, ecchymosis and a suspected pelvic fracture is class III to IV hemorrhagic shock. He is oriented and talking, so the airway is protected, and the immediate life threat is circulatory collapse; the next step is IV access with a warmed crystalloi
wo: A. Exploratory laparoscopy: never for an unstable trauma patient; unstable abdominal trauma needs resuscitation and laparotomy (or angioembolization for pelvic bleeding), not laparoscopy. | C. IV morphine: analgesia matters, but opioids worsen hypotension in profound shock and do not treat the life threat; give it in small titrated doses after resuscitation starts. | D. Supplemental O2: is given to every trauma patient in the primary survey and is reasonable with SpO2 92%, but it does not reverse a BP of 60/40; the decisive problem here is hemorrhage.

q: 30 smth male Post MVA in ER with increase WOB and dullness percussion over R lung base . GCS9 . Whats next appropriate management
k: Chest trauma: percussion note chooses the procedure. Dull + reduced breath sounds: hemothorax: chest tube Hyperresonant + hypotension + raised JVP: tension pneumothorax: needle then chest tube Simple pneumothorax: chest
r: After an MVA, dullness on percussion over the right lung base with increased work of breathing indicates a traumatic hemothorax. The treatment is a large bore chest tube, which drains the blood, re expands the lung and lets you measure the output. GCS 9 is above the ≤8 intubation threshold, so the a
kw: dullness percussion over R lung base
wo: B. Intubation: right for GCS ≤8, inability to protect the airway, or refractory hypoxia; at GCS 9 with a cause that a chest tube fixes, it is not the next step. | C. Supplemental O2: given to all trauma patients but does not treat the cause of respiratory compromise; the blood still needs draining. | D. Needle decompression: for tension pneumothorax with hyperresonance, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and hypotension; dullness means fluid, not air.

q: Pretty much the Q stem was asking when should we surgically intervene for chest tube for a hemothorax
k: Hemothorax: thoracotomy when the bleeding is massive or ongoing. Initial chest tube output >1500 ml Ongoing output 200 ml/hr for 2 to 4 hours Persistent hemodynamic instability or ongoing transfusion need Otherwise chest
r: After a chest tube for hemothorax, surgical intervention (thoracotomy) is indicated by an initial drainage of more than 1500 ml or by ongoing bleeding of about 200 ml per hour over 2 to 4 hours, or persistent instability or need for transfusion. Of the listed options, ongoing drainage of 200 ml/hr i
wo: A. Immediate 500 ml output: well below the 1500 ml immediate drainage threshold; most hemothoraces stop with a chest tube alone. | C. Concurrent hemo and pneumothorax: a hemopneumothorax is managed with a chest tube; its presence alone is not an indication for surgery. | D. (forgot): recalled as irrelevant; judge any option against the 1500 ml immediate or 200 ml/hr ongoing rules.

q: 44 YO woman presenting to post op clinic following an appendectomy for appendicitis ( no mention of any surgical complications ) (also don't remember exactly when it was i.e exactly what day post op ) . She complains of fould discharge from the wound . She is febrile 38.8 . inspection of the wound revels erythema with purulent discharge . How to manage
o: wound opening and either exploration or wash out (not sure which one)
k: Postoperative wound problems: Seroma: clear fluid, no inflammation: observe or aspirate Wound abscess or SSI with pus: open the wound, drain, wash out Cellulitis without collection: antibiotics Deep intra abdominal colle
r: After an appendectomy, foul purulent discharge , wound erythema and fever 38.8 indicate a surgical site infection with a wound abscess. The cornerstone of treatment is opening the wound (removing sutures or staples), draining the pus, exploring and washing it out, then leaving it to heal by secondar
wo: A. Conservative: right for a seroma (clear fluid, no inflammation, afebrile); pus and fever need drainage. | B. PO antibiotics: right for mild superficial cellulitis without collection; antibiotics alone cannot clear an abscess. | D. (don't remember): recalled as irrelevant.

q: Middle aged woman had alcoholic pancreatitis 5 weeks ago . Has been reporting 2 week history of nausea , post meal vomiting and upper abdominal fullness . What should be preformed next
k: Post pancreatitis collection: image first, then treat. Pseudocyst: >4 weeks after pancreatitis, early satiety, fullness, vomiting Best imaging: contrast CT Symptomatic or enlarging: endoscopic internal drainage Fever and
