wo: A. Abdominal US: can detect a pseudocyst and is the fallback if CT is absent, but CT defines anatomy and complications better before intervention. | B. ERCP: for biliary obstruction or cholangitis, or a duct leak, not as the first step for a suspected post pancreatitis collection in alcoholic disease. | C. Surgical drainage: treatment comes after imaging confirms a symptomatic mature pseudocyst, and endoscopic internal drainage is now preferred over surgery. | D. (forgot, maybe CT): if this option is CT, it is the answer.

q: present with head trauma . On examination, bilateral periorbital raccoon eye Which type of intubation is most appropriate?
k: Basal skull fracture: nothing through the nose. Signs: raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea, hemotympanum Avoid nasotracheal tube and nasogastric tube (use orogastric) Facial or maxillofacial trauma: oro
r: Bilateral periorbital (raccoon) eyes after head trauma indicate a fracture of the anterior skull base. Nasal routes are contraindicated because a tube can pass through the cribriform plate into the cranium, so the airway is secured by orotracheal intubation (with in-line cervical stabilization).
wo: A. Nasotracheal intubation: contraindicated in suspected basal skull or midface fracture (risk of intracranial tube placement, CSF leak, infection). | C. Cricothyrotomy: the surgical airway when oral intubation fails or is impossible, for example massive maxillofacial injury with the mouth full of blood. | D. Tracheostomy: a planned, slower procedure for prolonged ventilation or laryngeal injury, not the emergency airway in trauma.

q: 52 year old male medically free came to the clinic complaining of red urine for 2 days associated with right flank pain , no dysuria no fever no other symptoms On examination: right flank tenderness and palpable rectal prostate ( written like this) Urine culture : negative Urine analysis: + erythrocyte Nitrate: absent WBC: absent What is the most appropriate next investigation :
k: Hematuria: pain decides the first test. Painful hematuria with flank pain: non-contrast CT-KUB (stone) Painless visible hematuria, older or smoker: CT urography plus cystoscopy With fever, dysuria, pyuria: urine culture
r: Red urine with right flank pain and tenderness , no fever or dysuria, a negative culture and no nitrites or WBC is painful hematuria without infection, most likely a ureteric stone. Non-contrast CT-KUB is the investigation of choice for suspected urolithiasis.
wo: A. Urine cytology: adjunct for suspected urothelial cancer (painless hematuria, smoker); low sensitivity and not first line with flank pain. | C. Retrograde urethrogram: for suspected urethral injury after pelvic trauma (blood at meatus, high-riding prostate); no trauma here. | D. Cystoscopy: evaluates the bladder in painless visible hematuria over 40 to exclude bladder cancer; not the first test for flank pain.

q: A boy presents with periumbilical pain that shifted to the right iliac fossa , accompanied by vomiting. Physical examination reveals tenderness, and labs show leukocytosis . What is the most appropriate step to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Order abdominal US or CT scan
k: Appendicitis: clinical diagnosis, imaging to confirm when needed. Classic: migratory pain, anorexia, vomiting, RIF tenderness, fever, leukocytosis Children and pregnancy: ultrasound first Adults, obese, equivocal ultraso
r: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with vomiting , local tenderness and leukocytosis is suspected acute appendicitis. The lead-in asks how to confirm the diagnosis, which is imaging: ultrasound first in children (no radiation), CT if ultrasound is inconclusive or in adults.
wo: B. Give IV fluids and observe: fluids, analgesia and NPO are supportive and active observation suits an equivocal low-risk picture, but it does not confirm the diagnosis. | C. Discharge and reassess after 48h: unsafe with a high-probability picture; risk of perforation. | D. High fiber diet and laxative: management of constipation; laxatives are contraindicated in suspected appendicitis.

q: An old patient came with subdural hematoma with signs of lateralization imaging revealed 13 mm shifting . His GCS 7/15 then was intubated and resuscitated, what to do next?
k: Acute SDH: evacuate if mass effect is significant. Surgery: thickness over 10 mm or midline shift over 5 mm regardless of GCS Also: GCS drop of 2 or more, asymmetric or fixed pupils, ICP over 20 ICP bridges: head up 30 d
r: An acute subdural hematoma with lateralizing signs , a 13 mm midline shift and GCS 7 meets criteria for surgical evacuation (shift over 5 mm or thickness over 10 mm, or GCS ≤8 with deterioration). The airway is secured and he is resuscitated, so the next step is urgent craniotomy to relieve the mass
wo: A. IV mannitol: a temporizing measure for raised ICP or impending herniation while arranging surgery; it does not remove the clot. | B. Elevate head of bed: a simple supportive ICP measure, not definitive for a large hematoma with shift. | C. Hyperventilate: brief rescue for signs of herniation only; prolonged use causes cerebral ischemia.

q: Patient prepared for left adrenal adenoctomy what should be given postoperative
o: High dose glucocorticoid and gradual tapering
k: Steroid cover depends on what the tumour secreted. Cortisol-secreting (Cushing): stress dose hydrocortisone, then slow taper Bilateral adrenalectomy: lifelong glucocorticoid plus fludrocortisone Aldosteronoma: no steroid
r: The keyed scenario is a cortisol-secreting adenoma : its autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH and atrophies the contralateral adrenal, so after unilateral adrenalectomy the patient is cortisol deficient. Give a stress (high) dose of glucocorticoid perioperatively, then taper gradually over months as
wo: A. Lifelong glucocorticoid: needed after bilateral adrenalectomy; after unilateral surgery the other gland recovers, so steroids are tapered off. | B. Initiate fludrocortisone: the contralateral gland's zona glomerulosa is controlled by renin-angiotensin, not ACTH, so mineralocorticoid replacement is not routinely needed after unilateral surgery. | D. Nothing: right for a non-functioning adenoma or an aldosteronoma, where the axis is not suppressed; risky after removing a cortisol-secreting tumour.

q: A 25-year-old male with bilateral breast enlargement since the age of 18 , he's uncomfortable and reluctant to swim or exercise at the gym PE revealed grade 4 gynecomastia ,. Most appropriate management?
k: Gynecomastia management ladder. Pubertal: reassure and observe, most regress Find causes: drugs (spironolactone, anabolic steroids), liver disease, hypogonadism, testicular tumour, hyperthyroidism Recent and tender: medi
r: Gynecomastia that has persisted for about 7 years (since 18) is unlikely to regress, because long-standing glandular tissue becomes fibrotic. It is high grade (4) and is causing distress and avoiding activities ( reluctant to swim or exercise ). Surgical excision with bilateral subcutaneous mastecto
wo: A. Reassurance: right for pubertal gynecomastia in adolescents, which usually regresses within 1 to 2 years; not for persistent, symptomatic, high-grade disease. | B. Bilateral core needle biopsy: for a unilateral, hard, eccentric or fixed mass, skin or nipple changes suspicious for male breast cancer; bilateral symmetric enlargement does not need biopsy. | D. Endocrine and liver work up: the right step for new-onset adult gynecomastia, rapid growth or features of an underlying cause (testicular tumour, liver disease, drugs, hyperthyroidism).

q: During excision of a back lipoma under local lidocaine , the surgeon suspects an excessive dose . Earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity ? (p. 37)
k: Lidocaine toxicity runs from CNS warning signs to seizures to cardiac collapse. Early: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness Then: muscle twitching, confusion, seizures, coma Late: bradycardia, hypotensi

q: Male patient came with epigastric pain, came with history of using NSAIDs , now he is vitally stable , with erect chest x-ray showing AIR UNDER DIAPHRGM . What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Free air under the diaphragm = perforated viscus = surgery. Commonest cause: perforated peptic ulcer (NSAIDs, H. pylori) Steps: NPO, IV fluids, NG tube, PPI, antibiotics, then repair Repair: omental (Graham) patch, test
r: Epigastric pain in an NSAID user with air under the diaphragm on erect chest x-ray is a perforated peptic ulcer. Free intraperitoneal air means perforation and peritoneal contamination, so after resuscitation and IV antibiotics the definitive step is surgical exploration and repair (omental patch);
wo: A. Gastroduodenoscopy: for upper GI bleeding or ulcer diagnosis; insufflating air into a perforated viscus worsens the leak and it does not close the hole. | C. Laparoscopy: laparoscopic patch repair is an accepted option in stable patients where expertise exists, but the classic exam answer for free air is laparotomy. | D. Observation: non-operative management is only for highly selected sealed perforations; being vitally stable does not remove the need for repair.

q: A patient with comorbidity , with nothing in the question indicating it is uncontrolled , and the question stated that he walks to the mosque 3-4 times daily. What is the ASA classification?
k: ASA physical status: judge control and functional impact, not just the number of diseases. I: healthy II: mild, controlled systemic disease, no limitation III: severe disease with functional limitation IV: constant threa
r: He has a comorbidity but nothing suggests it is uncontrolled, and he walks to the mosque 3 to 4 times daily , showing no functional limitation. Mild, well controlled systemic disease without limitation of activity is ASA II .
kw: nothing in the question indicating it is uncontrolled
wo: A. 1: a normal healthy patient with no systemic disease; any comorbidity excludes ASA I. | C. 3: severe systemic disease with functional limitation (poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, COPD, morbid obesity, MI or stroke more than 3 months ago). | D. 4: severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (recent MI, ongoing ischaemia, severe valve dysfunction, sepsis).

q: An 8 year old boy presented with a history of being easily distracted , not listening when spoken to directly, avoiding his schoolwork, being restless, and talking excessively. Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive method ?
o: Avoiding prenatal exposure to addictive substances
Limit watching TV and playing rapid response video games
k: ADHD: diagnosis and risk factors. Symptoms before age 12, in 2 or more settings, at least 6 months Strongly heritable Modifiable risk factors: prenatal smoking, alcohol, drug exposure, prematurity, low birth weight, lead
r: Inattention (distracted, not listening, avoiding schoolwork) plus hyperactivity (restless, talking excessively) in an 8-year-old is ADHD. The question asks for a preventive method: ADHD is largely genetic, but the best-established modifiable risk factors are prenatal exposure to tobacco, alcohol and
wo: A. Early school screen programs: detect ADHD earlier (secondary prevention) but do not prevent it occurring. | B. Referral to specialized daycare centers: not a recognized prevention or treatment of ADHD. | D. Limit TV and rapid response video games: screen time may worsen attention but has no proven causal role; not an established preventive measure.

q: A 55-year-old man known to have psychiatric disease and hypertension was admitted to the hospital due to poor nutrition at home, as he was refusing food. During hospitalization, he became agitated, so they increased the dose of Haloperidol . Suddenly, he became confused and began sweating . He was shifted to the ICU, started on IV fluids, and intubated (see lab result). Which of the following should be added to the management plan?
k: NMS = dopamine blockade, so treatment = stop the drug and restore dopamine. Features: hyperthermia, lead pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, confusion Labs: high CK, leukocytosis, myoglobinuria Treatment: stop antipsyc
r: Symptoms started right after the haloperidol dose was increased : sudden confusion, sweating and a need for ICU and intubation is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, high CK). NMS is caused by dopamine blockade, so beside stopping the antips
wo: A. Naloxone: reverses opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression); haloperidol is not an opioid. | B. Glucagon: antidote for beta blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity with bradycardia and hypotension, not dopamine antagonist toxicity. | C. Meropenem: for severe or resistant sepsis; fever with rigidity after a neuroleptic dose increase is drug toxicity, not infection.

q: First time pregnant mom came for her first antenatal visit . Which vaccine should she be given?
k: Antenatal vaccines: inactivated influenza any trimester, Tdap at 27 to 36 weeks. Influenza: any gestational age, every pregnancy Tdap: 27 to 36 weeks, every pregnancy Live vaccines (MMR, varicella): avoid in pregnancy, g
r: At the first antenatal visit (no gestational age given, so early pregnancy) the vaccine that can be given now is inactivated influenza , which is recommended for every pregnant woman at any gestational age. It protects the mother, who is at higher risk of severe influenza, and gives the newborn pass
wo: A. Tdap is given in every pregnancy but timed for 27 to 36 weeks to maximise antibody transfer to the baby; it would be the answer if the stem said she is at about 28 weeks. | C. Pneumococcal vaccine is not routine in pregnancy; it is given only for specific indications such as asplenia or chronic disease. | D. Meningococcal vaccine is reserved for specific risks (asplenia, complement deficiency, outbreaks, travel such as Hajj); it is not a routine antenatal vaccine.

q: A 25-year-old woman presents at 10 weeks of gestation for booking in the antenatal clinic. She gave a history of previous intrauterine death with multiple congenital anomalies . Which of the following is the most appropriate time for a detailed anomaly scan ?
k: Antenatal ultrasound timing. Dating scan: about 10 to 13 weeks Nuchal translucency: 11 to 13+6 weeks Detailed anomaly scan: 18 to 22 weeks Growth scans: third trimester if indicated
r: The detailed anomaly (morphology) scan is done at 18 to 22 weeks , when fetal organs are large enough to be assessed in detail and there is still time for counselling and decisions. A previous IUFD with multiple anomalies raises concern but does not change the timing of the detailed scan; she is boo
kw: previous intrauterine death with multiple congenital anomalies
wo: A. 10 to 12 weeks is the dating scan window (and nuchal translucency at 11 to 13+6 weeks); organs are too small for a detailed anatomy survey. | B. 14 to 16 weeks is too early for a full anatomy survey; this window is used for second trimester serum screening or amniocentesis, not the detailed scan. | D. 24 to 28 weeks is too late: anomalies found then leave little time for counselling and options; this window is for the glucose challenge test.

q: Which of the following is the recommended folic acid daily dose for a HEALTHY (low-risk) woman who wants to conceive and has no prior diseases or risk factors?
k: Folic acid dose depends on NTD risk. Low risk: 0.4 mg (400 micrograms) daily, from at least 1 month before conception to 12 weeks High risk: 4 to 5 mg daily High risk = prior NTD, antiepileptics, diabetes, obesity, hemol
r: For a healthy, low risk woman the preconception folic acid dose is low dose, 400 micrograms (0.4 mg) daily, started at least one month before conception. Among the options, 1000 micrograms (1 mg) is the only low dose choice and the closest to the standard low risk dose; only 4000 micrograms correspo
wo: B. 2000 micrograms is not a standard regimen for either risk group. | C. 3000 micrograms is not a standard regimen for either risk group. | D. 4000 micrograms (4 mg, or 5 mg in some guidelines) is the high dose for high NTD risk: previous NTD baby, antiepileptic drugs, pregestational diabetes, obesity, sickle cell disease; she has none of these.

q: A 14-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea and recurrent cyclic lower abdominal pain . On examination, a bluish/purplish bulging membrane is seen at the vaginal opening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Outflow tract obstruction with normal secondary sexual characteristics. Imperforate hymen: bluish bulging membrane at introitus Transverse vaginal septum: short blind vagina, no bulge at introitus Vaginal (Mullerian) age
r: A 14 year old with primary amenorrhea , cyclic lower abdominal pain (menstruating behind an obstruction, hematocolpos) and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus is classic imperforate hymen. Treatment is hymenotomy (cruciate incision) to drain the retained blood.
wo: B. Primary amenorrhea is the presenting complaint, not a diagnosis; the question asks for its cause. | C. Endometriosis causes cyclic pain in women who already menstruate and has no bulging membrane at the vaginal opening. | D. Transverse vaginal septum also causes cryptomenorrhea with cyclic pain, but the obstruction is higher in the vagina, so no bulging bluish membrane is seen at the introitus; it does not bulge with Valsalva.

q: Pregnant women at 31 weeks of gestation diagnosed with pretrm premature rupture of membrane CTG shows late deceleration , on examination baby found in the vaginal cavity , what is the best next step?
k: Fetal distress: choose the fastest safe route. Not fully dilated or head high: emergency cesarean Fully dilated, head low (station +2 or below): instrumental delivery Preterm below 34 weeks: forceps, not vacuum Face pres
r: There is fetal compromise (late decelerations) and the head is already low in the vaginal cavity , so the fastest safe delivery is an operative vaginal delivery. At 31 weeks the vacuum is avoided (risk of scalp and intracranial bleeding in the preterm fetus, generally not used below about 34 weeks),
kw: baby found in the vaginal cavity
wo: A. Ventouse is contraindicated in a preterm fetus below about 34 weeks; it would be a choice at term with a low head and full dilatation. | C. Cesarean section is right for fetal distress when the cervix is not fully dilated or the head is high; with the baby in the vaginal cavity, an instrumental delivery is quicker and safer.

q: 33 y.o Female known case of asthma, Smoker , hypertension, epilepsy . Want to get pregnant . Which one oppose the greatest risk on pregnancy ?
k: Preconception risk: match the factor to the outcome asked. Malformation: antiepileptics (valproate), pregestational diabetes Growth restriction, abruption: smoking, hypertension Aneuploidy, miscarriage: age 35 or more As

q: A 44-year-old woman presented with heavy vaginal bleeding and a blood pressure of 93/73 mmHg . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Acute AUB management. Resuscitate (ABC, IV access, blood if needed) Medical: IV estrogen, high dose COCP or progestin, tranexamic acid Severe, unstable or failed medical: D&C Then long term: LNG IUD, ablation, hysterecto
r: This is acute, heavy abnormal uterine bleeding with borderline low blood pressure (93/73) , so the priority is to stop the bleeding quickly. Dilatation and curettage stops severe or refractory bleeding rapidly, and at 44 it also provides endometrial tissue to exclude hyperplasia or cancer.
wo: A. Hysterectomy is the definitive treatment for refractory bleeding, completed family, or structural disease such as adenomyosis or fibroids, but it is not the first step in an acute bleed. | B. Mefenamic acid (NSAID) modestly reduces chronic heavy menstrual bleeding; it is too weak for acute heavy bleeding with low blood pressure. | C. Hormonal IUD (levonorgestrel) is first line for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding, not for acute heavy bleeding with hemodynamic compromise.

q: Women with brief jerky movements involving only upper limb
k: Seizure type by movement. Myoclonic: brief shock like jerks, seconds Clonic: rhythmic repeated jerking Tonic: sustained stiffening Atonic: sudden loss of tone, drop attack Absence: staring spells, few seconds
r: Brief, jerky, shock like movements lasting about a second, here limited to the upper limbs, are myoclonic seizures. Consciousness is usually preserved; they typically occur in the morning (juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, often with dropping things in the morning).
wo: A. Atonic seizures are a sudden loss of muscle tone causing drop attacks or head drops, not jerks. | B. Clonic seizures are sustained, rhythmic, repetitive jerking that lasts longer, usually with impaired awareness, not single brief jerks. | C. Tonic seizures are sustained stiffening (increased tone) of the limbs and trunk, not jerky movements.

q: 46 years old female right handed, complaining of Sausage digits in the left hand and nail pitting , She Also Had morning stiffness and joint swelling in both PIPs and DIPs . what else you can find in the history?
k: Psoriatic arthritis clues. Dactylitis (sausage digits) Nail pitting, onycholysis DIP involvement, asymmetric oligoarthritis Skin psoriasis (may follow the arthritis) Pencil in cup deformity on X ray
r: Sausage digits (dactylitis), nail pitting and DIP joint involvement point to psoriatic arthritis. The history question that completes the picture is skin disease: a history of psoriatic plaques (scalp, extensor surfaces, natal cleft) or a family history of psoriasis.
wo: B. Heat intolerance points to hyperthyroidism (thyroid acropachy can cause finger clubbing and swelling) but does not explain nail pitting, dactylitis and DIP arthritis. | C. Dyspnea from lung disease fits rheumatoid arthritis (interstitial lung disease) or scleroderma, not the dactylitis and nail pitting pattern of psoriatic arthritis.

q: A 62-year-old woman known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and ischemic stroke 1 month ago , presented to the Emergency Room complaining of central stabbing continuous chest pain for 3 hours . She denied any dyspnea, palpitation, or change in consciousness. The patient is taking insulin, lisinopril, metoprolol, lipitor, and aspirin. Examination revealed she is in pain. She was started on oxygen, morphine, and sublingual nitroglycerin (see image). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: ACS reperfusion choice. STEMI: primary PCI preferred Fibrinolysis only if PCI cannot be done in time and no contraindication Absolute contraindications include ischemic stroke within 3 months, any prior intracranial hemo
r: Multiple risk factors with 3 hours of continuous central chest pain treated with oxygen, morphine and nitrate is acute coronary syndrome. The definitive next step is urgent coronary angiography with PCI where indicated. Thrombolysis is not an option because of her ischemic stroke 1 month ago .
kw: central stabbing continuous chest pain for 3 hours
wo: A. IV magnesium is for torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemia related arrhythmias; it has no role in ACS here. | B. CT angiography is used when aortic dissection is suspected (tearing pain to the back, pulse or BP differential) or for stable low risk chest pain; it cannot treat and only delays reperfusion in an active ACS. | D. Fibrinolysis is contraindicated: ischemic stroke within the last 3 months is an absolute contraindication; it would be used for STEMI only when PCI is not available in time and there is no contraindication.

q: A 35-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis maintained on methotrexate 15 weekly . She is currently in remission. 4 months ago, her LFTs were normal but the most recent LFTs show: AST 300 (10x normal), ALT 280 (10x normal), Albumin 30 (low). What is the most appropriate action for her abnormal liver function tests?
k: Methotrexate and LFTs. Monitor LFTs regularly ALT/AST 1 to 3 times normal: reduce dose and recheck Above 3 times normal: stop methotrexate Give folic acid weekly to reduce toxicity
r: Her transaminases are about 10 times normal on methotrexate, with a falling albumin, after normal LFTs 4 months ago. Methotrexate is hepatotoxic, and a rise above 3 times the upper limit of normal requires stopping methotrexate to prevent further liver injury; she is in remission, so the drug can be
wo: A. Liver ultrasound may be part of later workup, but the priority action is removing the offending drug. | B. Glucocorticoids treat autoimmune hepatitis or RA flares; they do not reverse drug induced liver injury and she is in remission. | D. Liver biopsy is invasive and considered only for persistent abnormalities after the drug is stopped, not as the first action.

q: lady in her fourties recurrent uti what is the best for prevention
k: Recurrent UTI prevention ladder. Behavioural: fluids, postcoital voiding, avoid spermicides Postmenopausal: vaginal estrogen Most effective: continuous or postcoital antibiotic prophylaxis
r: For a woman with recurrent UTI (2 or more in 6 months or 3 or more in a year), the most effective prevention is antibiotic prophylaxis , either continuous low dose or postcoital (for example nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole). It has the strongest evidence for reducing recurrences.
wo: A. Cranberry products have weak and inconsistent evidence; they may be an option for women who wish to avoid antibiotics, but they are not the best. | B. Increased fluid intake is a reasonable first behavioural measure, but it is less effective than prophylactic antibiotics.

q: A patient presented with severe diarrhea . Which of the following is the most expected abnormalities ?
k: GI losses and acid base. Vomiting / NG suction: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis Diarrhea / fistula: normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia
r: Stool below the stomach is rich in bicarbonate and potassium . Severe diarrhea loses both, giving a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia ; volume depletion and secondary hyperaldosteronism worsen the potassium loss.
wo: B. Metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia fits renal failure, type 4 RTA (hypoaldosteronism) or adrenal insufficiency, not GI loss of potassium. | C. Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia is the pattern of vomiting or gastric outlet obstruction (loss of HCl), or diuretics; diarrhea loses bicarbonate, not acid. | D. Metabolic alkalosis with hyperkalemia is an unusual combination and does not fit any GI loss.

q: Patient with diabetes, hypertension and renal failure . Blood pressure is around 159/105-110 and glucose around 7-8 . What is the cause of the renal failure?
k: Diabetic vs hypertensive kidney disease. Diabetic: long DM duration, albuminuria/nephrotic range proteinuria, retinopathy, normal or large kidneys Hypertensive: long HTN, mild proteinuria, small kidneys, other end organ
r: This recall is built on which disease drove the kidney damage. Blood pressure is markedly high and poorly controlled ( 159/105 to 110 ) while glucose is near target ( 7 to 8 ); in the earlier version, hypertension had been present for about 20 years versus only 2 to 3 years of diabetes. Diabetic nep
wo: A. Diabetic nephropathy is the commonest cause of CKD overall, but it needs long standing (usually over 10 years), poorly controlled diabetes, with proteinuria and often retinopathy; here diabetes is short and controlled.

q: Patient who's a known case of alcoholic liver cirrhosis , presents with hematemesis , he is drowsy but arousable . Vitals: Hypotensive (80/40?). PLT: 40000 . INR was elevated but not sure. What's the initial next step ?
o: IV pantoprazole and prepare for endoscopy
k: Variceal bleed order. Airway (intubate if drowsy or massive bleed), IV access Restrictive transfusion, avoid overfilling Octreotide (vasoactive) + IV ceftriaxone Endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours No routine FFP or
r: A cirrhotic with hematemesis is a variceal bleed until proven otherwise. He is drowsy (cannot protect his airway, high aspiration risk) and hypotensive , so ABC comes first: airway protection with intubation and restoring volume with blood (restrictive target, about Hb 7 to 8). Octreotide, IV ceftri
wo: A. PPI and endoscopy are part of management (endoscopy within 12 hours), but not before securing the airway and circulation in a drowsy, hypotensive patient. | B. Octreotide is correct early variceal therapy and lactulose treats encephalopathy, but neither addresses the immediate airway and shock. | C. IV antibiotics reduce mortality in variceal bleeding, but platelet (and FFP) transfusion should not be given to reach a platelet or INR target; and ABC still comes first.

q: An Elderly Patient On Day 2 Post Hip Surgery Developed Confusion And Drowsiness . During Surgery, He Was Given Hypotonic Fluids D5W . Serum Na: 121 , Serum Osm: ~260, Urine Osm: 600, Urine Sodium 46. What is the most appropriate step in management ?
o: D50 with saline something like that
k: Hyponatremia: symptoms and timing decide the speed. Severe or moderate symptoms (confusion, drowsiness, seizures): 3% saline bolus Acute (under 48 hours): faster correction is safer Chronic: limit rise (about 8 to 10 mmo
r: Na 121 with low serum osmolality (about 260), inappropriately concentrated urine ( urine osm 600 ) and urine Na 46 is post operative SIADH made worse by hypotonic D5W. The key clues are new confusion and drowsiness (symptomatic) arising within 2 days ( acute , under 48 hours). Symptomatic acute hypo
wo: A. Fluid restriction is right for chronic or asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic SIADH; it is too slow for a confused, drowsy patient. It was the alternative answer favoured in an earlier version. | B. Normal saline is for hypovolemic hyponatremia; in SIADH, the salt is excreted and water retained, which can drop sodium further. Adding furosemide is used for hypervolemic states or with hypertonic saline in SIADH, not as the first step here. | D. Dextrose gives more free water and would worsen the hyponatremia that hypotonic D5W helped cause.

q: An (forget age) female patient with (memory impairment not sure about it )was admitted to the hospital and found elevated blood pressure ( 167/98 mmHg ). She was prescribed antihypertensive medication but refused to take it because she was concerned about its potential side effects. What complication could develop if she does not take her antihypertensive medication ?
k: Complications of uncontrolled hypertension. Heart: LVH, heart failure, coronary disease, atrial fibrillation Brain: stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic), vascular dementia Kidney: nephrosclerosis, CKD Eye: hypertensive reti
r: Untreated high blood pressure ( 167/98 ) increases afterload chronically, causing left ventricular hypertrophy , diastolic dysfunction and eventually heart failure . Hypertension is one of the commonest causes of heart failure, alongside stroke, coronary disease and CKD as the main complications of
kw: does not take her antihypertensive medication
wo: A. Pericarditis is caused by viral infection, uremia, post MI or autoimmune disease, not by hypertension. | B. Amyloidosis can cause a restrictive cardiomyopathy, but it is a deposition disease, not a complication of high blood pressure. | D. Infective endocarditis is caused by bacteremia on damaged or prosthetic valves, IV drug use, or dental procedures; hypertension does not cause it.

q: An elderly patient presents with acute heart failure and has atrial fibrillation on ECG. What is the best next step?
k: AF rate control choice. Unstable: synchronized DC cardioversion Stable, normal LV: beta blocker or diltiazem/verapamil Acute heart failure or hypotension: digoxin or amiodarone WPW with AF: procainamide (avoid AV nodal b
r: AF in a patient with acute heart failure needs rate control without depressing contractility. Beta blockers (and non dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) are negatively inotropic and are avoided in acute decompensated heart failure, so digoxin (positively inotropic, slows AV conduction) is the
wo: B. Adenosine is used to terminate or unmask regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT); it does not control AF. | C. Beta blockers are first line rate control in stable AF and in chronic stable heart failure, but they can worsen acute decompensated failure. | D. Procainamide is used for AF with pre-excitation (WPW, irregular wide complex tachycardia) or stable VT, not rate control in heart failure.

q: A 49-years-old male smoker for many years came to clinic for lung cancer screening . What is the most appropriate screening tools ?
k: Lung cancer screening (USPSTF 2021). Age 50 to 80 At least 20 pack years Current smoker or quit within 15 years Test: annual low dose CT Stop when quit over 15 years or not fit for surgery
r: Lung cancer screening with annual low dose CT is offered to adults aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack years who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years (USPSTF). This smoker is 49 , below the starting age, so screening is not indicated yet; the priority is smoking cessation.
wo: A. Low dose CT is the screening test, and becomes the answer at 50 or above with 20 or more pack years, or when 'no need' is not among the options. | B. Chest X ray is not used for screening; it has not been shown to reduce lung cancer mortality. | C. Bronchoscopy is a diagnostic test for a suspected lesion or symptoms such as hemoptysis, never a screening tool.

q: Patient, vitally stable, only has fatigue. He has CKD . Labs are all normal EXCEPT for K (6.6 exactly) , no ECG changes ! What is the INITIAL step ? (INITIAL!!!)
k: Hyperkalemia ladder. Stabilise: IV calcium gluconate (K 6.5 or more, or ECG changes) Shift: insulin + dextrose, nebulised salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic Remove: potassium binders, loop diuretics, dialysis
wo: A. Hemodialysis is the definitive removal of potassium but comes after medical stabilisation, or when hyperkalemia is refractory or there is severe renal failure; it is not the initial step. | C. Normal saline does not lower potassium and adds volume in CKD; it would be for hypovolemia or prerenal AKI.

q: 14 year old child has h-pylori positive doudnal ulcer , started on triple therapy what is the duration of tx ?
k: H. pylori eradication. Triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin, 7 to 14 days (14 preferred) Failure: bismuth quadruple therapy Test of cure: urea breath test or stool antigen at least 4 weeks after therapy
r: Triple therapy for H. pylori (PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin or metronidazole) is given for 7 to 14 days , with 14 days preferred in current guidelines because of better eradication. Eradication is then confirmed with a urea breath test or stool antigen at least 4 weeks after therapy, off
wo: B. 3 days is far too short and leads to treatment failure and resistance. | C. 3 months is not an eradication regimen; prolonged courses add side effects without benefit. | D. 4 weeks is the length of PPI continuation for ulcer healing, or the interval before testing for eradication, not the antibiotic course.

q: A child presents with shortness of breath and exercise intolerance . Chest X-ray demonstrates a characteristic boot-shaped (coeurensabot) heart. The child has an underlying cardiac disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate management? X-ray was clear no pulmonary edema ONLY boot shaped heart
o: Reassurance because the symptoms/findings are expected as part of the underlying disease
k: Tetralogy of Fallot. CXR: boot shaped heart, decreased pulmonary markings ECG: right axis deviation, RVH Diagnosis: echocardiography Tet spell: knee to chest, oxygen, morphine, IV fluids, beta blocker Definitive: surgica

q: A mother is worried about her son who has asthma . What is the most appropriate counseling ?
o: He will develop chronic lung disorder
Childhood asthma will disappear by adolescence
He will have asthma for the rest of his life
No correlation between childhood and adulthood asthma
k: Childhood asthma prognosis. Many children outgrow it by adolescence Persistence more likely with atopy, severe disease, parental asthma, female sex in adolescence Remission may relapse in adulthood
r: The reassuring, evidence based counselling is that many children with asthma improve or go into remission by adolescence , especially those with mild disease and episodic viral triggered wheeze. Atopy, severe disease, and parental asthma make persistence more likely.
kw: worried about her son who has asthma
wo: A. Most children with well controlled asthma do not develop chronic lung disease; that is more a concern with severe, poorly controlled disease or other conditions like bronchopulmonary dysplasia. | C. Lifelong asthma is not the usual course; many children outgrow it, although some relapse later in adult life. | D. There is a correlation: childhood asthma, especially severe or atopic, increases the risk of adult asthma, and remission can relapse later.

q: 65 years man brought to the clinic due to the finding of reducible inguinal hernia , he said it bulge when he coughs and when he stands but it return back when lying back, mild discomfort without significant pain . What is The Most Appropriate Management
k: Hernia management. Inguinal, symptomatic and fit: elective mesh repair Femoral: always repair (high strangulation risk) Irreducible or strangulated: emergency surgery Recurrent or bilateral: laparoscopic repair Infant um
r: A reducible inguinal hernia with a cough impulse that causes mild discomfort is symptomatic. In a fit patient the standard treatment is elective surgical repair (open mesh repair for a primary unilateral hernia), to relieve symptoms and remove the risk of incarceration and strangulation, which rises
wo: B. Lifestyle measures (weight loss, stopping smoking, treating cough or constipation) improve surgical outcomes but do not treat the hernia. | C. Avoiding heavy lifting may reduce discomfort but does not cure the hernia or remove the strangulation risk. | D. Watchful waiting is acceptable for men with asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic hernias, especially if unfit for surgery, but most cross over to surgery over time; in a fit patient with a symptomatic reducible hernia the standard exam answer is repair.

q: women presented with lower GI bleeding . On examination, diffusely tender abdomen and perianal exam showing fresh Blood . The patient is stable . What is the most appropriate management?
k: Acute lower GI bleed. Unstable: resuscitate, then CT angiography, embolisation Stable, bleed settled: colonoscopy after bowel prep Colonoscopy negative: CT angiography, then tagged RBC scan or small bowel evaluation Alwa
r: The decisive clue is that the patient is stable . In stable lower GI bleeding the main investigation is colonoscopy after bowel preparation: it locates the source (diverticula, angiodysplasia, colitis, tumour) and can treat it. CT angiography and angiographic embolisation are reserved for unstable p
wo: A. Laparotomy is the last resort for persistent, life threatening bleeding when endoscopic and angiographic methods fail, or for peritonitis or perforation. | B. Angiography (CT angiography then catheter embolisation) is right if the patient is unstable or still actively bleeding; it is not first in a stable patient. | D. Transfusion is part of resuscitation when hemoglobin is low or the patient is unstable; it does not find or treat the source in a stable patient.

q: 9~11 yo boy got into a fight in school, the teacher bring him after assessment the doctor decided that he needs suturing in the head , asks about consent
o: the patient can give consent himself
k: Consent in minors. Legal consent: parent or legal guardian Child: give explanation and seek assent Life threatening emergency, guardian unreachable: treat without consent Teachers, neighbours, other relatives without gua
r: A 9 to 11 year old is a minor and cannot give legal consent for a procedure. A scalp laceration needing sutures is not life threatening, so there is time to contact the parents (legal guardian) for consent before suturing.
wo: A. A teacher is not a legal guardian and cannot consent for medical treatment, even when responsible for the child at school. | B. A child of this age cannot give valid legal consent; his assent should be sought, but consent comes from the guardian. | C. Consent can be waived only in a life or limb threatening emergency when the guardian cannot be reached; a simple scalp laceration can wait.
